cadmus: In the usual telling Cadmus was the son of Agenor, ruler of a Phoenician kingdom, and his wife Telephassa, although some sources give other parents. When Zeus carried off his sister Europa, Cadmus was sent by his father to find her and told not to return without her. Unsuccessful, or unwilling to go against Zeus, he came to Samothrace, the island sacred to the Great Gods, where he took Harmonia as his bride; according to Diodorus Siculus the wedding was the first on earth to which the gods brought gifts.

Cadmus went to Delphi, where the oracle told him to follow a cow marked with a half moon and to build a town where she lay down exhausted. The cow led him to Boeotia, where he founded Thebes. He killed the dragon that guarded the Ismenian spring and, on Athena's instruction, sowed its teeth. Armed men called the Spartoi sprang up and fought one another until five survived, who helped him build the Cadmeia, the citadel of Thebes, and became the ancestors of its noblest families.

The dragon had been sacred to Ares, and the family met with misfortunes. Cadmus abdicated in favour of his grandson Pentheus and went with Harmonia to Illyria to fight beside the Enchelii, and he founded the cities of Lychnidos and Bouthoe. Troubled by his ill fortune, he said that if the gods so loved the life of a serpent he might wish it for himself, and he began to change; Harmonia asked to share his fate.

Herodotus credited Cadmus with bringing the Phoenician alphabet to the Greeks. Modern scholarship almost unanimously agrees that the Greek alphabet came from the Phoenician, but the earliest Greek inscriptions match Phoenician letter forms of the late 9th or 8th centuries BCE, far later than Herodotus supposed. Frederick Ahl suggested that the legend might preserve memories of Linear B, which has been found in abundance at Thebes.

Albert Schachter suggested that Cadmus was an invented hero named after the Theban acropolis and made Phoenician through the influence of eastern immigrants. Others have proposed that he was a Mycenaean, a Cretan or an Argive.
caernarfon: Caernarfon lies on the eastern shore of the Menai Strait in Gwynedd, opposite the island of Anglesey, with Snowdonia to the east and south-east. The mouth of the River Seiont forms a natural harbour. The name combines caer, meaning fortress, either the Roman fort of Segontium or the Norman castle near the mouth of the Seiont, with Arfon, meaning opposite Môn, Anglesey, and so means the fortress in the land opposite Anglesey. The town is the historic county town of Caernarfonshire.

The resources of the Menai Strait supported prehistoric habitation. During the Roman conquest the fort of Segontium was established around 80 CE to subjugate the Ordovices, a Celtic tribe. Roman rule ended in 382, after which Caernarfon became part of the Kingdom of Gwynedd. In the late 11th century William the Conqueror ordered a motte-and-bailey castle to be built there as part of the Norman invasion of Wales, but the invasion failed and Wales remained independent until about 1283.

Llywelyn ap Gruffudd, ruler of Gwynedd, refused to pay homage to Edward I of England, and the English conquest of Gwynedd followed. The present castle was built between 1283 and 1330 on Edward's order, and its banded stonework and polygonal towers are thought to imitate the Walls of Constantinople. The town walls, with eight towers and two gateways, were built between 1283 and 1285. In 1284 the Statute of Rhuddlan created the county of Caernarfonshire, and Edward granted the town a charter making it a borough and the seat of English government in north Wales. St Mary's Church was begun in 1307 as a chapel for the castle and garrison.

When the Welsh House of Tudor came to the English throne hostilities eased and the castle fell into disrepair. In the 19th century Caernarfon was an important port, exporting slate from the Dyffryn Nantlle quarries, helped from 1828 by the Nantlle Railway.

Caernarfon is a royal town, a status granted by Queen Elizabeth II as a royal borough in 1963 and amended in 1974. The castle and town walls form part of the World Heritage Site of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd, which UNESCO listed in 1986. Gwynedd Council has its headquarters there. The town has the highest percentage of Welsh speakers of any community in Wales, and its residents are known colloquially as Cofis. It has hosted the National Eisteddfod several times, from 1862 to 1979. Tourism, the harbour and the marina are central to its economy.
caesarion: Caesarion, whose name means Little Caesar, was born in Egypt in 47 BCE; an Egyptian demotic stele from the Serapeum at Memphis records his birth on 23 June 47 BCE. He was conceived during Julius Caesar's stay in Egypt, when Caesar supported Cleopatra's claim to the throne against her brother Ptolemy XIII. Mark Antony later testified before the Roman Senate that Caesar had privately acknowledged the boy as his son, but Caesar never recognised him legally as his heir, and when his will was read after his assassination on 15 March 44 BCE, Caesarion was omitted and Octavian was named as heir.

Cleopatra returned to Alexandria with her two-year-old son in mid-April 44 BCE, and on 2 September 44 BCE Caesarion was proclaimed King of Egypt at the age of three, although Cleopatra kept absolute authority. She presented herself as the goddess Isis and him as Horus. In 34 BCE, in the Donations of Alexandria, Antony granted lands and titles to Caesarion, proclaimed him a god and King of Kings, and declared him Caesar's true son and heir. That threatened Octavian, whose position rested on his adoption by Caesar, and he used Roman resentment of the Donations to win support for war against Antony and Cleopatra.

When Octavian invaded Egypt in 30 BCE, Caesarion was seventeen. Plutarch says he was sent with much treasure towards India, and that his tutor Rhodon persuaded him to return by saying that Octavian invited him to take the kingdom. Octavian took Alexandria on 1 August 30 BCE.

Octavian is supposed to have had Caesarion killed in Alexandria in late August 30 BCE. According to Plutarch he followed the advice of Arius Didymus, who said that too many Caesars was not good. Little is recorded of the death. Caesarion was the last of the Ptolemaic line and the last pharaoh.
cahors: Cahors lies in a meander of the Lot, surrounded by steep, dry limestone hills, 115 km north of Toulouse. It covers 64.72 km2, and its altitude ranges from 105 to 332 metres. It is the historical centre of the Quercy and the main town of the Lot department.

The town's original name was Divona, or Divona Cadurcorum, Divona of the Cadurci. Divona was a fountain, now called the fontaine des Chartreux, worshipped by the Cadurci, a Celtic people of Gaul. They were among the last Celtic tribes to resist the Roman conquest in the 50s BCE. Romanisation was rapid and profound, and Cahors became a large Roman city whose remains include the Arc de Diane, a relic of Roman baths.

In the Middle Ages the town was notorious for financiers known as Cahorsins, Christians who charged interest on loans. The church held that this was the sin of usury, so Cahors became a byword for it, and Dante's Inferno names it alongside Sodom. Pope John XXII, born Jacques Duèze, came from Cahors, the son of a shoemaker. On 7 June 1331 he granted a charter to the University of Cahors, which was annexed to the University of Toulouse in 1751.

The Valentré Bridge, the symbol of the town, was begun in 1308 and finished in 1378. A Devil's Bridge legend is attached to it, and when the bridge was restored in 1879 the architect Paul Gout placed a small sculpture of the devil on one of its towers.

Cahors is the prefecture of the Lot department and the seat of a diocese. Its monuments include the Saint-Étienne cathedral, a national monument, and the Valentré bridge, a World Heritage Site as part of the pilgrimage path to Santiago de Compostela. The wine of the Cahors appellation is a robust, tannic red that must contain at least 70% Malbec.
cai-lun: Cai Lun was born in Guiyang Commandery, in what is now Leiyang in Hunan, to a poor family. His year of birth is unknown, and estimates run from about 50 to about 62. Almost nothing is known of his early life, and it is not known how he came into imperial service in Luoyang. He is known to have been a eunuch official by 75 CE, and eunuchs were the only people eligible for certain tasks of the Han imperial household. Around 80 CE he was promoted to Xiao Huangmen, a messenger between the palace and the outer court.

In 82 CE Lady Dou, who wished to place her adopted son Prince Zhao in line for the throne, falsely accused Consort Song of witchcraft and ordered Cai to interrogate her and her sister; both killed themselves. When Prince Zhao became Emperor He in 88 CE, at the age of ten, Dou ruled as empress dowager and promoted Cai to Zhongchang shi, the highest post open to eunuchs, and made him Prefect of the Palace Workshop, responsible for instruments and weapons. Emperor He overthrew the Dou family in 92 CE but left Cai undisturbed.

In 105 CE Cai announced a new composition for paper and a new process. It used bamboo and also hemp waste, old rags, fishnets and, above all, tree bark, probably mulberry, boiled to a pulp, beaten, mixed with water, sieved and dried. Before then writing was usually on heavy bamboo and wooden slips or on costly silk. The Hou Hanshu records that he submitted the process to the emperor and that the paper came to be called the paper of Lord Cai. In 110 CE he oversaw a new edition of the Five Classics, and in 114 CE he was made a marquis.

After Empress Dowager Deng's death in 121 CE, Emperor An, remembering Cai's part in the death of his grandmother Consort Song, ordered him to answer to the Ministry of Justice. Cai bathed, dressed formally and drank poison.

Paper existed in China as early as the 3rd century BCE, so scholars regard his work as an improvement, not an invention, though paper did not see widespread use until his changes. Papermaking spread across China and by the 600s appeared in Turkestan, Korea and India. Chinese prisoners from the Battle of Talas passed the knowledge to the Arabs of the Abbasid Caliphate, and it reached Europe, where paper was widely made by the 12th century. In China Cai was deified in the early Tang dynasty as god of papermaking, and Leiyang is still a centre of paper production.
cajamarca: Cajamarca stands at about 2,750 m above sea level in an inter-Andean valley irrigated by three rivers, the Mashcon, the San Lucas and the Chonta; the first two join here to form the Cajamarca river. The climate is subtropical highland, pleasant by day and cold at night, with rain mostly from October to April. The soil is very fertile. The Quechua name, Kashamarka, is usually explained as town or province of thorny plants, from kasha, thorn, and marka, town or region. Inca Garcilaso de la Vega proposed qasa, frost, instead, and that false etymology still appears in some dictionaries.

The city and its surroundings have been occupied by several cultures for more than 2,000 years. Nearby sites such as Cumbe Mayo and Kuntur Wasi preserve traces of cultures older than Chavín. Huacaloma, a ceremonial centre where fire rituals were performed, dates from about 1500 to 1000 BCE. The Cajamarca culture, known mainly from fine ceramics of white kaolin clay fired above 1,000 degrees, kept an unbroken style from about 200-100 BCE until the Spanish conquest. Its pottery reached its widest distribution between 700 and 900, when it is found at many sites of the Wari Empire, as far south as Pikillacta.

Between 1463 and 1471 the generals Capac Yupanqui and his nephew Tupac Inca Yupanqui conquered Cajamarca for the Inca Empire, then ruled by Tupac Inca Yupanqui's father, Pachacutiq. The town had been founded by other peoples about a century earlier, around 1320. Colonial chroniclers tell of a Cuismancu kingdom that ruled the area before the Incas. The Incas rebuilt the city to their own canons, but little survives, since the Spanish also rebuilt it after the conquest. When Francisco Pizarro reached Cajamarca in 1532, he learned that Atahualpa was resting at the nearby hot springs of Pultumarca and sent Hernando de Soto to invite him to a feast.

Cajamarca is the capital and largest city of the Cajamarca Region and a commercial centre of the northern Andes, known for its dairy products, notably the mantecoso cheese, and for mining nearby. The Organization of American States designated it a site of Historical and Cultural Heritage of the Americas in 1986. Its six Spanish colonial churches were all built in the 17th century; the Cathedral took 80 years to build, from 1682 to 1762, and its facade remains unfinished. Baños del Inca, the hot springs town nearby, is a popular visiting place. The city celebrates Carnival each year with parades and dances.
calabash: The calabash, or bottle gourd (Lagenaria siceraria), is a vine of the family Cucurbitaceae, native to tropical Africa and grown across the tropics. The English word comes from Middle French calebasse and Spanish calabaza, meaning gourd or pumpkin. The gourd was one of the first plants cultivated not mainly for food but for use as containers. Bottle gourds have been recovered from archaeological contexts in China and Japan dating to about 8,000 to 9,000 years ago, while in Africa the earliest record is a gourd reported in 1884 from a 12th Dynasty tomb at Thebes, about 4,000 years old. Genetic and archaeological evidence suggest that it was domesticated independently, first in Asia and over 4,000 years later in Africa.

Calabash fruits take many shapes: huge and round, small and bottle-shaped, or slim and serpentine, and some grow longer than a metre. The fruit can be harvested young and eaten as a vegetable, or left to mature and dried for use as a ladle, bowl, beverage container or musical instrument. The name is also given to the unrelated calabash tree, Crescentia cujete. How the gourd reached the Americas, where it was grown over 8,000 years ago, has long puzzled scholars. A study of 2005 proposed that Paleo-Indians carried it there, but a fuller genetic study of 2014 concluded that American gourds are most closely related to wild African ones and could have drifted across the ocean many times.

Hollowed and dried calabashes are a typical household utensil across West Africa, used to clean rice, carry water and hold food. They are made into instruments such as the Yoruba ṣẹ̀kẹ̀rẹ̀, a rattle similar to a maraca. In many African legends the calabash is a vessel for knowledge and wisdom. Because it is watertight, it was used to ship seeds across the transatlantic slave trade and by enslaved people to carry seeds for planting. In China the hulu is an ancient symbol of health, and in India a dried calabash forms the resonator of the sitar and tanpura.
calakmul: Calakmul lies in the jungles of the greater Petén Basin in Campeche, about 35 kilometres from the Guatemalan border and 38 kilometres north of the ruins of El Mirador. Its name is modern, read by Cyrus L. Lundell as the City of the Two Adjacent Pyramids. In ancient times its core was known as Ox Te' Tuun, the Place of Three Stones. The site core covers about 2 square kilometres, and Structure 2, a pyramid over 45 metres high and one of the tallest in Mesoamerica, holds four tombs.

Occupation runs from the Middle Preclassic to the Postclassic. Its rulers called themselves Divine Lords of the Snake, and the snake head emblem glyph, read Kaan, is widely distributed over its domain. Epigraphic studies show that before the 7th century the city's emblem glyph was a bat, so a different polity may have ruled there, and the Kaan polity may have moved to Calakmul from Dzibanché in the late 6th or early 7th century.

In the Classic period Calakmul and Tikal were rivals, described as two Maya superpowers, and Calakmul tried to surround Tikal with allies. It held the upper hand from the second half of the 6th century to the late 7th. King Uneh Chan attacked Palenque on 23 April 599 and defeated Queen Lady Yohl Ik'nal. Tikal won a decisive battle in 695 and half a century later won major victories over Calakmul's most important allies. Both cities succumbed to the Classic Maya collapse.

At its height the city is estimated to have had 50,000 inhabitants and to have ruled a regional state of about 13,000 square kilometres. Thirteen reservoirs held over 200 million litres of water. The site has 117 stelae, the most in the Maya region, and murals showing market scenes.

Cyrus L. Lundell reported the ruins in 1931 after seeing them from the air, and Sylvanus G. Morley visited in 1932. Excavation resumed in 1982 under William J. Folan and continues under Mexico's National Institute of Anthropology and History.
calatayud: Calatayud lies on the river Jalón in the Province of Zaragoza, in Aragón, in the midst of the Sistema Ibérico mountain range. It occupies a strategic position between the central meseta of Spain and the Ebro valley, which explains its lasting importance. It is the second-largest town of the province after Zaragoza and the seat of the comarca of Calatayud. Its motto calls it very noble, loyal, always august and most faithful.

The Romans founded a city called Augusta Bilbilis on the site of a Celt-Iberian settlement. Its ruins lie about four kilometres north of the modern town, and the poet Martial was born there in 40 CE. The modern town was founded by the Moors around a castle of Ayyub, about 716 CE, and its name comes from the Arabic Qal‘at ’Ayyūb, the fortress of Ayyub. The former inhabitants of Bilbilis moved to the new site. By the eleventh century a substantial Jewish community lived there, and it survived until the expulsion of the Jews of Spain in 1492.

Alfonso I of Aragón conquered the town from the Muslims, and many surviving mudéjar churches show that Islamic influence remained. The church of San Pedro is said to have housed the first cortes of Aragon, held in 1411. During the Peninsular Wars the French-occupied town was besieged and taken by guerrillas in 1811. Calatayud was the capital of its own province in 1822–23, during the Trienio Liberal.

The population was 20,658 in 2014. One of the most notable mudéjar towers of Aragón is the 15th-century bell tower of the collegiate church of Santa María, built on the site of a mosque, with a Renaissance doorway added in 1528. The church of Santo Sepulcro, built in 1141 and restored in 1613, was long the principal church of the Spanish Knights Templar. The Muslim fortress is described as the biggest and oldest on the Iberian peninsula. Most employment is in services and agriculture, mainly apple and pear orchards.
california: California covers 163,696 square miles and is bordered by Oregon to the north, Nevada to the east, Arizona to the south-east, the Mexican state of Baja California to the south and the Pacific Ocean to the west. In the middle lies the Central Valley, bounded by the Sierra Nevada and the coastal ranges, the state's agricultural heartland. The name most likely comes from the mythical island of California in the 1510 romance The Adventures of Esplandián by Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo, whose Queen Calafia ruled a remote land rich in gold and pearls. The name was on a map by 1541. The Spaniards called the peninsula of Baja California Las Californias, and the name spread north to Alta California.

Before European colonisation California was one of the most culturally and linguistically diverse areas of pre-Columbian North America. Historians generally agree that at least 300,000 people lived there, in more than 70 ethnic groups. They managed their environments in complex ways, with forest gardening and controlled burning to prevent destructive wildfires, and political organisation ranged from bands and villages to large chiefdoms on the rich coasts, among them the Chumash, Pomo and Salinan.

European exploration in the 16th and 17th centuries led to colonisation by the Spanish Empire. The area became part of Mexico in 1821. In the Mexican-American War the United States conquered California, and Mexico ceded it in 1848. The gold rush that began that year brought social and demographic changes, among them what has been called the California genocide of the Indigenous peoples. California was admitted as the 31st state in 1850, as a free state, following the Compromise of 1850.

Sacramento is the state capital, and Los Angeles is its most populous city. California is the most populous US state, with over 39 million people. Hollywood has been an important centre of the film industry since the 1920s, and Silicon Valley in the San Francisco Bay Area is a centre of the technology industry.
caliphate: A caliphate is an institution led by a caliph, regarded as a political and religious successor to Muhammad and a leader of the whole Muslim community, the ummah. The word comes from the Arabic khalifah, meaning successor, steward or deputy. Before Islam, Arabian rulers used the title malik, king. After Muhammad's death the Ansar of Medina met in the courtyard of the Banu Sa'ida clan, and at the meeting at Saqifah Abu Bakr was elected the first caliph.

Three major caliphates followed one another in the medieval period: the Rashidun (632 to 661), the Umayyad (661 to 750) and the Abbasid (750 to 1517). After Ali was assassinated by a Kharijite, his son Hasan gave way to Mu'awiyah, who founded the Umayyad dynasty and made the title hereditary. The Umayyad Caliphate took in the Caucasus, Transoxiana, Sindh, the Maghreb and most of the Iberian Peninsula. In 750 the Abbasids overthrew the Umayyads, and their capital Baghdad became a centre of knowledge, culture and trade. The Abbasids lost effective power outside Iraq by about 920, and the Mongols under Hulagu Khan sacked Baghdad in 1258.

The Fatimid Caliphate, from 909 to 1171, was an Isma'ili Shi'i caliphate that began in Tunisia, founded Cairo in 969 and made Egypt its centre. The Ottoman sultans claimed the caliphate from Murad I, and the claim strengthened after Selim I annexed the Mamluk Sultanate of Cairo in 1517 and became defender of Mecca and Medina. The title gained a practical use only in the late 18th century, when it allowed the sultans to answer Russian claims to protect Ottoman Christians. The Ottoman Caliphate was formally abolished in 1924.

Sunni Muslims developed the belief that the caliph is a temporal ruler, elected by the community and bound by Islamic law, and many call the first four caliphs the Rashidun, the rightly guided. Most Shia Muslims hold instead that rulers should be imams chosen by God from the family of the Prophet, descended from Ali. Since the Umayyads every caliphate has been dynastic. Some Sufi orders and the Ahmadiyya movement, which has had caliphs since 1908, use the title for spiritual leaders. Since the 1920s the political caliphate has lain dormant.
callao: Callao stands on and around the peninsula of La Punta, which separates the bays of Miraflores and Callao. Stone workshops on Chivateros Hill are more than 10,000 years old, and in the mid-15th century the territory was annexed to the Inca Empire. The name comes from callao, a Spanish nautical word for a pebble; a definition of 1667 that mentioned the rocky coast was considered decisive, though historians had suggested a Quechua or Aymara origin. Its people are called chalacos.

On 6 March 1537 Diego Ruiz obtained a licence to open a tambo, a supply post, in the port of Lima, and the first Spanish neighbourhood began to be built in 1555. As the main port of the Viceroyalty of Peru it attracted pirates: Francis Drake attacked it in 1579 and Jacques l'Hermite in 1624, and walls were built between 1634 and 1647. It received city status in 1671. Goods from Lower Peru, Upper Peru and the River Plate were carried by mule to Callao and shipped to Panama, and the port was a node on the Manila galleon route.

The earthquake and tsunami of 28 October 1746 destroyed the city; of about five thousand inhabitants only 200 survived. Viceroy José Manso de Velasco founded Bellavista inland, but the people of Callao stayed by the sea, and work on the Real Felipe Fortress began in October 1747. San Martín's troops first took the fortress in 1821. After the Battle of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824 a 13-month siege ended in 1826, when General José Ramón Rodil surrendered it to General Bartolomé Salom. Callao became a Littoral Province on 20 August 1836 and a Constitutional Province under Ramón Castilla after the fighting of April 1857.

Callao is Peru's chief seaport and the site of Jorge Chávez International Airport, and it forms part of the Lima metropolitan area, its centre about 15 km west of Lima's Historic Centre. It is a city and a constitutional province outside any department, and includes the islands of San Lorenzo, El Frontón, Cavinzas and Palomino. The Real Felipe Fortress still overlooks the harbour. Callao celebrates no founding date; on 20 August it marks its autonomy from Lima.
callimachus: The main source for the life of Callimachus is an entry in the Suda, a 10th-century Byzantine encyclopaedia, which contains factual inaccuracies but also some otherwise unattested information. He was born into a prominent family in Cyrene, a Greek city on the coast of modern Libya, and called himself the son of Battus, though this may allude to the city's mythical founder rather than to his father. His grandfather, also named Callimachus, had been a general of the city. His date of birth is unknown and is placed around 310 BCE.

In the 280s BCE he is thought to have studied at Alexandria under the philosopher Praxiphanes and the grammarian Hermocrates. He appears to have worked as a schoolteacher in the suburbs of the city and to have been poor for a time, a claim the classicist Alan Cameron calls almost certainly fiction. He then entered the patronage of the Ptolemies and worked at the Library of Alexandria under Ptolemy II Philadelphus. His poetry suggests that he was writing until about 240 BCE.

At the Library of Alexandria Callimachus was responsible for cataloguing. From its shelf-lists he compiled the Pinakes, a bibliography of all Greek literature that ran to 120 volumes, five times the length of Homer's Iliad. It has not survived, but scholars have reconstructed its content from later writers. Authors were divided into poetry and prose, each split into subcategories such as drama, epic and lyric, or philosophy, oratory, history and medicine. Entries were alphabetical and gave an author's biography and list of works. The classicist Lionel Casson called it the first comprehensive bibliographic resource for Greek literature.

According to the Suda, Callimachus wrote more than 800 works in prose and poetry. Only the Epigrams and Hymns survive complete in the main; the rest, including all his prose, is known from fragments. The Aetia, a poem of about 4,000 lines in four books, collects origin stories told in elegiac couplets, among them the Victory of Berenice and the Lock of Berenice. The Iambs, 13 satirical poems, defend his style against critics. The Hecale, an epyllion of about 1,000 lines, tells how Theseus was hosted by a poor old woman. He also wrote six hymns and at least 60 epigrams.

At the start of the Aetia he set out his programme in words he gave to Apollo: keep the Muse slender and tread an untrodden path. He preferred small, learned and sometimes obscure subjects to the long heroic epic that dominated his day. Catullus, Horace, Vergil, Propertius and Ovid took him as a principal model, and Propertius called himself a Roman Callimachus. Richard Hunter argues that this reception through Roman poets has simplified the picture of his work.
calw: Calw lies in the valley of the Nagold in the Northern Black Forest, at an altitude between 330 and 630 metres, about 18 kilometres south of Pforzheim and 33 kilometres west of Stuttgart. The historic centre is on the west bank of the river, and newer districts have grown on the surrounding slopes. Calw is the capital and largest town of its district.

Calw is first mentioned in records in 1037. In the 11th century the town grew around the older castle of the counts of Calw, whose coat of arms, a red lion on a three-ridged hill, is still the town's. In the Middle Ages it was an important commercial town, especially in the cloth and leather trades. In 1345 it passed to Württemberg, and by the 16th century it had become a summer residence of the dukes of Württemberg. The Reformation took force there in 1534, and in 1555 Calw became the seat of a deanery. In the 18th century the town flourished on the lumber trade and the rafting of timber down the Nagold.

In 1945 a small subcamp of the Natzweiler-Struthof concentration camp was located in Calw, where female Jewish forced labourers assembled aircraft parts. The town then fell into the French occupation zone and in 1947 became part of Württemberg-Hohenzollern, which merged into Baden-Württemberg in 1952.

The most prominent person from Calw is the author Hermann Hesse, winner of the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1946. His stories use Gerbersau as a literary name for Calw, and a Hermann Hesse Prize for literary journals and translators is awarded there every other year. Calw has a small historic centre that the wars of the 20th century largely left untouched, with its marketplace and the Nikolausbrücke, a historic bridge.
cambodia: Cambodia covers about 181,035 km2 and lies entirely within the tropics, with a 443 km coastline along the Gulf of Thailand. Its landscape is a low-lying central plain surrounded by uplands and low mountains, including the Tonle Sap, the Great Lake, and the upper Mekong delta. The Tonle Sap's most distinctive feature is its flooding, from about 2,590 km2 in the dry season to about 24,605 km2 in the rainy season, and the plain around it, devoted to wet rice cultivation, is the heartland of the country.
The highest peak is Phnom Aural, at 1,813 metres. The Khmer name derives from the Sanskrit Kambujadeśa, the land of the sons of Kambu, after a sage from whom the Khmer kings claimed descent.

Cambodia has been inhabited for over 5000 years. The cave of Laang Spean, with radiocarbon dates around 6000 BCE, is considered the most ancient archaeological site in the country, and the first rice farmers came from the north from the third millennium BCE. Iron was worked by about 500 BCE. In the 3rd, 4th and 5th centuries the Indianised kingdoms of Funan and its successor Chenla coalesced in what became Cambodia and southwestern Vietnam, and for more than 2,000 years the region absorbed influences from India and passed them to other Southeast Asian civilisations.

In 802 Jayavarman II declared himself king, uniting the warring Khmer princes of Chenla under the name Kambuja, and the Khmer Empire became the centre of power. Over 600 years it facilitated the spread of first Hinduism and then Buddhism across Southeast Asia. In the 15th century Cambodia declined and lost territory to its neighbours, and during the Post-Angkor period Vietnam and Thailand each attempted to vassalise it. It became a French protectorate in 1863 and secured independence in 1953.

The Khmer Rouge regime carried out the Cambodian genocide from 1975 to 1979 and was deposed by a Vietnamese intervention and occupation, though insurgencies continued until 1999. By 1993 a United Nations peacekeeping mission had restored the monarchy and established a democratic constitution with elections. Cambodia is a constitutional monarchy. About 17 million people live there, 95.8% of them ethnic Khmer.
cambridgeshire: Cambridgeshire is a ceremonial county in the East of England and East Anglia, bordered by Lincolnshire, Norfolk, Suffolk, Essex, Hertfordshire, Northamptonshire and Bedfordshire. The north and east are dominated by the Fens, an extremely flat, drained marsh maintained by drainage ditches and dykes, where Holme Fen is the lowest physical point in the United Kingdom, 2.75 metres below sea level. The south and west are gently undulating. The principal rivers are the Nene, the Great Ouse and its tributary the Cam, which flows through Cambridge.

Must Farm quarry at Whittlesey has been described as Britain's Pompeii for the best-preserved Bronze Age dwellings ever found in the United Kingdom, and many archaeological finds from the Stone Age, the Bronze Age and the Iron Age have come from East Cambridgeshire. Anglo-Saxons settled the area from the fifth century. Genetic testing of seven skeletons from Anglo-Saxon graves at Hinxton and Oakington found that five were migrants or descended from migrants from the continent, one was a native Briton and one had both continental and native ancestry, suggesting intermarriage.

The Domesday Book records the county as Grantbridgeshire, a name related to the river Granta. In 1888 separate county councils were set up for the area around Cambridge and for the liberty of the Isle of Ely. In 1965 these were merged as Cambridgeshire and the Isle of Ely, and under the Local Government Act 1972 this merged with Huntingdon and Peterborough, formed in 1965 from Huntingdonshire and the Soke of Peterborough. The resulting county was called simply Cambridgeshire. Since 1998 Peterborough has been a separate unitary authority.

Because of the flat terrain and the nearness of the continent, many airfields were built in the county in the Second World War for RAF Bomber Command, RAF Fighter Command and the American air forces. The Cambridge American Cemetery and Memorial lies at Madingley.

Peterborough is the largest settlement, and the county also contains the cities of Cambridge and Ely and the towns of Wisbech, Huntingdon and St Neots. Most of it is agricultural. The University of Cambridge, the second-oldest university in the English-speaking world, stands in Cambridge.
cambyses-ii: Cambyses was the eldest son of Cyrus the Great and Cassandane, and his younger brother was Bardiya. In April 538 BCE Cyrus appointed him governor of northern Babylonia, and he received the royal sceptre in the temple of Marduk at the New Year festival. Cyrus dismissed him after nine months, for unknown reasons. Babylonian records give both men the title King of Babylon, King of the Lands, which suggests that Cyrus made him co-ruler some years before his campaign against the Massagetae. Cambyses was sent back to Persia before Cyrus fell in that campaign, and he had his father's body carried to Pasargadae for burial.

The conquest of Egypt had been planned by Cyrus, who wished to unite Babylonia with the Trans-Euphrates lands. Cambyses seized Cyprus, founded the Achaemenid navy with men and equipment from Phoenicia and Asia Minor, and made a treaty with the Arabs of the desert between Gaza and Egypt for water. In the spring of 525 BCE he defeated Psamtik III at Pelusium, then besieged and captured Memphis. By summer all Egypt was under Persian suzerainty. The Greeks of Cyrene and Barca acknowledged his authority, and he set a garrison at Elephantine against Kush. At Sais he was crowned in the temple of Neith and took the titles of the pharaohs.

Greek writers such as Herodotus accuse him of brutality, of looting temples, of killing the sacred Apis bull, and of madness. Pierre Briant holds that this bias casts doubt on Herodotus's account. An epitaph and sarcophagus show that Cambyses took part in the burial of an Apis, and the Demotic Chronicle says that he reduced the income of most Egyptian temples, which may explain hostile stories spread by priests. Herodotus also reports a disastrous expedition against Kush, but archaeology shows a Persian stronghold at Dorginarti.

In the spring of 522 BCE Cambyses left Egypt in haste to put down a revolt in Persia. On the way through Syria he received a wound in the thigh that became gangrenous, and he died about three weeks later, probably at Hama. Herodotus tells of an accident with his sword, Ctesias of a self-inflicted wound, and some modern historians suspect assassination. He died childless and was succeeded by his brother Bardiya, whom Darius the Great soon overthrew. Cambyses was buried at Neyriz in southeastern Persis. At his death the empire stretched from Cyrenaica to the Hindu Kush.
camel: The camel is an even-toed ungulate of the genus Camelus, marked by fatty deposits known as humps. Three species survive. The one-humped dromedary makes up 94% of the world's camel population and the two-humped Bactrian camel 6%. The wild Bactrian is a distinct species, not the ancestor of the domestic Bactrian. Camels provide milk, meat, fibre and felt, and are a vital means of transport for passengers and cargo.

The hump is a reservoir of fatty tissue, a reserve of calories and not of water, as is commonly believed. A dromedary can drink as seldom as once every 10 days even in great heat, and can lose up to 30% of its body mass through dehydration.

Camelids originated in North America during the Eocene. Paracamelus, the ancestor of modern camels, crossed the Bering land bridge into Asia during the late Miocene, around 6 million years ago. The camels that stayed in North America were wiped out 10 to 12,000 years ago, when the first indigenous peoples spread there from Asia, although fossils have never been associated with definitive evidence of hunting.

When humans first domesticated camels is disputed. Dromedaries may have been domesticated in Somalia or South Arabia in the 3rd millennium BCE, and the Bactrian in central Asia around 2,500 BCE, as at Shahr-e Sukhteh in Iran. A study of 2016 using mitochondrial DNA suggested that the dromedary was first domesticated in the southeast Arabian Peninsula.

Excavations in the Timna Valley in 2009 to 2013, led by Lidar Sapir-Hen and Erez Ben-Yosef, found what may be the earliest domestic camel bones in Israel or outside the Arabian Peninsula, dating to around 930 BCE. The find drew attention because camels appear in the biblical stories of Abraham, Jacob, Esau and Joseph, and it is taken as strong evidence that those stories were written after that time. The archaeologist William F. Albright had earlier seen the camels of the Bible as an anachronism.

Camels introduced to Australia as transport animals in the 19th and early 20th centuries became a large feral population. The United States Camel Corps experiment of the 19th century also brought camels to the Southwestern United States.
camera-obscura: The effect is a natural phenomenon. Perforated gnomons that projected a pinhole image of the sun are described in the Chinese Zhoubi Suanjing, and the Mozi explains that the image is inverted because light crosses at the pinhole: rays from a person's foot strike below it and form the top of the image. The Greek philosopher Aristotle, or a follower, asked in the Problems why sunlight passing through square gaps in wickerwork forms round images.

Al-Kindi, who lived from about 801 to about 873, used pinhole images to show that light travels in straight lines. Ibn al-Haytham, known in the West as Alhazen (965 to 1040), gave the first experimental and mathematical analysis of the phenomenon in the early 11th century.

A camera obscura is a box, tent or room with a small hole in one side or the top. Light from the scene outside passes through the hole and forms on the opposite surface an image that is inverted and reversed left to right, with colour and perspective kept. A smaller hole gives a sharper but dimmer image, until diffraction spoils it, so practical instruments use a lens, which allows a larger aperture. Mirrors can set the image upright.

Leonardo da Vinci wrote the oldest known clear description in 1502 and drew about 270 diagrams of it, though his writings were deciphered and published only in 1797. The oldest published drawing is in Gemma Frisius's book of 1545, where he used it to watch the solar eclipse of 24 January 1544. The name first appears in Johannes Kepler's book of 1604. From 1611 David and Johannes Fabricius and Christoph Scheiner projected the sun to study sunspots, since looking at it directly could damage the eyes.

As a drawing aid it allowed an image to be traced and was valued as an easy way to achieve correct perspective. Lenses were fitted from the second half of the 16th century. In the first half of the 19th century camera obscura boxes were used to expose light-sensitive materials, and the technology developed into the photographic camera.
camerino: Camerino stands in the Apennines on the border with Umbria, between the valleys of the rivers Potenza and Chienti, about 64 kilometres from Ancona. It occupies the site of ancient Camerinum, whose inhabitants became allies of Rome in 310 or 309 BCE, bound to it by an equal treaty, the foedus aequum. Under the empire the town was a municipium. No ancient building is visible today, since the Roman remains lie as much as a metre below ground level.

Camerino was part of the Exarchate of Ravenna until 592, when the Lombards captured it. Under them it was the seat of a marquisate and then of a duchy, which the Franks later conquered. Around 1050 Boniface III of Tuscany occupied the duchy and ceded it to his daughter Matilda, who donated it to the Papal States. After the year 1000, however, it had become an independent commune. The troops of Manfred of Sicily destroyed it in 1256 and killed much of its population. Gentile Da Varano, one of the refugees who returned in 1262, founded a fiefdom for his family that lasted three centuries.

In 1382 Giovanni da Varano built a wall 12 kilometres long to defend the city, and Giulio Cesare Da Varano built a Ducal Palace, now one of the most important Renaissance buildings in central Italy. Giulio Cesare's daughter Camilla Battista da Varano was canonised in 2010. Cesare Borgia nearly extinguished the family in 1502. The university was founded in 1336, was recognised by the Kingdom of Italy in 1861 and became the public University of Camerino in 1958.

Camerino is a town in the province of Macerata in Marche. Its Ducal Palace is the seat of the university's Faculty of Jurisprudence. Its cathedral was rebuilt in the early 19th century, and the Porta Malatestiana dates from 1511.
cameroon: Cameroon covers 475,442 square kilometres in Central and West Africa, on the Bight of Bonny, part of the Gulf of Guinea. It is often called Africa in miniature because it has the coast, desert, mountains, rainforest and savanna of the continent. The country divides into five major geographic zones, among them a hot and humid coastal plain and the South Cameroon Plateau, covered by equatorial rainforest.

A chain of mountains, hills and plateaus, the Cameroon range, runs from Mount Cameroon on the coast, the highest point at 4,095 metres, almost to Lake Chad in the north. Volcanism there has created crater lakes. On 21 August 1986 one of them, Lake Nyos, released carbon dioxide and killed between 1,700 and 2,000 people.

Excavations at Shum Laka in the Northwest Region show human occupation dating back 30,000 years. The Baka are counted among the longest continuous inhabitants, and Bantu migrations into eastern, southern and central Africa are believed to have begun from this area about 2,000 years ago. The Sao culture arose around Lake Chad about 500 CE and gave way to Kanem and its successor, the Bornu Empire, while kingdoms, fondoms and chiefdoms arose in the west. Portuguese sailors reached the coast in 1472 and named the Wouri River Rio dos Camarões, the Shrimp River, after the ghost shrimp they found there. In 1896 Sultan Ibrahim Njoya created the Bamum script for the Bamum language.

Germany built a warehouse on the Wouri estuary in 1868, and in 1884 the German Empire claimed the territory as the colony of Kamerun after Gustav Nachtigal made a treaty with a local king. The people resisted in the Bafut Wars and Adamawa Wars. Commercial companies ran local administration and used forced labour on banana, rubber, palm oil and cocoa plantations, a policy criticised by other colonial powers. After World War I the territory was divided between France and the United Kingdom as League of Nations mandates. The French-administered part became independent as the Republic of Cameroun in 1960 under Ahmadou Ahidjo, and the southern part of British Cameroons federated with it in 1961.

Yaoundé is the capital and Douala, the economic capital and main seaport, is among the largest cities. Cameroon is a unitary presidential republic. Its official languages are French and English, and its people speak some 250 native languages. Christianity is the majority religion, with significant minorities practising Islam and traditional faiths. Cameroon is a member of the African Union, the United Nations, the Commonwealth of Nations and the Organisation Internationale de la Francophonie.
camille-pissarro: Jacob Abraham Camille Pissarro was born on 10 July 1830 at Charlotte Amalie to Frederick Abraham Gabriel Pissarro, a merchant of Portuguese Jewish descent who held French nationality, and Rachel Manzano-Pomié. His father's marriage to his late uncle's widow caused a stir in the small Jewish community, and the four children were sent to an all-black primary school. In 1855, at 25, Camille moved to Paris and worked as an assistant to the painter Anton Melbye. He found the teaching at the École des Beaux-Arts and the Académie Suisse stifling and asked Corot for instruction instead.

His first painting was accepted by the Paris Salon in 1859. Corot inspired him to paint outdoors, and at the Académie Suisse he met Claude Monet, Armand Guillaumin and Paul Cézanne, who shared his dissatisfaction with the Salon. During the Franco-Prussian War he moved his family to Norwood near London, since he had only Danish nationality. Of the 1,500 paintings he left in France, only 40 remained, since soldiers had used many as floor mats. In 1871 he married Julie Vellay, with whom he had seven children, six of them painters. The family settled at Éragny-sur-Epte in April 1884.

The first Impressionist exhibition, in 1874, shocked critics, who found the subjects vulgar and the brushwork sketchy. Pissarro showed five landscapes, and Émile Zola praised them. In 1885 he met Georges Seurat and Paul Signac and for about three years used their method of small dabs of pure colour, showing such works in 1886 at the eighth exhibition. By the end of the 1880s he found the method too restrictive, but kept a stronger attention to colour. He was also drawn to anarchist circles, and in 1889 made an album of thirty drawings, Turpitudes sociales.

In 1892 Monet helped Pissarro and Julie buy the Éragny house, and in 1893 Pissarro converted the barn into a studio. In old age a recurring eye infection kept him from working outdoors except in warm weather, so he painted from hotel windows in Rouen, Paris, Le Havre, Dieppe and London. He died in Paris on 13 November 1903, aged 73, of sepsis, and was buried in Père Lachaise Cemetery. The art historian Diane Kelder wrote that no member of the Impressionist group did more to mediate the disputes that threatened to break it apart. Cézanne said that Pissarro had been a father for him.
camille-saint-saens: Saint-Saëns was born in Paris, the only child of Jacques-Joseph-Victor Saint-Saëns, an official in the French Ministry of the Interior, and Françoise-Clémence, née Collin. Less than two months after the christening his father died of consumption. The boy was taken to the country for his health and lived for two years with a nurse at Corbeil, 29 kilometres south of Paris. He always considered himself a true Parisian.

On leaving the Conservatoire in 1853, Saint-Saëns became organist at Saint-Merri, where weddings and funerals gave him a comfortable income and spare time to compose. In 1861 he took his only teaching post, at the École Niedermeyer, in charge of piano studies. He scandalised some austere colleagues by introducing his students to Schumann, Liszt and Wagner, and Gabriel Fauré remembered the lessons with lasting gratitude.

In 1870, with Romain Bussine, he discussed a society to promote new French music. He served in the National Guard in the Franco-Prussian War. The Société Nationale de Musique, with the motto Ars Gallica, was founded in February 1871, with Bussine as president and Saint-Saëns as vice-president. He was elected to the Institut de France in 1881, and in 1906 and 1909 he made successful tours of the United States as pianist and conductor.

Saint-Saëns was the first major French composer to write piano concertos. The Second, in G minor (1868), became one of his most popular works, and the pianist Zygmunt Stojowski said it begins like Bach and ends like Offenbach. The Fifth, the Egyptian concerto of 1896, was written while he was wintering in Luxor. His Third Symphony has prominent parts for piano and organ and is dedicated to the memory of Liszt.

He wrote twelve operas. Henry VIII became a repertory piece in his lifetime, but since his death only Samson et Dalila has been regularly staged. He composed more than 140 mélodies and set Victor Hugo most often. Committed to the structures of earlier French composers, he came into conflict in later years with the impressionist and expressionist schools.
camillo-benso-count-of-cavour: Camillo Benso was born in Turin on 10 August 1810, during Napoleonic rule, into a family that had acquired estates during the French occupation. His godparents were Napoleon's sister Pauline and her husband, Prince Camillo Borghese. He joined the Engineer Corps of the Royal Sardinian Army in 1827. Reading Jeremy Bentham and Benjamin Constant made him a liberal and a suspect to the police, and he resigned his commission in November 1831. He managed the family estate at Grinzane and served as its mayor until 1848, held that economic progress had to come before political change, and backed railways and canals.

The Revolutions of 1848 let him enter politics, and he founded the newspaper Il Risorgimento. After the Piedmontese defeat at Novara and the abdication of Charles Albert in favour of Victor Emmanuel II, he became minister of agriculture, commerce and the navy in 1850 and of finance in 1851. His railway programme gave Piedmont 800 kilometres of track by 1860. With Urbano Rattazzi he formed a coalition that brought down Massimo d'Azeglio's cabinet in November 1852, and he became prime minister. His methods included heavy use of emergency powers and rigging elections, and the national debt rose sixfold. Piedmont joined the Crimean War on 10 January 1855, which earned it a place at the Congress of Paris.

At Plombières in July 1858 Cavour agreed with Napoleon III that France would help Piedmont fight Austria in return for Savoy and Nice. After Magenta and Solferino Napoleon signed the Armistice of Villafranca on 11 July 1859, and Cavour resigned in fury. Recalled on 20 January 1860, he ceded Savoy and Nice to France to annex Tuscany and Emilia. Garibaldi's thousand volunteers landed at Marsala on 11 May 1860 and conquered Sicily and then Naples. Cavour invaded Umbria and Marche to stop them marching on Rome, and Garibaldi handed the south to the king.

In 1861 Victor Emmanuel II declared the Kingdom of Italy and Cavour became its first prime minister. He held that Rome should be the seat of a free church in a free state. Exhausted, he fell ill, presumably with malaria, and was bled several times. He died on 6 June 1861 and was buried at Santena. Venice joined Italy in 1866 and Rome in 1870. Cavour had at first aimed to expand Piedmont rather than to unite Italy, but by his death the state was five times its earlier size and ranked among Europe's great powers.
camino-de-santiago: The Camino de Santiago is a network of pilgrim routes leading to the shrine of the apostle James in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela in Galicia, where tradition holds that his remains are buried. The main route follows an earlier Roman trade road that continues to Cape Finisterre on the Atlantic coast, which the Romans called Finisterrae, the end of the world. Pilgrims can take one of dozens of routes, and traditionally the way begins at one's own home. The Camino Francés, the French Way, is the most popular, and the Via Regia forms its last portion.

The Way was established in the early 9th century after the discovery of the relics of Saint James the Great, and the earliest records of visits to the shrine come from the time of the Kingdom of Asturias and Galicia. The earliest recorded pilgrims from beyond the Pyrenees came in the mid-11th century, and by the early 12th century the pilgrimage was highly organised.

Pope Callixtus II promoted it and began the Compostelan Holy Years. The Codex Calixtinus, published around 1140, served as the guide: four routes from France met at Puente la Reina, and from there a defined road crossed northern Spain through Burgos, León and Astorga.

Hospitals along the route met the pilgrims' needs, and contributed to the modern idea of the hospital. Romanesque churches with massive arches were built for the crowds, and pilgrims took home a Galician scallop shell as proof of completion, which became the badge of the pilgrim. The Church also imposed the pilgrimage as penance for grave sins. The Black Death, the Reformation and political unrest in the 16th century brought a decline, though in 1779 John Adams followed part of the route in reverse on his way to Paris. Few modern pilgrimages predate the 1957 publication of Walter Starkie's The Road to Santiago.

Whenever St James's Day, 25 July, falls on a Sunday, the cathedral declares a Holy Year. In 1987 the Camino was named the first Cultural Route of the Council of Europe, and the French Way and the Northern routes in Spain were inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List, followed by the routes in France in 1998. Pilgrims come mostly on foot, some by bicycle or horse, and many walk the final 100 kilometres to earn the Compostela certificate.
campeche: Campeche lies in southeast Mexico, bordered by Tabasco, Yucatán and Quintana Roo, by the Petén department of Guatemala to the south and the Orange Walk District of Belize, with 523 kilometres of shoreline on the Gulf of Mexico. The name derives from Can Pech, the Maya name of a chiefdom of the southwestern Yucatán Peninsula at the time the Spanish arrived; its capital, Ah-Kin-Pech, stood where the city of Campeche is now. The native name means place of snakes and ticks.

The Maya were the first people to dominate the area, and their main cities were Edzná, Xtampak and later Calakmul and Becán. The civilization reached its height between 600 and 900 CE, and from about 1000 the cities were abandoned for unknown reasons. In 1517 Francisco Hernández de Córdoba and Antón de Alaminos landed at Can-Pech and renamed it San Lázaro. At Champotón Hernández de Córdoba was attacked and died of his wounds, so the Spanish called the bay the Bay of the Bad Fight. The conquest of the peninsula began in earnest in 1540 under Francisco de Montejo, father and son, and the capital was founded that year.

The city was a rich port during the colonial period and suffered more than 21 major pirate attacks. After the sack of 1685 by English and French buccaneers, who plundered the surroundings for two months, fortifications were begun that took 24 years to complete: a wall with four main gates, three to the land and one to the sea, and forts including San Carlos, Santa Rosa, San Juan and San Francisco. Only one pirate, Barbillas, found a way in, in 1708. After Mexican independence the city declined, and Campeche split from the province of Yucatán in the mid-19th century, mostly because of political friction with Mérida.

Campeche is one of the 31 states that, with Mexico City, make up the 32 federal entities of Mexico, and has thirteen municipalities. Much of its territory is filled with archaeological sites, almost all Maya, among them Calakmul, Edzná, Becán, Chicanná and Río Bec. The Calakmul Biosphere Reserve was created in 1989. The historic buildings of the capital, formally San Francisco de Campeche, are protected by decree.
campi-flegrei: The Phlegraean Fields are a large volcanic caldera west of Naples, part of the Campanian volcanic arc, which also includes Mount Vesuvius. The caldera area consists of 24 craters and volcanic edifices, most of them under the Gulf of Naples. Part of the city of Naples is built over it, and the area also takes in Pozzuoli, Bacoli, Ischia and Procida. The Solfatara crater has steaming fumaroles and many pools of boiling mud, and was believed in ancient Rome to be the home of Vulcan, the god of fire. Lake Avernus fills one of the tuff craters.

Geologists distinguish three phases. In the first, about 39,280 years ago, the Campanian Ignimbrite eruption, rated VEI 7, spread ash across a large part of eastern Europe; one theory holds that it contributed to the extinction of the Neanderthals. The second period, 35,000 to 10,500 years ago, produced the Neapolitan yellow tuff, with Pozzuoli at its centre; the last major eruption came about 12,000 years ago. The third, from 8,000 to 500 years ago, formed Lake Avernus and Monte Nuovo, which an eight-day eruption built as a new hill in 1538.

The ground rises and falls slowly, a process called bradyseism, most evident at the Macellum of Pozzuoli, where bands of holes bored by marine molluscs in marble columns show that the level of the site against the sea has varied. Between 1982 and 1986 an uplift raised the ground by 1.8 metres.

The ancient Greeks had a colony at Cumae, seat of the Cumaean Sibyl. Lake Avernus was believed to be an entrance to the underworld and is portrayed so in Virgil's Aeneid. Baiae was a fashionable coastal resort with summer villas of Julius Caesar, Nero and Hadrian, who died there.

Pozzuoli has the Flavian Amphitheatre, the third largest in Italy, and Baiae, now partly submerged, had the largest ancient dome before the Pantheon. Quarries of piperno stone supplied much of the building stone of Naples from Roman times to the early 20th century. The tombs of Agrippina the Elder and Scipio Africanus lie in the area. In 2022 the International Union of Geological Sciences listed the site among 100 geological heritage sites, for its part in the development of volcanology in the 18th and 19th centuries.
canaan: Canaan was an ancient Semitic-speaking civilization and region of the southern Levant in the late 2nd millennium BCE. Egyptian texts of that millennium use the name for an Egyptian-ruled colony whose boundaries broadly match those of the Hebrew Bible: the Mediterranean Sea to the west, the vicinity of Hamath in Syria to the north, the Jordan Valley to the east and a line from the Dead Sea to around Gaza to the south. The Egyptians also called the Levantine coast Retjenu, and the region between Ascalon and the Lebanon, inland to the Sea of Galilee, Djahy.

The name appears as Kinâḫna in the Amarna letters of the 14th century BCE. Its origin is uncertain; one early explanation derives it from a Semitic root meaning to be low or subjugated. The Akkadian word kinahhu referred to purple-dyed wool, a key export, and the Greeks may have taken the name Phoenikes for the Canaanites from their word for crimson or purple.

Scholars use several periodizations. Metalworking Ghassulian settlers entered Canaan around 4500 BCE, at the start of the Chalcolithic. In the Early Bronze Age Ebla was incorporated by about 2300 BCE into the Akkadian Empire of Sargon the Great and Naram-Sin. In the Middle Bronze Age, from 2000 to 1550 BCE, urbanism returned and the region was divided among small city-states, of which Hazor seems to have been the most important, within a wide international trading network.

In the early Late Bronze Age, Canaanite confederacies centred on Megiddo and Kadesh were fully brought into the Egyptian and Hittite empires. By the Early Iron Age the southern Levant was dominated by the kingdoms of Israel and Judah, the Philistine city-states, and Moab, Ammon, Aram-Damascus and Edom. The Neo-Assyrian Empire conquered the whole region in the 10th and 9th centuries BCE and held it for three hundred years.

The name Canaanites is attested many centuries later as the endonym of the people the Greeks called Phoenicians from about 500 BCE, and the Punics of North Africa used a form of it of themselves. In the Hebrew Bible Canaan and the Canaanites appear some 160 times, and Canaan is the land of the Promised Land. The biblical scholar Mark Smith, citing archaeology, holds that Israelite culture largely overlapped with and derived from Canaanite culture.
canada: Canada is the second-largest country by total area, encompassing 9,984,670 square kilometres, and has the world's longest coastline, of 243,042 kilometres. It shares the world's largest land border with the United States, spanning 8,891 kilometres. The country has seven physiographic regions, among them the Canadian Shield, the Interior Plains and the Western Cordillera. It has over 2,000,000 lakes, and boreal forests prevail throughout. Canadian Forces Station Alert, on the northern tip of Ellesmere Island, is the world's northernmost settlement.

Indigenous peoples have continuously inhabited what is now Canada for thousands of years, and they include the First Nations, Inuit and Métis. Their population at the time of the first European settlements is estimated at between 200,000 and 2 million, and it declined by 40 to 80 percent as a consequence of colonization, through European diseases, conflicts over the fur trade, conflicts with colonial authorities and settlers, and the loss of land.

British and French expeditions explored and later settled along the Atlantic coast from the 16th century, and France ceded nearly all of its colonies in North America in 1763. Early interactions were relatively peaceful, but friendship and peace treaties gave way to the dispossession of Indigenous lands.

Canada was formed in 1867 through Confederation as a federal dominion of four provinces. Settler colonialism peaked in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, when the government funded Indian residential schools administered by Christian churches. These are considered part of a genocide of Indigenous peoples because of their forced assimilation and the large-scale removal of children from their families. A reconciliation commission was formed in 2008. Autonomy from the United Kingdom grew through the Statute of Westminster, 1931, and the Canada Act 1982 severed the remaining legal dependence.

Canada has ten provinces and three territories, with Ottawa as the capital and Toronto, Montreal and Vancouver as the three largest metropolitan areas. It is a parliamentary democracy and a constitutional monarchy, and it is officially bilingual in English and French in the federal jurisdiction. The 2021 census enumerated 36,991,981 people, and the population is estimated to have passed 40,000,000 in 2023. About 80 percent live within 150 kilometres of the border with the contiguous United States. Multiculturalism is official state policy.
canal-du-midi: A canal between the Atlantic and the Mediterranean was an old idea. Leaders including Augustus, Nero, Charlemagne, François I, Charles IX and Henry IV are said to have dreamed of it. In 1516 François I brought Leonardo da Vinci to France and commissioned a survey of a route from the Garonne at Toulouse to the Aude at Carcassonne. Such a waterway would spare ships and goods a voyage around the Iberian Peninsula that could take a month and carried the danger of piracy.

Royal authority for the work came in October 1666, when Jean-Baptiste Colbert authorised it by edict after a committee of experts had studied the route for several months. Colbert believed that trade favoured the Dutch rather than the kingdom, and grain prices and wine production had fallen. The edict gave the work to its designer, Pierre-Paul Riquet, and his descendants, with rights of expropriation, a tax-exempt fief and the right to levy tolls.

The canal is about 240 km long. It was first called the Canal Royal en Languedoc and was renamed the Canal du Midi in 1789. It climbs from Toulouse over 52 km to the Seuil de Naurouze, its summit level at 189.43 m, and then descends 188 km to Les Onglous on the Étang de Thau. The central difficulty was bringing water from the Montagne Noire to the summit. Riquet sent François Andreossy and Pierre Roux there to work on the supply, which uses the reservoirs of Lampy, Cammazes and Saint-Ferréol and channels called rigoles.

The first locks, rectangular and built on wooden stilts, collapsed, and Riquet redesigned them with thicker, rounded walls, a form later called Baroque. Construction lasted from 1666 to 1681. Riquet died in October 1680, shortly before completion, and the first inspection began on 2 May 1681. In 1686 Vauban found the canal in poor repair and ordered new work, including the Cammazes tunnel and a strengthening of the Saint-Ferréol reservoir.

At first the canal was used mainly by small sailing barges with lowered masts, hauled by gangs of men. By the middle of the 18th century horses had largely taken over, and steam tugs appeared in 1834. By 1838 273 vessels worked the canal regularly, and mail boats carried passengers. The record year for trade was 1856, with nearly 100,000 passengers.

Railways then took the traffic. In 1858 Napoleon III entrusted the canal for 40 years to the railway company Chemins de fer du Midi, which favoured its own line, and boat traffic declined. Commercial shipping ended around the late 1980s, and the canal is now used mainly by boaters and tourists. It was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996.
canary-islands: The Canary Islands are an archipelago in the Atlantic Ocean, about 100 kilometres off the northwest coast of Africa. The seven main islands, from largest to smallest by area, are Tenerife, Fuerteventura, Gran Canaria, Lanzarote, La Palma, La Gomera and El Hierro. All are volcanic in origin, and with the Azores, Cape Verde, Madeira and the Savage Isles they form the Macaronesia ecoregion. Historically the chain was called the Fortunate Isles.

The western islands, El Hierro, La Palma and La Gomera, are influenced by the moist Canary Current and carry extensive subtropical laurisilva forest, while Fuerteventura and Lanzarote, nearest to Africa, are effectively desert or semi-desert. Mount Teide on Tenerife is the highest peak in Spain.

Linguistic, genetic and archaeological analyses indicate that indigenous peoples were living on the islands at least 2,000 years ago, possibly 3,000, and shared a common origin with the Amazighs of the nearby North African coast. They may have reached the islands in several small boats, landing first on Lanzarote and Fuerteventura. They came to be known collectively as the Guanches, although that name had belonged only to the indigenous inhabitants of Tenerife.

According to a 2024 study by the University of Las Palmas de Gran Canaria, archaeological evidence shows that the Romans were the first to establish contact, between the 1st century BCE and the 1st century CE. During the Age of Sail the islands were the main stopover for Spanish galleons on the way to the Americas, which sailed that far south to catch the prevailing northeasterly trade winds.

The archipelago is the southernmost autonomous community of Spain, established in 1982. It has two provinces, Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas, created by splitting the Province of Canary Islands in 1927, and the cities of Santa Cruz de Tenerife and Las Palmas de Gran Canaria are joint capitals.

The name Islas Canarias probably derives from the Latin Canariae Insulae, meaning Islands of the Dogs, from Pliny the Elder's account of vast multitudes of very large dogs on Canaria. The canary bird takes its name from the islands. San Cristóbal de La Laguna on Tenerife is a World Heritage Site, as is Mount Teide.
canberra: Canberra lies near the Brindabella Ranges, part of the Australian Alps, about 150 km inland from Australia's east coast. Its urban area has an elevation of about 580 m, and the highest point near it is Mount Majura at 888 m. The Molonglo River was dammed to form Lake Burley Griffin, and it then flows into the Murrumbidgee. The area was a flood plain before the lake was filled.

The name derives from the Ngunnawal language of a local clan that the first British colonists called the Canberry, Kanberri or Nganbra tribe. Joshua John Moore, the first European landowner in the region, named his grant Canberry in 1823. The form Canberra began to appear around 1857. Suggested meanings include meeting place.

The first peoples of the area include the Ngunnawal and Ngambri. Archaeological evidence suggests human activity there 21,000 years ago. The Canberry or Nganbra clan lived mostly around Sullivan's Creek and had ceremonial grounds at the base of Galambary (Black Mountain), while the Pialligo clan had land around what is now Canberra Airport. The people managed the land with fire, farmed yams and hunted. Galambary was a meeting and business site, mainly for men, and an initiation site.

European settlement began in the first half of the 19th century. The federation of the Australian colonies was achieved on 1 January 1901, and the new capital was founded and formally named Canberra in 1913, as a compromise between Sydney and Melbourne. It is an entirely planned city, based on a design by the American architects Walter Burley Griffin and Marion Mahony Griffin, influenced by the garden city movement and aligned with landmarks such as Black Mountain, Mount Ainslie and Capital Hill.

Canberra is the capital of Australia and the largest population centre in the Australian Capital Territory, with an estimated 484,630 people. It is the country's largest inland city. It is the seat of the federal government, with Parliament House, Government House and the High Court, and it hosts all foreign embassies in Australia.

Among its national institutions are the Australian War Memorial, the Australian National University, established in 1946, the National Gallery, the National Museum and the National Library. The Royal Military College Duntroon is also there, and Floriade is the largest flower festival in the Southern Hemisphere.
candide: Voltaire was already a well-established author when he wrote Candide, which became a model for the contes philosophiques of the 18th and early 19th centuries, a genre that included his earlier Zadig and Micromegas. Several events lie behind it: the publication of Leibniz's Monadology, the Seven Years' War and the Lisbon earthquake of 1755, which posed a problem for the optimism founded on the theodicy of Gottfried Wilhelm Leibniz, which insisted on God's benevolence in spite of such disasters.

It is not known exactly when Voltaire wrote it. Scholars estimate that it was mainly composed in late 1758 and begun as early as 1757, in part at Les Délices near Geneva. A popular legend that he wrote it in three days probably rests on a misreading of an 1885 book. He did not openly admit his authorship until 1768, and signed it until then as Doctor Ralph.

The story has thirty short chapters. Candide, the illegitimate nephew of a baron in Westphalia, lives in the baron's castle, where the tutor Pangloss teaches that all is for the best in the best of all possible worlds. Expelled for his love of the baron's daughter Cunégonde, he is swept through war, earthquake and cruelty, first in Europe, then in the Americas, where he reaches El Dorado, and finally back to Europe and the Ottoman Empire. Many of the events are based on real happenings.

Its method is to set great tragedy against comedy, told in a matter-of-fact tone. At Portsmouth Candide sees an admiral, thought to stand for John Byng, shot for failing to engage a French fleet, merely pour encourager les autres, a phrase Voltaire is credited with originating. The book ends with Candide dismissing optimism but offering no system in its place, only the practical precept that we must cultivate our garden, and critics still dispute what that means.

Immediately after publication the work and its author were denounced by secular and religious authorities because it openly derides government and church, and it was widely banned on grounds of blasphemy and sedition. A sequel by other hands appeared in 1760. Candide is the most widely read of Voltaire's works and is listed in Harold Bloom's The Western Canon. Its parody and picaresque methods influenced later black humorists such as Joseph Heller, Thomas Pynchon and Kurt Vonnegut.
cangas-de-onis: Cangas de Onís is a municipality in the eastern part of the province and autonomous community of Asturias, in the north-west of Spain. Its Asturian name, Cangues d'Onís, is explained as the valleys of Onís. More than seventy square kilometres of the municipality form part of the Parque nacional de los Picos de Europa. Because of its range of heights it has many kinds of plants, among them mountain shrubs, heather, oak and ash, surrounded by grassland. The municipality is divided into eleven parishes, and the capital is the parish of Cangas de Onís, with 4,326 inhabitants according to the figures of 2005.

Within the national park lies the village of Covadonga, where the battle of Covadonga, about 722, was the first major victory of a Christian military force in Iberia after the Islamic conquest and is taken to mark the starting point of the Reconquista. Cangas de Onís is known as the first capital of the Kingdom of Asturias and is the site of the first church built in Iberia after the conquest, Santa Cruz de Cangas de Onís of 737, which was built on an ancient dolmen.

A parish named Cangas de Onís is attested for the 14th century, and the stone bridge over the Sella River was built in the 14th or 15th century. The town was represented in the Junta General of the principality of Asturias in 1504. Covadonga began to develop as a pilgrimage site in the 16th century, which attracted commerce, and the settlement of Cangas de Onís grew rapidly in the middle of the 19th century. It was bombarded several times in the Spanish Civil War, and it was the seat of the Regional Council in the pre-autonomous regime of 1978 to 1981, before the Statute of Autonomy of the Principality of Asturias came into force on 31 January 1982.

The main economic activities of the region are agriculture, cattle rearing and rural tourism, and the nearby Covadonga Sanctuary and its surrounding lakes are among the main tourist destinations in Asturias, within the national park.
canillo: Canillo is the name of one of the seven parishes of Andorra and of its main town. It borders France to the north and east and is the largest parish of Andorra, at 121 square kilometres. Its localities include Soldeu, El Tarter, Incles, Prats and Meritxell, and the Estany de Juclà in the Incles valley is the largest lake in Andorra. Much of the parish is still characterised by active farms.

The name of the parish is pre-Roman in origin. It is first documented in the 9th century, in the deed of consecration of the cathedral of La Seu d'Urgell, as Kanillave, and appears as Canilau in 1176. At Prats stands the sanctuary of Roc de les Bruixes, a set of rock engravings dating from the Bronze Age to the early Middle Ages. Remains of the late 7th and 8th centuries show early Christianity in Andorra. The church of Sant Joan de Caselles, Romanesque and from the end of the 11th century, holds a 12th-century Romanesque Majesty on a mural painting.

Canillo is also the site of the sanctuary of Our Lady of Meritxell. According to legend a shepherd found an image of the Virgin under flowering roses, and when he took it home it returned three times to the same place, so a chapel was built there. In 1873 she was declared patron saint of the country, and 8 September 1921 was declared the national holiday. The Romanesque sanctuary burned down in 1972, and the architect Ricardo Bofill Levi designed the new one, inaugurated in 1976.

The parish had 4,826 inhabitants in 2011 and is a tourist destination, notably for the ski resort of Soldeu-El Tarter, though farming continues. The sanctuary of Meritxell was declared a minor basilica in 2014.
cankiri: Çankırı lies about 140 kilometres north-east of Ankara, some 800 metres above sea level. Its ancient name Gangra seems to mean a goat in Paphlagonian. The earlier town stood on the hill behind the modern city, where the ruins of a late fortress remain, while the Roman city occupied the site of the present one.

Gangra seems once to have been the capital of Paphlagonia, since Strabo says that Deiotarus Philadelphus, the last king of Paphlagonia, lived there, though he also calls it only a small town and a garrison. It was absorbed into the Roman province of Galatia on the king's death in 6 or 5 BCE. It was later named Germanicopolis, after Germanicus or possibly the emperor Claudius. In Christian times it was the metropolitan see of Paphlagonia, and its bishop Hypatios, venerated as a saint in the Orthodox tradition, was killed by Arians on his return from the Council of Nicaea in 325.

In the 4th century Gangra was the scene of an important synod, whose date is disputed. Twenty-one bishops met to act against Eustathius of Sebaste and his followers, who disowned marriage and denounced riches. The synod issued twenty canons, declared ecumenical by the Council of Chalcedon in 451, and said it condemned not virginity but the dishonouring of marriage, and not poverty but disparagement of honest wealth. In 1400 and 1401 the patriarch Matthew I appointed George Kontophe metropolitan of Gangra, at the request of its people, who were threatened by the Turkomans.

Çankırı is the seat of Çankırı Province and of Çankırı District, with about 90 thousand inhabitants. Wheat, maize, beans and apples are grown in the surrounding fields, and Çankırı Karatekin University was founded there in 2007.
cannon: The word cannon derives from the Old Italian cannone, meaning large tube, from the Latin canna and the Greek kanna, reed. It has referred to a gun since 1326 in Italy and 1418 in England. The earliest known depiction of cannons may appear in Song dynasty China as early as the 12th century, but solid evidence does not appear until the 13th century. The cannon was probably a parallel development or evolution of the fire lance, a short-range weapon combining a gunpowder-filled tube and a polearm, whose paper and bamboo barrels were eventually replaced by metal.

Elsewhere the dates are less settled. There is no clear consensus on when the cannon first appeared in the Islamic world, with dates ranging from 1260 to the mid-14th century. Documentary evidence of cannons in Russia does not appear until 1382, and Ivan III established the first Russian cannon foundry in Moscow in 1475. Cannons reached the Javanese Majapahit Empire when a Mongol-Chinese army under Ike Mese invaded Java in 1293.

A cannon has the form of a truncated cone with an internal cylindrical bore that holds the charge and the projectile. The thickest and strongest part lies near the charge, which is ignited through a thin tube called the vent. The main body is divided into the chase, the reinforce and the cascabel, and a cannon's calibre is determined by the diameter of its bore. By the 16th century cannons were made in great variety, and the general rule was that the longer the barrel, the longer the range.

Cannons were used primarily as anti-infantry weapons until around 1374, when large cannons were recorded breaching walls for the first time in Europe. In 1464 the Ottoman Empire cast the Great Turkish Bombard, which weighed 16,000 kilograms.
