Larger guns forced engineers to build stronger castle walls, and in India the fort of Raicher had gun ports built into its walls for defensive cannons. Field artillery became more important after the introduction of the limber, which greatly improved mobility.

In the 1770s a cannon was manned by two gunners, six soldiers and four officers of artillery. The bore was cleaned with a wet sponge, powder was added, then wadding and the ball, which was rammed down; at 45 degrees the ball had its utmost range. Decoys also had a use: the Quaker gun, a painted log, was used by Colonel William Washington's Continental Army in 1780, when about 100 Loyalists surrendered rather than face bombardment.
cantar-de-mio-cid: The poem is anonymous and survives in a 14th-century codex in the Spanish National Library in Madrid, which lacks its first page and two others in the middle. A colophon names Per Abbad, in English Abbot Peter, and puts the date 1207 after his name. Current thinking is that this claim was simply copied with the text of an earlier manuscript now lost. Ramón Menéndez Pidal counted the work among the poems passed down and varied by minstrels, while others believe a single learned author wrote it. Date and authorship remain open to debate.

The original title is unknown, and the present one was proposed by Menéndez Pidal. Cid comes from the Arabic sidi or sayyid, a title like Sir. The poem has been translated into English many times since 1879, among others by John Ormsby, W. S. Merwin and Burton Raffel.

Since 1913 the poem, of more than 3,700 verses, has been divided into three parts. In the first, enemies accuse Rodrigo Díaz of keeping tribute owed to King Alfonso VI, who exiles him from Castile and León. He leaves his wife, Doña Ximena, and his daughters, Doña Elvira and Doña Sol, at the monastery of Cardeña and grows rich from raids on Moorish territory. In the second he takes Valencia and defeats the Almoravid king Chufa ibn Tashfin, and the king pardons him and allows his daughters to marry the infantes of Carrión.

In the third part the infantes show cowardice, fleeing a lion in the court and a campaign against the Moors. In revenge they beat their wives and leave them tied to trees at Corpes. The Cid asks the court of Toledo for justice, his men defeat the infantes in a duel, and his daughters marry the heirs of Navarre and Aragon. The tone is realist, with no magic: the archangel Gabriel appears only in a dream.

The poem is the oldest preserved Castilian epic and is considered a national epic of Spain. It departs from history: it does not mention the Cid's son, and his daughters were not called Elvira and Sol. It echoes the plot devices of the Song of Roland.
canterbury: Canterbury lies on the River Stour, not far from its mouth on the Strait of Dover, in east Kent. The site has been occupied since prehistoric times. The Roman name Durovernum Cantiacorum means Durovernum of the Cantiaci, and replaced an earlier British name reconstructed as Durouernon, meaning stronghold by the alder grove. In Sub-Roman Britain it was Cair Ceint, the stronghold of Kent, and the Jutes who occupied it called it Cantwareburh in Old English.

Canterbury was first recorded as the main settlement of the Cantiaci. In the 1st century CE the Romans captured it and rebuilt it with a grid of streets, a theatre, a temple, a forum and public baths. They kept no major garrison, but its position on Watling Street, in relation to the ports of Richborough, Dover and Lymne, gave it strategic importance. In the late 3rd century they built an earth bank and a wall with seven gates round it. It later served as capital of the Jute kingdom of Kent.

A large Viking army besieged Canterbury in 1011, and the city was pillaged. Remembering the destruction caused by the Danes, its inhabitants did not resist William the Conqueror in 1066, and William ordered a wooden castle built beside the Roman wall, rebuilt in stone in the early 12th century. In the mid-16th century Canterbury hosted the first congregation of Huguenot refugees in England, founded around 1548 and scattered in 1553–4 under Mary I. In 1647, during the English Civil War, the Plum Pudding Riots broke out, and the trial of the rioters led to a Kentish revolt.

Canterbury is a World Heritage Site and its cathedral is the seat of the Archbishop of Canterbury. Its surviving past includes a city wall founded in Roman times and rebuilt in the 14th century, the Westgate Towers, the ruins of St Augustine's Abbey and the Norman castle. The Canterbury and Whitstable Railway, which ran from 1830 to 1953, was the first regular passenger steam railway in the world. The city's economy rests on tourism, higher education and retail.
canusium: Canusium, the modern Canosa, lies on the right bank of the Ofanto river, the ancient Aufidus, nearly 20 kilometres from the Adriatic Sea. The town stands on the edge of the Murgia plateau at between 105 and 140 metres above sea level. Its soil is sand or clay over a layer of soft limestone tuff, which is easily excavated. This allowed the digging of underground grottoes and a hypogeum, and the stone taken out of them went into buildings above ground.

The ancient Greeks and Romans ascribed the foundation of the town to the Homeric hero Diomedes. Archaeologists place human presence in the area as far back as the 7th millennium BCE. The surrounding fields were one of the main centres of the Dauni, a northern branch of the Iapyges, and buildings and tombs at Toppicelli point to a wealthy aristocracy. The town became an important commercial centre for craftsmen, above all of ceramics and pottery, and is thought to have become a Greek polis in the age of Magna Grecia.

After Hannibal defeated the consuls Paullus and Varro at Cannae in 216 BCE, Canusium sheltered the fleeing remnants of the Roman army within its walls. In the second year of the Social War it joined the rebels and resisted a Roman siege. It suffered heavily in that conflict or in the civil wars that followed, but became a self-governing municipium in 88 BCE. Some of its bishops are known from the 4th century, and it came to be called the city of bishops. Bishop Stercorius attended the Council of Sardica in 343, and the diocese reached its height under Saint Sabinus (514 to 566), later the town's patron saint.

Earthquakes damaged the town repeatedly, notably in 1361, 1456, 1627, 1659, 1694 and 1851. It was sacked by the Tarantini in 1451 and by Napoleon in 1803. As a fief it passed through several families, and Tiberio Capece was named prince of Canosa in 1712.

Canosa di Puglia is a town and comune in the province of Barletta-Andria-Trani in Apulia, between Bari and Foggia, and is counted among the oldest continually inhabited cities in Italy. Its Cathedral of San Sabino was founded in the 8th century by Duke Arechis II of Benevento and was named after Sabinus in 1101. Bohemond I of Antioch, a commander of the First Crusade, is buried in its mausoleum. The so-called castle is the acropolis of the ancient town, and the remains of a Roman amphitheatre lie at its southern foot. The archaeological museum, founded in 1934, holds about 2,000 finds from the tombs and the town.
cao-cao: Cao Cao, courtesy name Mengde, came from Qiao County in Pei State, in present-day Bozhou, Anhui. His father, Cao Song, bought his way into the office of Grand Commandant under Emperor Ling and served less than half a year; Cao Song was the foster son of the eunuch Cao Teng. Nominated as a xiaolian around the age of 19, Cao Cao became Commandant of the North District of Luoyang and later Chancellor of Jinan State, where he proposed dismissing about 80 percent of its officials for corruption.

In 189 Cao Cao spent his family fortune on an army to oppose Dong Zhuo, and between 191 and 192 Yuan Shao made him Administrator of Dong Commandery, which marks the start of his career as a warlord. His attacks on Tao Qian in Xu Province followed the murder of his father there, and he massacred thousands of civilians. In 196, on the advice of Xun Yu and Cheng Yu, he received Emperor Xian, who had escaped his captors, and set up the capital at Xuchang. The emperor and government came under his control, though he kept up nominal allegiance.

After defeating Yuan Shao at the Battle of Guandu in 200, he spent seven years defeating Yuan Shao's sons and allies and brought much of northern China under his rule. In 208 he marched south but was defeated at the Battle of Red Cliffs by Sun Quan and Liu Bei, when disease had also broken out in his army. Emperor Xian made him Duke of Wei in 213 and King of Wei in June 216, with privileges once reserved for emperors.

Cao Cao died in Luoyang on 15 March 220. In November 220 his son Cao Pi accepted the abdication of Emperor Xian and founded the state of Cao Wei, an event commonly seen as a usurpation, and gave his father the title Emperor Wu. Opinion of Cao Cao has been divided since the Jin dynasty: some praise his poetry and career, others condemn his cruelty and alleged treachery. Traditional Chinese culture stereotypically shows him as a sly tyrant opposed to Liu Bei, a portrait shaped by the 14th-century novel Romance of the Three Kingdoms.
cape-coast: Cape Coast lies on the Gulf of Guinea, about 130 km from Accra. Its traditional name is Oguaa, from the Guan Awutu word gua, meaning market. Early Portuguese navigators called it Cabo Corso, short cape, which the British later corrupted to Cape Coast. It became the principal town of the Fetu Kingdom, an old Guan kingdom whose paramount seat lay about 16 km to the north. A market called Ogua grew into an active commercial centre, and the King of Fetu appointed a chief to represent it.

The English navigator William Towerson, the first documented English visitor to reach the Guinea coast, landed in 1555. Around 1650 Hendrik Carloff bought a plot from the King of Fetu for Dutch privateers working against the Dutch West India Company. The fort built on the site of Carolusborg changed hands several times before 1664, when a joint English and Dutch force captured it from the Dutch. The Danes built Fort Frederiksborg on a hill plot, which the English later bought.

The Asante invaded the coast in 1806. Cape Coast escaped the attack, but the townspeople's confidence in British protection fell. The town had been largely burnt down in 1817. It was the most important anchorage on the coast until Sekondi Harbour was built in the 1890s. Cape Coast was capital of the Gold Coast from 1821 until 1877, when the seat moved to Accra, which badly damaged its economy.

Cape Coast is the capital of the Central Region of Ghana. Its 2010 census population was 108,374, mostly Fante. Cape Coast Castle is a World Heritage Site. The University of Cape Coast, established in 1962, helped make it an educational centre. The main festival is Fetu Afahye, held on the first Saturday of September.
cape-cod: Cape Cod extends into the Atlantic Ocean from the south-eastern corner of Massachusetts and is coextensive with Barnstable County, running from Provincetown in the north-east to Woods Hole in the south-west. It is divided into fifteen towns. Most of the land consists of glacial landforms, terminal moraine and outwash plains, which mark the southernmost extent of glacial coverage in south-eastern New England. Geologically it is young, laid down some 16,000 to 20,000 years ago. Since 1914 the Cape Cod Canal has separated most of the peninsula from the mainland.

The Wampanoag have lived on Cape Cod for centuries. They lived from the sea, farmed, and lit controlled fires to keep the underbrush in check. They helped the Pilgrims, who arrived in the fall of 1620, to survive at Plymouth Colony, and later gradually lost their lands through cessions and violent conflict with settlers. The Wampanoag tribe was federally recognized in May 2007.

Bartholomew Gosnold coined the name Cape Cod in 1602, and it is the ninth-oldest English place-name in the United States. It applied at first only to the tip of the peninsula. The Cape was among the first places settled by Puritan colonists, with Sandwich founded in 1637 and Barnstable and Yarmouth in 1639. The canal was developed from 1870 to 1914. Lighthouses were built from 1797, and from the end of the 19th century improved rail transport made the Cape a summer haven for city dwellers from Boston.

Cape Cod has a year-round population of about 220,000 and a tourist season in the warmer months. Henry David Thoreau wrote about his 1849 travels there in Cape Cod, published in 1865, and Henry Beston's The Outermost House of 1928 describes a year spent in a cottage in Eastham.
cape-horn: Cape Horn lies on Hornos Island in the Hermite Islands group, at the southern end of the Tierra del Fuego archipelago in southern Chile, at about 56 degrees south. It is not the most southerly point of South America, which is Águila Islet, but it marks the northern boundary of the Drake Passage, the strait between South America and Antarctica, and the place where the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans meet. The cape lies in Chilean territorial waters, within Cabo de Hornos National Park, and the Chilean Navy maintains a station on the island with a residence, chapel and lighthouse.

The Dutchmen Willem Schouten and Jacob Le Maire first rounded the cape in 1616 and named it Kaap Hoorn after the city of Hoorn in the Netherlands. The Strait of Magellan, between the mainland and Tierra del Fuego, had been used for trade well before the Horn was discovered, but is narrow, and for decades Cape Horn was a major milestone on the clipper route by which sailing ships carried trade around the world. The need to round it was greatly reduced by the opening of the Panama Canal in August 1914.

The passage is regarded as perhaps the most dangerous ship route in the world, and many ships have been wrecked and many sailors have died attempting it. Winds in these latitudes blow from west to east almost uninterrupted by land, and the Andes and the Antarctic Peninsula funnel them into the narrow Drake Passage. The waves become shorter and steeper over the shallow water south of the Horn, and rogue waves of up to 30 metres are reported west of it. Icebergs are a further hazard. Passage from east to west, against the winds and currents, was a particular problem for traditional sailing ships.

There are no regular commercial routes around the Horn, although cruise ships and vessels bound for the Antarctic Peninsula pass it. Rounding the Horn remains one of the major challenges in yachting. A memorial near the station, a sculpture by José Balcells of the silhouette of an albatross, was erected in 1992 in remembrance of the sailors who died attempting to round the Horn. The cape belongs to the commune of Cabo de Hornos, whose capital is Puerto Williams.
cape-of-good-hope: The Cape of Good Hope is a rocky headland on the Atlantic coast of the Cape Peninsula in South Africa, about 2.3 kilometres west and a little north of Cape Point. It is a common misconception that it is the southern tip of Africa; the southernmost point is Cape Agulhas, about 150 kilometres to the east-southeast. Following the western African coastline from the equator, however, the Cape of Good Hope marks the point where a ship begins to travel more eastward than southward. Cape Town lies about 50 kilometres to the north, in Table Bay.

Herodotus records that around 600 BCE Necho II reputedly commissioned Phoenicians to sail from the Red Sea around Africa to the mouth of the Nile, which would be the first completion of the Cape Route. The account came to him by oral tradition. Eudoxus of Cyzicus, a Greek navigator for Ptolemy VIII, found in about 116 BCE the wreck of a ship that appeared to have come from Gades, and concluded that it had sailed round Africa; his own later attempt failed and his fate is unknown. The Fra Mauro map of 1450 depicts the Indian Ocean as connected to the Atlantic and records a voyage by an Indian junk around 1420.

The first European to reach the cape was the Portuguese explorer Bartolomeu Dias, who named it the Cape of Storms, Cabo das Tormentas. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope because of the optimism the opening of a sea route to India and the East engendered. The Khoikhoi lived in the area when the Dutch first settled in 1652. On 6 April of that year Jan van Riebeeck established a resupply camp for the Dutch East India Company in Table Bay, which developed into Cape Town and became known as the Tavern of the Seas. On 31 December 1687 a community of Huguenots arrived from the Netherlands, since the Company needed skilled farmers.

British troops occupied the Cape Colony in 1795, after the Dutch Republic was occupied by France, and again on 19 January 1806 following the Battle of Blaauwberg. The colony existed from 1795 to 1802 and again from 1806 to 1910. Today the cape is a section of Table Mountain National Park, with fynbos vegetation that belongs to the Cape Floristic Kingdom, and at least 250 bird species, including a mainland colony of African penguins. In legend it is the home of the Flying Dutchman, and the poet Luís de Camões invented the giant Adamastor in Os Lusíadas, first printed in 1572, as a symbol of the dangers of rounding the Cape of Storms.
cape-town: Cape Town stands on the shore of Table Bay, at a latitude of about 33.55 degrees south. Table Mountain, with near vertical cliffs and a flat summit more than 1,000 metres high, forms a mountainous backdrop with Devil's Peak and Lion's Head on either side and creates the City Bowl, which holds the central business district. To the south the Cape Peninsula runs 40 kilometres into the Atlantic Ocean and ends at Cape Point, and many suburbs lie on the Cape Flats, a plain that joins the peninsula to the mainland. Robben Island in Table Bay is part of the city, and Table Mountain National Park lies within its boundaries.

The earliest known remains of human occupation in the region were found at Peers Cave in Fish Hoek in the late 1920s; earlier estimates of an upper Pleistocene origin have since been revised to the mid-Holocene. Bartolomeu Dias, the first European to reach the area, arrived in 1488 and named it the Cape of Storms. John II of Portugal renamed it the Cape of Good Hope, because the opening of a sea route to India raised such optimism, and Vasco da Gama recorded sighting it in 1497. In 1510, at the Battle of Salt River, the Portuguese admiral Francisco de Almeida and sixty-four of his men were killed by the Khoikhoi Goringhaiqua, who used cattle trained to respond to whistles and shouts.

Ships of several nations, mainly Portuguese, regularly stopped in Table Bay in the late sixteenth century on the way to the Indies. They traded tobacco, copper and iron with the Khoikhoi clans of the region for fresh meat and other provisions. In 1652 Jan van Riebeeck and other employees of the United East India Company were sent to establish a way-station for ships travelling to the Dutch East Indies, and they built the Fort de Goede Hoop, later replaced by the Castle of Good Hope.

The settlement grew slowly because adequate labour was hard to find. The shortage led the local authorities to import enslaved people from Indonesia and Madagascar, many of whom are ancestors of the present Cape Coloured and Cape Malay communities.

Cape Town is the legislative capital of South Africa, the seat of its Parliament, and the capital of the Western Cape. It is the country's oldest city. It has the highest density of Cape Dutch buildings in the world, a style that combines the architectural traditions of the Netherlands, Germany, France and Indonesia. Mostert's Mill in Mowbray, built in 1796, is the only complete windmill in South Africa. The Cape Floristic Region, including Kirstenbosch National Botanical Garden, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004.
cape-verde: Cape Verde is a horseshoe-shaped cluster of ten volcanic islands, nine of them inhabited, and eight islets, with a land area of about 4,033 square kilometres. They lie between 600 and 850 km west of Cap-Vert on the Senegalese coast, from which the country takes its name. Cap-Vert comes from the Portuguese Cabo Verde, meaning green cape, a name Portuguese explorers gave to the headland in 1444. The islands are divided into the Barlavento or windward group in the north and the Sotavento or leeward group in the south. Santiago is the largest and holds the capital, Praia.

The islands were uninhabited before the arrival of Europeans. Genoese and Portuguese navigators found them around 1456. Portuguese records credit the first discoveries to António de Noli, born in Genoa, who was later appointed governor by King Afonso V. In 1462 Portuguese settlers founded Ribeira Grande on Santiago, today called Cidade Velha, the first permanent European settlement in the tropics.

In the 16th century the islands prospered from the Atlantic slave trade. The English privateer Francis Drake sacked Ribeira Grande twice in 1585, when it was part of the Iberian Union, and after a French attack in 1712 the town declined relative to Praia, which became the capital in 1770. The decline of the slave trade in the 19th century brought economic crisis, but the islands' position on mid-Atlantic shipping lanes made them a good place to resupply ships, and the harbour of Mindelo grew into a commercial centre. In 1951 Portugal changed the status of Cape Verde from a colony to an overseas province in an attempt to blunt nationalism. The country became independent in 1975.

Cape Verde is a unitary semi-presidential republic whose constitution was adopted in 1980 and revised in 1992, 1995 and 1999. Praia is the capital and largest city. Portuguese is the official language, and Cape Verdean Creole, called Kriolu, is the mother tongue of virtually all Cape Verdeans. The people descend from Africans, free or enslaved, and Europeans of various origins, and the diaspora outnumbers the people on the islands.
capetian-dynasty: The Capetian dynasty, also called the House of France, is of Frankish origin. Agnatically it is a branch of the Robertians, and it descends from the Carolingians through female lines. It takes its name from its founder, Hugh Capet, whose nickname Capet has an unknown meaning; one suggestion links it to the Latin caput, head. Nineteenth-century historians applied the name to the ruling house of France and to all the male-line descendants of Hugh; it was not a contemporary practice. In 987 Hugh Capet was elected to succeed Louis V, the last of the Carolingian dynasty that had ruled France for over three centuries.

The Capetian monarchy began as one of the weakest in Europe, its direct rule confined to the Île-de-France. The early Capetians associated their elder sons with them in the kingship, which established hereditary succession and turned a theoretically elective kingship into a sacral one. By the reign of Philip II Augustus, who became king in 1180, the hold was so strong that the practice was dropped. The kings extended their power slowly while the great peers of the realm lost theirs in succession crises. The senior line ruled until the death of Charles IV in 1328.

Charles IV died without male heirs, and the French lords, who rejected the claim of Edward III of England through his mother Isabella, made Philip of Valois king. From then on the succession excluded females and claims through the female line, a rule known as Salic law. The crown passed to the House of Valois and then to the House of Bourbon. The Revolution abolished the monarchy in 1792 and Louis XVI was executed in 1793. The Bourbons returned in 1814 and left the throne in 1830 for Louis Philippe I of the House of Orléans, the last Capetian king of France, who reigned until 1848.

By tradition, younger sons and brothers of the king received appanages to maintain their rank and discourage them from claiming the crown. Capetian cadets therefore aimed at foreign thrones, and the family has reigned in Portugal, Sicily and Naples, Navarre, Hungary, Poland, Spain and Sardinia, in the grand duchies of Lithuania and Luxembourg, and in the Latin and Brazilian empires. Cadet branches of the House of Bourbon still reign in Spain and Luxembourg.
capitalism: Capitalism in its modern form is traced to agrarian capitalism and mercantilism in the early Renaissance, in city-states such as Florence. Capital had existed on a small scale for centuries in merchant, renting and lending activities. During the Islamic Golden Age, Arabs promulgated policies such as free trade and banking, and their use of Indo-Arabic numerals facilitated bookkeeping; these innovations reached Europe through Venice and Pisa.

In 16th-century England the manorial system broke down, land became concentrated in fewer landlords and workers were increasingly employed in a money-based economy instead of as serfs. From the 16th to the 18th centuries mercantilism prevailed, a system of trade for profit, though goods were still largely produced by non-capitalist methods. Most scholars see it as the origin of the modern system, but Karl Polanyi held that capitalism required generalised markets for land, labour and money, and so could not be said to exist before 1834, when a competitive labour market was established in England.

Capitalism is an economic system based on private ownership of the means of production and its use to obtain profit. Its elements include private property, the profit motive, capital accumulation, competitive markets and wage labour. Its forms, among them laissez-faire, state and welfare capitalism, differ in their degree of free markets, public ownership and regulation. There is no universally agreed definition.

The term capitalist, meaning an owner of capital, dates to the mid-17th century. Louis Blanc in 1850 and Pierre-Joseph Proudhon in 1861 are credited with the first modern use of capitalism, and Karl Marx wrote of the capitalist mode of production in Das Kapital (1867). Because socialist critics coined the word, Robert Hessen called it a term of disparagement.

The Industrial Revolution of the 18th century made capitalism the dominant mode of production, characterised by factory work and a complex division of labour. It spread across the world in the 19th and 20th centuries. In the 19th century it was largely unregulated; after World War II it became more regulated through Keynesianism, followed from the 1980s by a return of less regulated capitalism termed neoliberalism.
capitoline-hill: The Capitoline Hill lies between the Forum and the Campus Martius. It was earlier known as Mons Saturnius, after the god Saturn. The word Capitolium first meant the Temple of Jupiter Optimus Maximus and then came to cover the whole hill. Ancient sources connected the name with caput, Latin for head, through a tale that a man's head was found when the temple's foundations were laid. The Romans regarded the Capitolium as indestructible and adopted it as a symbol of eternity. On its eastern lower slopes stood the Vulcanal, a sacred precinct of the 8th century BCE.

The temple of the Capitoline Triad was started by Rome's fifth king, Tarquinius Priscus, and completed by the last, Tarquinius Superbus. It was nearly as large as the Parthenon. Temples of Juno Moneta and of Virtus also stood on the hill. When the Senones Gauls raided Rome in 390 BCE, the Capitoline was the one part of the city they did not take, because its defenders had fortified it. According to legend, the sacred geese of Juno warned Marcus Manlius Capitolinus of the attack. In the Year of Four Emperors, 69 CE, Vespasian's brother and nephew were besieged in the temple, and it burned down.

In the Middle Ages the hill's religious role was overshadowed by its use as the seat of Rome's civic government, revived as a commune in the 12th century. After a revolt against the pope and the nobles in 1144, a senator took up residence there. His palace turned its back on the ancient Forum, a change of orientation that Michelangelo later accentuated. Pope Paul III commissioned Michelangelo Buonarroti in 1536 to redesign the piazza, partly to impress Emperor Charles V, who was expected in 1538. The work ran from 1536 to 1546, and the Campidoglio was completed in the 17th century. Michelangelo faced the new piazza towards St. Peter's Basilica, and the paving design was finished only in 1940, on the order of Benito Mussolini.

The Palazzo dei Conservatori, the Palazzo Nuovo and the Palazzo Senatorio enclose the trapezoidal Piazza del Campidoglio, which is approached by the wide ramped stair called the cordonata. The first two palazzi, with the Palazzo Senatorio, now house the Capitoline Museums, and the Palazzo Senatorio is also the Roman city hall. The equestrian statue of Marcus Aurelius in the piazza is a modern copy; the original is in the Palazzo dei Conservatori. The church of Santa Maria in Aracoeli stands beside the square, and the English word capitol derives from Capitolium.
caracalla: Caracalla was born Lucius Septimius Bassianus at Lugdunum in Gaul, the elder son of Septimius Severus and Julia Domna. At seven he was renamed Marcus Aurelius Antoninus as part of his father's attempt at union with the families of Antoninus Pius and Marcus Aurelius.

His father, acclaimed Augustus in 193, had himself adopted posthumously by Marcus Aurelius, and Caracalla was made Caesar in 195 or 196. On 28 January 198, aged nine, he became joint Augustus, on the day of his father's triumph over the Parthian Empire, and in 202 he was consul with his father.

Severus died at Eboracum on 4 February 211 while on campaign in Caledonia, leaving Caracalla and his brother Geta as joint rulers. On 26 December 211, at a reconciliation meeting arranged by their mother, Geta was killed by Praetorian Guards loyal to Caracalla, and it is widely accepted that Caracalla ordered it. He persecuted Geta's supporters, and the Senate pronounced a damnatio memoriae on Geta, whose name it became a capital offence to speak or write; an estimated 20,000 people were massacred. Julia Domna took on more of the government, since Caracalla found administration mundane.

In 212 he issued the Constitutio Antoniniana, granting full Roman citizenship to all free inhabitants of the empire except the dediticii. In 213 he left Rome, never to return, and campaigned against the Alamanni on the German frontier, defeating some tribes and settling others by diplomacy. In December 215 he slaughtered a deputation of leading citizens at Alexandria after the city mocked his claim to have killed Geta in self-defence, and set his troops loose on the city for several days of looting.
He raised the annual pay of a legionary from 2,000 sesterces to 2,700 to 3,000, and the cost led him to debase the coinage. In 215 he introduced the antoninianus, intended as a double denarius.

In 216 Caracalla began a campaign against the Parthians after King Artabanus IV refused a marriage proposal. On 8 April 217, travelling from Edessa to Carrhae to visit a temple of the moon god Sin, he was stabbed by a Roman soldier, Justin Martialis, and the two Praetorian tribunes completed the killing. Macrinus succeeded him three days later, and had him deified.

Cassius Dio, Herodian and the Historia Augusta portray him as a cruel tyrant and a soldier first and an emperor second, a view that has largely persisted. The Constitutio Antoniniana goes almost unnoticed in the classical records. In the late 18th century French painters revived his image, as the tyranny ascribed to him seemed to parallel that ascribed to Louis XVI.
caracas: Caracas lies along the Guaire River in the Caracas Valley of the Venezuelan Central Range, a small and irregular valley close to the Caribbean Sea. A steep range, Cerro El Ávila, rises 2,200 metres between the valley and the shore, and about 15 kilometres of El Ávila National Park separate the city from the coast. The valley floor lies between 870 and 1,043 metres above sea level, and the historic centre stands at about 900 metres. The highest point of the Capital District, Pico El Ávila, reaches 2,159 metres.

The Guaire crosses the city and empties into the Tuy River. The city is occasionally struck by earthquakes, notably in 1641, 1812 and 1967. The region was formed in the Late Cretaceous, and the city sits mostly on metamorphic rock.

Before the city was founded in 1567, the valley was populated by indigenous peoples. Francisco Fajardo, the son of a Spanish captain and a Waikeri cacique, began establishing settlements around La Guaira and the Caracas valley between 1555 and 1560. His plantation of 1562 did not last, as natives of the region led by Terepaima and Guaicaipuro destroyed it, as they had destroyed the Villa de San Francisco founded by Juan Rodríguez de Suárez in 1561.

The settlers who eventually founded Caracas came from Coro, the capital of the German colony of Klein-Venedig, which Spaniards had controlled in practice from the 1540s. Moving eastward, they founded inland towns including Barquisimeto and Valencia before reaching the valley. In 1591 Simón de Bolívar, an ancestor of the liberator Simón Bolívar, petitioned King Philip II for a coat of arms. The king granted it by Royal Cedula on 4 September 1591 and declared Caracas The Most Noble and Very Loyal City of Santiago de León de Caracas.

Caracas is the capital and largest city of Venezuela and the centre of a metropolitan region estimated at over 5 million people. Its historic centre is the Caracas Cathedral on Bolívar Square. The Central University of Venezuela, founded in 1721, is the oldest university in the country, and its campus, designed by the architect Carlos Raúl Villanueva, was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2000.

In the 1940s and 1950s, after the Second World War, a wave of European immigrants, mainly Spanish, Italian and Portuguese, settled in the country, and the city has been shaped by many ethnic and cultural groups. The Caracas Metro has operated since 27 March 1983.
caravanserai: The word caravanserai is Persian, combining karvan, a group of traders, pilgrims and travellers, with sarai, a building with enclosed courts. Depending on region and period such buildings were also called khan, funduq and wikala. Rural staging posts are ancient: an early forerunner appears at an Urartian site of the 8th or 9th century BCE in western Iran, and Herodotus reports royal stations and excellent caravanserais along the Royal Road of the Achaemenid Empire. In the Islamic period their use grew, linked to a shift from wheeled vehicles to camels and caravans for long-distance travel. The oldest identified Islamic example is a courtyard structure at Qasr al-Hayr al-Sharqi, an Umayyad complex of the early 8th century in the Syrian desert.

A caravanserai was typically a square or rectangular building with a single entrance wide enough for laden camels. Its central courtyard, open to the sky, was surrounded by identical stalls and chambers for merchants, their animals and merchandise. A fountain or well supplied water, and many had a small mosque, shops, fodder and sometimes a hammam. Rural examples stood about a day's journey apart, which in Iran meant 30 to 40 km in open country and about 10 km or less in mountains. Seljuk examples in Iran and Central Asia were of brick with decorated façades, while those of Anatolia were of stone with tall carved portals.

Rural caravanserais let merchants and travellers rest safely along the way. Urban ones, concentrated near the main bazaars of cities such as Damascus, Aleppo, Cairo and Istanbul, lodged merchants, especially foreign ones, stored their goods and served as places to do business. The oldest surviving urban example is the Khan al-Mirjan in Baghdad, from 1359. Many earned revenue for charitable or religious buildings through a waqf, an endowment guaranteed under Islamic law. Under the Safavids their number grew to encourage trade with India, especially under Shah Abbas I, who ruled from 1587 to 1629, and in the Indian subcontinent they stood along the Grand Trunk Road.
caravel: The caravel developed from small, single-masted fishing vessels used in the thirteenth century along the coasts of Galicia, Portugal and Atlantic Andalusia. Mediterranean trade carried lateen rigging westward through the Strait of Gibraltar, and shipwrights there adapted it to small, shallow-draft open boats built for the swells and river mouths of the Atlantic coast. These boats first weighed less than 20 tons and had a crew of five, but grew larger through the fourteenth century, and records of 1307 note caravels of up to 30 tons in Biscay. By the early fifteenth century decked versions were widely used across the Iberian Peninsula.

In the mid to late fifteenth century Prince Henry the Navigator of Portugal wanted better ships to explore the Atlantic and the African coast. At Sagres he brought together experts in mapmaking, navigation, astronomy and ship design. The caravel could sail in difficult winds and open ocean, and was easier to steer than the square-rigged barca. It became the main vessel of Portuguese explorers such as Diogo Cão and Bartolomeu Dias, and of Christopher Columbus's expedition of 1492, in which the Pinta and Niña were caravels and the Santa María a small carrack.

Fifteenth-century caravels averaged 12 to 18 m in length and carried 50 to 60 tons, which made them fast and manoeuvrable but limited their cargo. Columbus re-rigged the Niña with square sails for the Atlantic crossing. Towards the end of the 15th century the Portuguese developed a larger round caravel with a square-rigged foremast, used as an escort on the routes to Brazil and round the Cape.

Caravels found new trade routes, but their small size made them poor cargo ships, and on commercial routes the much larger carrack replaced them. After the colonisation of the Americas the galleon replaced them as well, being stronger and able to carry more. The caravel remains a poorly understood type, since few wrecks have been investigated that are likely to be caravels.
carcassonne: Carcassonne lies in the plain of the Aude, about 80 kilometres east of Toulouse, between the historic trade routes linking the Atlantic to the Mediterranean Sea and the Massif Central to the Pyrénées. Settlement there dates to about 3500 BCE. The hill site of Carsac, a Celtic place-name, became an important trading place in the 6th century BCE, when the Volcae Tectosages fortified it as an oppidum. The popular story of a lady named Carcas and the ringing of bells is a modern reconstruction of a 16th-century depiction.

The Romans fortified the hilltop around 100 BCE and made it a colonia; the lower courses of the northern ramparts date from Gallo-Roman times. In 462 the Romans officially ceded Septimania to the Visigothic king Theodoric II, who had held Carcassonne since 453. The first count known by name is Bello, of the time of Charlemagne, who founded the Bellonid dynasty. In 1067 the county passed to Raimond-Bernard Trencavel through his marriage with Ermengard, sister of the last count.

In August 1209 the crusading army of the Papal Legate, the abbot Arnaud Amalric, besieged the city, a stronghold of Occitan Cathars. Viscount Raymond-Roger de Trencavel was imprisoned while negotiating its surrender and died in mysterious circumstances three months later. The people were allowed to leave with nothing but the shirts on their backs, and Simon de Montfort became the new viscount and added to the fortifications. The city submitted to France in 1247 and became a border fortress against the Crown of Aragon under the 1258 Treaty of Corbeil. Edward the Black Prince failed to take it in 1355, though his troops destroyed the lower town.

The Treaty of the Pyrenees of 1659 moved the border away and reduced Carcassonne's military importance. A decree of 1849 ordered the decayed fortress demolished, but a campaign led by the mayor Jean-Pierre Cros-Mayrevieille and the writer Prosper Mérimée saved it, and Eugène Viollet-le-Duc restored it from 1853 until his death in 1879. His slate roofs and pointed tips, more typical of northern France, were criticised in his lifetime. The citadel was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 1997, and Carcassonne is the prefecture of the Aude.
cardiff: Cardiff is the county town of the historic county of Glamorgan. The centre of the city is relatively flat and bounded by hills to the east, north and west, and the River Taff flows past Cardiff Castle. The highest point in the local authority area is Garth Hill, at 307 m. The position, with easy access to the coalfields of the South Wales Valleys, influenced the city's development as the world's largest coal port. The Welsh name, Caerdydd, derives from Middle Welsh Caerdyf, meaning the fort of the Taff, the fort probably being the one the Romans established.

People had settled in the area by about 6000 BCE, in the early Neolithic, and burial chambers such as Tinkinswood and St Lythans lie a few miles to the west. Four Iron Age hill forts and enclosures have been identified within the county boundary, among them Caerau Hillfort, which encloses 5.1 hectares. Cardiff Castle has stood at the heart of the city since the Norman period, within the walls of the old Roman fort. Welsh was the majority language from the 13th century until the Victorian growth of the city; as late as 1850, five of the twelve Anglican churches within the present boundaries held services only in Welsh.

In 1536 the Laws in Wales Acts made Glamorganshire and Cardiff its county town, and in 1538 Henry VIII closed the Dominican and Franciscan friaries. John Crichton-Stuart, 2nd Marquess of Bute, born in 1793, spent his life building the Cardiff docks and was later called the creator of modern Cardiff. A boat service to Bristol opened in 1815. Dic Penderyn was tried and hanged in 1831, after unrest that followed the Napoleonic Wars. Cardiff became a county borough on 1 April 1889, with more than 123,000 people.

Edward VII granted Cardiff city status on 28 October 1905, and in 1955 it was proclaimed capital of Wales. National institutions followed, including the National Museum of Wales and the Welsh National War Memorial, though the National Library of Wales went elsewhere, partly because its founder, Sir John Williams, thought Cardiff had a non-Welsh population. Since 1922 the city has included Llandaff, with its cathedral. The Senedd, the Welsh Parliament, has sat in Cardiff Bay since 1999, when it was founded as the National Assembly for Wales, and its building opened on 1 March 2006. The 2021 census counted 362,400 people in the city.
cardinal-richelieu: Armand du Plessis was born in Paris on 9 September 1585, the fourth of five children, and was delicate from childhood. His family belonged to the lesser nobility of Poitou; his father, François du Plessis, seigneur de Richelieu, was a soldier and courtier who died of fever in the French Wars of Religion when Armand was five. In 1606 Henry IV nominated him to the Bishopric of Luçon, which the family held. Since he was below the canonical minimum age, he travelled to Rome for a dispensation from Pope Paul V and was consecrated bishop in April 1607. On his return he was heralded as a reformer and became the first bishop in France to implement the reforms of the Council of Trent.

In 1614 Richelieu represented the clergy of Poitou at the Estates-General. He rose by serving the queen mother Marie de' Medici's favourite, Concino Concini, and in 1616 was made Secretary of State with responsibility for foreign affairs. He became a cardinal in 1622 and Louis XIII's principal minister in 1624. His policy had two aims: to centralize power in France and to oppose the Habsburg dynasty, which ruled in Austria and Spain. In 1626 he abolished the position of Constable of France and ordered all fortified castles razed, except those needed against invaders, which made him hated by most of the nobility. In 1627 he personally commanded the troops besieging the Huguenot stronghold of La Rochelle.

Abroad he subsidized the Dutch Republic against Spain, and in 1629, alarmed by Emperor Ferdinand II's growing influence, he gave money to incite Sweden to intervene in Germany. He encouraged Louis XIII to colonize the Americas through the Company of New France, and the Ordonnance of 1627 deemed Indians who converted to Catholicism natural Frenchmen. He also renovated the Sorbonne and patronised the arts.

Near the end of his life Richelieu faced a plot by the marquis de Cinq-Mars, whom he had introduced at court. He suffered from recurrent fevers, intestinal tuberculosis and migraine, and he died on 4 December 1642, naming Jules Mazarin as his successor. He left his library, with some 900 manuscripts, to be open to scholars. Historians credit him with replacing a largely feudal political structure with centralized power, work that Louis XIV continued. He is also noted for authoritarian measures: he censored the press, kept a network of spies and had those who conspired against him prosecuted and executed.
carhaix-plouguer: Carhaix-Plouguer, commonly called Carhaix, lies in the Poher, an important territory of Brittany between the Arrée Mountains to the north and the Black Mountains to the south. The town grew mainly on a plateau about 140 metres above sea level, bounded on the north by the valley of the Hyères, which in Roman times required the building of an aqueduct to cross it. Carhaix and Plouguer became separate communes at the French Revolution and merged in 1957.

In the Roman Empire the city was called Vorgium and was the chief town of the Osismii. Modern archaeological digs have uncovered evidence of the Roman city, including its aqueduct system. Its function as a crossroads persisted, together with a decline in the late empire, and this may explain why the Osismii, although Carhaix was their capital, did not leave their name to it, as happened more often in Gaul.

The oldest form of the name, Carahes, appears in a charter of Hoel, Count of Cornouaille, written before his death in 1084; the Breton prefix kaer means a fortified place. In the 19th century it was believed that the name came from Ahès, the daughter of Gradlon in Breton tradition who brought about the loss of the city of Ys. In the continental romances Carhaix is thought to be the Carohaise of King Leodegrance, where King Arthur meets Guinevere.

Carhaix is in the department of Finistère, in the region of Brittany. It has the only lycée of the Diwan schools, which teach in Breton, moved there from Brest in 1999. The town holds the Vieilles Charrues music festival every July and the Book Festival in Brittany every October.
caribbean: The Caribbean is a region of thousands of islands, islets, reefs and cays centred on the Caribbean Sea and lying largely on the Caribbean plate. Island arcs mark its northern and eastern edges: the Greater Antilles, including Cuba, Hispaniola, Jamaica and Puerto Rico, in the north, and the Lesser Antilles in the east and south. The Bahamas, the Turks and Caicos Islands and Barbados are counted as part of the region though they do not border the sea. The term West Indies is often used interchangeably with the Caribbean. The region takes its name from the Caribs, after whom Spanish colonists named it.

The oldest evidence of human presence is at Banwari Trace in southern Trinidad, where remains about 7,000 years old have been found. Consistent dates of 3100 BCE appear in Cuba and of 2000 BCE in Antigua. At the time of European contact the dominant groups were the Taíno of the Greater Antilles and the Island Caribs of the southern Lesser Antilles, and the population is estimated to have been about 750,000.

Christopher Columbus arrived on Hispaniola in 1492. The Spanish assigned enslaved people to conquistadors under the encomienda system, and the Laws of Burgos of 1512 were meant to protect the rights of the native peoples. Smallpox and measles, to which they had no immunity, and social disruption sharply reduced the Amerindian population, and from 1503 enslaved people from Africa, among them Kongo, Igbo, Akan, Fon and Yoruba, were brought in. England, the Netherlands and France sought colonies of their own, and colonial rivalries made the region a battleground of European wars for centuries. Spain ceded Jamaica to England, while Martinique and the western third of Hispaniola passed to France.

The principal official languages are Spanish, French, English and Dutch, with Haitian Creole and Papiamento, and almost every country has a creole language or dialect as its everyday speech. Christianity is the main religion, alongside Hinduism, Islam and Rastafari. The islands hold about 8 per cent of the world's coral reefs. In 1973 English-speaking states created the Caribbean Community, CARICOM, in Guyana.
caribbean-community: The Caribbean Community was first called the Caribbean Community and Common Market. It was established by the Treaty of Chaguaramas, signed by the leaders of Barbados, Guyana, Jamaica and Trinidad and Tobago and in effect from 1 August 1973. It superseded the Caribbean Free Trade Association of 1965-1972, which had kept up an economic link between the English-speaking countries of the Caribbean after the West Indies Federation dissolved. That federation had lasted from 3 January 1958 to 31 May 1962.

CARICOM began as an organisation of the English-speaking Caribbean, and English was its sole working language into the 1990s. It became multilingual as Suriname joined in 1995 and Haiti in 2002, and Spanish was added as a fourth official language in 2003. On 5 July 2001 the heads of government signed a revised Treaty of Chaguaramas at Nassau, which cleared the way for the CARICOM Single Market and Economy and established the Caribbean Court of Justice. Haiti's participation was suspended from 29 February 2004 until June 2006.

CARICOM took part in founding wider bodies. The Association of Caribbean States was formed on 24 July 1994, from a recommendation of the West Indian Commission that CARICOM's heads of government set up in 1989. CARICOM was also involved in creating the Community of Latin American and Caribbean States in 2010.

The Conference of Heads of Government and the Community Council, made up of ministers responsible for community affairs, are the two principal organs. The chairmanship rotates among the heads of government. The Secretariat in Georgetown is the chief administrative organ; its Secretary-General is the chief executive, with a five-year term that may be renewed. Its main activities are coordinating economic policy and development planning, running a regional single market, handling trade disputes and devising projects for the less developed members. Its flag, first flown on 4 July 1984, shows two interlocking Cs as broken chain links, which stand for unity and a break with the colonial past.
carl-gustaf-emil-mannerheim: Mannerheim was born on 4 June 1867 at Louhisaari Manor in Askainen parish, into a Swedish-speaking aristocratic family. The Mannerheims, originally from Germany as Marhein, became Swedish noblemen in 1693. His great-grandfather, Count Carl Erik Mannerheim, became the first head of the executive of the newly autonomous Grand Duchy of Finland after Sweden lost Finland to the Russian Empire in 1809. His father, heavily in debt, left the family in 1880, and his mother died the following year.

In 1882 he entered the Hamina Cadet School, and in 1889 he was hired as a cornet in a dragoon regiment at Kalisz in Poland. He married Anastasia Arapova in 1892; they had two daughters. He served in the Russo-Japanese War, travelled through Turkestan to Beijing as a secret intelligence officer, and fought on the Austro-Hungarian and Romanian fronts in the First World War, rising to lieutenant general in April 1917.

After Finland declared independence in December 1917, the Senate of Finland faced the socialist Reds in a civil war. On 13 January 1918 Mannerheim was given command of the army of the Whites, about 24,000 mostly untrained men, against some 30,000 Red Guards. At Vaasa he surrounded a Russian garrison of 1,500 to 2,000 men with recruits, only the front rank of them armed, and the garrison surrendered its weapons. The Whites held a victory parade in Helsinki in May.

He was regent from December 1918 to July 1919, won recognition of independence from several Entente powers and ratified the republican constitution although he was a monarchist. He lost the first presidential election to K. J. Ståhlberg in 1919 and held no public office in the interwar years. As chairman of the Defence Council from 1931 he prepared for a possible war with the Soviet Union, and after the Soviet attack of 30 November 1939 he became commander-in-chief at 72, a post he held for five years.

In 1944 the Parliament of Finland unanimously appointed Mannerheim president, and he oversaw peace negotiations with the Soviet Union and the United Kingdom. Finland had made him a field marshal in 1933 and gave him the title Marshal of Finland in 1942, which no one else has held. In poor health, he resigned in March 1946, wrote his memoirs at a sanatorium in Montreux, Switzerland, and died there on 27 January 1951.

Mannerheim is often called the father of modern Finland. According to the historian Tuomas Tepora, a cult of personality grew around him after the civil war, and the Mannerheim Museum in Helsinki memorialises his life.
carl-linnaeus: Carl Linnaeus was born on 23 May 1707 in the village of Råshult in Småland, Sweden, the first child of Nicolaus (Nils) Linnaeus and Christina Brodersonia. His father, a Lutheran minister and amateur botanist, taught him Latin as a small child, and the family moved to the rectory of Stenbrohult when his father became rector there. Linnaeus liked plants from his earliest years, and his father gave him his own patch of land to grow them.

In 1727, at the age of 21, he enrolled at Lund University. Most of his higher education was at Uppsala University, where he began giving lectures in botany in 1730. In May 1732 he set out on an expedition to Lapland, funded by a grant from the Royal Society of Sciences in Uppsala, curious about the Sami people.

In April 1735 Linnaeus travelled to the Dutch Republic to study medicine at the University of Harderwijk, and he published the first edition of his Systema Naturae in the Netherlands. After returning to Sweden on 28 June 1738 he worked as a physician at the Admiralty in Stockholm and helped found the Royal Swedish Academy of Science, becoming its first Praeses by drawing of lots. He later became professor of medicine and botany at Uppsala, and in the 1740s he was sent on several journeys through Sweden to find and classify plants and animals.

He taught many students, 17 of whom he called his apostles, and they made botanical expeditions around the world, so that his system spread without his travelling outside Sweden again. He was ennobled in 1761. Illness troubled his last years, and he died on 10 January 1778 in Hammarby.

The first edition of Systema Naturae, printed in 1735, ran to twelve pages. By its 10th edition in 1758 it classified 4,400 species of animals and 7,700 species of plants. Linnaeus's main contribution to taxonomy was the establishment of universally accepted conventions for naming organisms, and his work marks the starting point of the consistent use of binomial nomenclature.

The Linnaean system placed nature in a nested hierarchy of three kingdoms divided into classes, orders, genera and species. His taxonomy of human races has been criticised in the 21st century: some regard him as a forebear of scientific racism, while others hold that his classification was stereotyped but did not imply that any race was superior.
carl-menger: Carl Menger von Wolfensgrün was born on 28 February 1840 in Neu-Sandez, in the Kingdom of Galicia and Lodomeria in the Austrian Empire, now Nowy Sącz in Poland. His father, Anton Menger, was a lawyer. He studied law at the universities of Prague and Vienna and received a doctorate from the Jagiellonian University in Kraków. In the 1860s he reported and analysed market news for the Lemberger Zeitung and then the Wiener Zeitung, and noticed a gap between what classical economics said about prices and what people in markets believed.

In 1867 Menger began a study of political economy that led in 1871 to his Principles of Economics. In 1873, aged 33, he received the chair of economic theory at the University of Vienna. From 1876 he tutored Archduke Rudolf von Habsburg, the crown prince, accompanying him on journeys through Europe and the British Isles; their association lasted until the prince's death in 1889.

His Investigations into the Method of the Social Sciences (1883) set off a dispute with the historical school. Gustav von Schmoller reviewed it unfavourably and used the term Austrian school as a gibe, and in 1884 Menger answered with The Errors of Historicism in German Economics, opening the Methodenstreit, or methodological debate. His disciples included Eugen von Böhm-Bawerk and Friedrich von Wieser. He headed a commission to reform the Austrian monetary system, and in 1903 he resigned his chair to concentrate on study.

Menger rejected the cost-of-production theory of value held by Adam Smith, David Ricardo and Karl Marx. His subjective theory of value held that price is determined at the margin and that both sides gain from exchange. Unlike William Jevons, he did not believe that goods provide units of utility; goods are valuable because they serve various uses whose importance differs. He explained money as a development of exchange, in which gold and silver, being especially saleable, came to be a general medium of exchange. Friedrich Hayek wrote that the fundamental ideas of the Austrian school belong fully and wholly to Menger.
carl-philipp-emanuel-bach: Carl Philipp Emanuel Bach was born on 8 March 1714 in Weimar to Johann Sebastian Bach and his first wife, Maria Barbara. The composer Georg Philipp Telemann was his godfather. At ten he entered the St. Thomas School in Leipzig, which his father directed as Thomaskantor, and he was trained in music almost entirely by his father. Like his brothers, he also studied law, at Leipzig University in 1731 and at Frankfurt an der Oder in 1735. He took his degree in 1738 at the age of 24 but never practised law, and turned at once to music.

A few months after graduating, Bach was appointed at Berlin to the service of Crown Prince Frederick of Prussia, and when Frederick came to the throne in 1740 he joined the royal orchestra. His reputation was made by two sets of sonatas, dedicated in 1742 to Frederick the Great and in 1744 to Charles Eugene, Duke of Württemberg. In 1746 he became chamber musician, serving alongside Carl Heinrich Graun, Johann Joachim Quantz and Franz Benda. In Berlin he wrote nearly two hundred sonatas and other keyboard pieces, symphonies, songs and a Magnificat of 1749, and was known as the Berlin Bach, to tell him from his brother Johann Christian, the London Bach.

In 1768, after long negotiations, he was released from court service to succeed Telemann as Kapellmeister in Hamburg, and was named court composer to Frederick's sister, Princess Anna Amalia. The post required steady music for Protestant services, and he turned more to church and choral music: twenty-one settings of the Passion, some seventy cantatas, litanies and motets, and the oratorios Die Israeliten in der Wüste and Die Auferstehung und Himmelfahrt Jesu. In 1773 he wrote an autobiography, one of the first by a composer.

Bach was the chief representative of the empfindsamer Stil, the sensitive style, working between his father's Baroque and the Classical style that followed. His keyboard works, especially the fantasias, are full of dramatic silences and harmonic surprises. His treatise Versuch über die wahre Art das Clavier zu spielen, written in Berlin, became a definitive work on keyboard technique, studied by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He died in Hamburg on 14 December 1788 and was buried in the Michaeliskirche. His reputation stood above his father's in the later 18th century, fell into neglect in the 19th, and revived chiefly from the 1960s.
carlisle: Carlisle lies on a slight rise at the confluence of the rivers Eden, Caldew and Petteril, about eight miles (13 km) south of the present Anglo-Scottish border, which earned it the nickname of the Great Border City. Its name comes from the Cumbric Caer Luel. Luguvalium took its name from a native name reconstructed as Brittonic Luguwaljon, the city of Luguwalos, a Celtic given name meaning strength of Lugus.

The earliest recorded inhabitants were the Carvetii. Luguvalium was founded to serve the forts along Hadrian's Wall, though it may have earlier origins. After Roman rule the region was the British kingdom of Rheged, whose capital, associated with Urien and his son Owain, has been identified with the Cair Ligualid listed by Nennius. Rheged came under Northumbrian control before 730, and for the rest of the first millennium Carlisle was contested between the kingdom of Strathclyde and Anglian Northumbria. In 685 St Cuthbert was shown its walls and a Roman fountain.

A priory built in the early 12th century became Carlisle Cathedral in 1133, when the Diocese of Carlisle was created, and as a diocesan seat the town gained city status. It was county town of Cumberland, and its earliest recorded charter was issued by Henry II.

Mary, Queen of Scots was held in the castle in 1568. In 1539 Henry VIII employed the engineer Stefan von Haschenperg to modernise the defences. Carlisle has been besieged at least ten times, and the reiving of the border families was suppressed more firmly after James VI of Scotland became James I of England in 1603. In the 19th century textile mills and engineering works opened in the Caldew Valley and Carlisle became a railway town, with seven companies sharing its station.

Carlisle is the only city in Cumbria and its largest settlement, with a population of 77,730 in 2021. The castle houses the Border Regiment Museum, and Tullie House Museum, opened in 1893, shows the Roman occupation, Hadrian's Wall and the Border Reivers. The cathedral remains the seat of the Diocese of Carlisle.
carloforte: Carloforte is a fishing and resort town and comune in the province of Sulcis Iglesiente, in the autonomous island region of Sardinia. It stands on the Isola di San Pietro, or Saint Peter's Island, about 7 kilometres off the south-western coast of the Sardinian mainland. Its Tabarchino name, U Pàize, means the village or the town. Ferries link its port with the mainland at Portovesme and with Calasetta on the island of Sant'Antioco, another fishing port that has a community of Tabarchini.

According to a legend, a church on the island, the Chiesa dei Novelli Innocenti, was founded in the early 14th century in honour of hundreds of participants in the Children's Crusade of 1212 who died in a shipwreck just off the island in a gale. It was the only visible building the settlers found when they came.

The town was founded in the 18th century by around 30 families of coral fishers. They descended from people of the Ligurian town of Pegli, near Genoa, who had left it in 1541 and settled on the island of Tabarka, off the coast of Tunisia, to fish for coral. After centuries the coral there was exhausted. On their way back towards Italy the families found plenty of coral in the sea off western Sardinia, and they asked Charles Emmanuel III, King of Piedmont-Sardinia, for permission to settle on the then uninhabited island of San Pietro. When he agreed, the island was colonised and the town was named Carloforte in his honour, meaning Charles the Strong or Carlo's Fort.

Carloforte has 5,851 inhabitants and keeps strong cultural ties with Pegli and Genoa. Most of its people speak tabarchino, a variety of Ligurian separate from both Italian and Sardinian, which most children also use and which is taught in the island's schools. The town has a long tradition of wooden boatbuilding, and traditional lateen-sail fishing boats can be seen in its harbour. North of the town stand the buildings of a former communal tuna-processing plant, which served the island's tonnare tuna fishing. The Capo Sandalo Lighthouse, on the far side of the island, dates from the 1880s. Fishing and tourism are its main sources of income, with money sent home by merchant mariners from Carloforte.
carloman-i: Carloman was born on 28 June 751, the second surviving son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon. At the age of three he was anointed King of the Franks, with his father and his brother Charlemagne, and given the title Patrician of the Romans by Pope Stephen II, who had left Rome to ask the Frankish king for help against the Lombards.

On Pepin's death the kingdom was divided between the brothers. Carloman's share lay in the centre of the realm, with its capital at Soissons, and took in the Parisian basin, Provence, Burgundy and Alemannia among other regions. It was easier to defend than Charlemagne's lands but poorer. The brothers disliked each other, though the reasons are unclear. When Aquitaine rebelled, Carloman marched to help Charlemagne but quarrelled with him at Moncontour and withdrew, which damaged his standing. Rosamond McKitterick argues that there is no evidence of lasting animosity.

In 770 their mother Bertrada began diplomacy that left Carloman isolated. Charlemagne married Desiderata, daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, and Bertrada won him the friendship of Tassilo III of Bavaria. Carloman sought the support of Pope Stephen III, but after Desiderius had the papal official Christopher the Primicerius murdered the pope favoured the Lombards and Charlemagne. Charlemagne then repudiated his Lombard wife, and Desiderius appears to have allied with Carloman.

Carloman died on 4 December 771 at the villa of Samoussy. The death was set down to natural causes, and a severe nosebleed is sometimes named. He was buried at Reims and reburied in the Basilique Saint-Denis in the 13th century. His widow Gerberga fled with her two sons to Desiderius, after his supporters invited Charlemagne to annex his lands, and Desiderius asked Pope Hadrian I to anoint the boys as kings. Charlemagne responded by invading Italy and ending the Lombard kingdom. What became of Gerberga and her sons is unknown.
carlos-fuentes: Carlos Fuentes Macías was born in Panama City on 11 November 1928, the son of Berta Macías and Rafael Fuentes, a Mexican diplomat. As the family moved with his father's career, he spent his childhood in several Latin American capitals, an experience he later said gave him the ability to see Latin America as a critical outsider. From 1934 to 1940 his father was posted to the Mexican Embassy in Washington, where he attended an English-language school and began to write. In 1940 the family moved to Santiago, Chile, where his interest in the poetry of Pablo Neruda led him to socialism.

He lived in Mexico for the first time at 16, when he went to study law at the National Autonomous University of Mexico with a diplomatic career in mind, and he later attended the Graduate Institute of International Studies in Geneva.

In 1957 Fuentes became head of cultural relations at the Mexican Secretariat of Foreign Affairs. His first novel, Where the Air Is Clear, appeared in 1958 and made him a national celebrity, allowing him to write full-time. In 1959 he moved to Havana after the Cuban Revolution. He served as Mexico's ambassador to France from 1975 to 1977 and resigned in protest at the appointment of the former president Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as ambassador to Spain. He taught at Cambridge, Princeton, Harvard, Columbia and other universities.

He was long a critic of the Institutional Revolutionary Party government that ruled Mexico from 1929 until 2000. In the 1980s he broke with the poet Octavio Paz over the Sandinistas, and a feud began that lasted until Paz's death in 1998. He received the Miguel de Cervantes Prize and, in 1999, Mexico's highest award, the Belisario Domínguez Medal of Honor. He died on 15 May 2012.

Fuentes named Cervantes, William Faulkner and Balzac as the writers most important to him, and his main theme was Mexican history and identity. Where the Air Is Clear is built around Federico Robles, a former revolutionary turned powerful financier, and presents Mexico City in vignettes. The Death of Artemio Cruz (1962) begins like Citizen Kane with its protagonist on his deathbed and tells his life in flashbacks: a soldier of the Mexican Revolution who becomes wealthy through violence, blackmail and bribery. Fuentes was a leading figure of the Latin American boom of the 1960s and 1970s, with Gabriel García Márquez, Mario Vargas Llosa and Julio Cortázar.

Terra Nostra (1975) tells the story of Hispanic civilisation, moving between the sixteenth and twentieth centuries. The Old Gringo (1985), loosely based on the disappearance of Ambrose Bierce during the Mexican Revolution, became the first United States bestseller by a Mexican author. His work has been translated into 24 languages.
carlos-menem: Carlos Saúl Menem was born on 2 July 1930 in Anillaco, a small town in northern La Rioja Province, to parents of Syrian Arab ancestry from Yabroud. He was raised a Muslim and later converted to Roman Catholicism to pursue a political career. On a visit to Buenos Aires in 1951 he met Juan Perón and Eva Perón, which led him to become a Peronist. He studied law at the National University of Córdoba. Elected governor of La Rioja in 1973, he was deposed and detained after the coup of 1976 and not released until 1978. He was re-elected governor in 1983 and again in 1987 with 63% of the vote.

In 1989 Menem defeated Antonio Cafiero in the Peronist primaries by building a broad coalition, and took office after hyperinflation and riots forced Raúl Alfonsín to leave early. He abandoned party orthodoxy for a market-oriented policy in line with the Washington Consensus and in 1991 introduced the Convertibility plan, complemented by privatisations and at first a success. Argentina aligned itself with the United States, joined the Gulf War and re-established relations with the United Kingdom. His government suffered two terrorist attacks, on the Israeli embassy on 17 March 1992 and on the AMIA centre in 1994.

Menem pardoned the leaders of the military juntas convicted in the 1985 Trial of the Juntas, despite popular opposition, and put down a mutiny led by Colonel Mohamed Alí Seineldín, the last military mutiny in Argentina. The Pact of Olivos with Alfonsín allowed the constitutional amendment of 1994 and his re-election in 1995. A new economic crisis began in his second term, and an opposition coalition won the 1999 presidential election.

Menem ran again in 2003 and led the first round with 24%, but withdrew before the run-off against Néstor Kirchner, who was likely to win by a wide margin. He was arrested in 2001 over a weapons export scandal and later received a sentence of seven years for arms trafficking and four and a half years for embezzlement, but his position as senator, to which he was elected in 2005, protected him from imprisonment. He died on 14 February 2021 at the age of 90.

He is regarded in Argentina as a polarising figure, chiefly because of corruption and economic mismanagement. Supporters credit his first presidency with ending a period of economic uncertainty and bringing stability. Contrary to Peronist tradition he addressed the public through television rather than rallies at the Plaza de Mayo.
carlos-saavedra-lamas: Carlos Saavedra Lamas was born in Buenos Aires on 1 November 1878 into a family descended from an early Argentine patriot, and he later married a daughter of President Roque Sáenz Peña. He studied at Lacordaire College and then at the Faculty of Law of the University of Buenos Aires, where he earned a doctorate in law summa cum laude in 1903. After further study in Paris he became a professor of law and constitutional history at the University of La Plata, beginning a teaching career of more than four decades.

Saavedra Lamas entered public life in 1906 as director of public credit and became secretary-general of the municipality of Buenos Aires the next year. Elected to Parliament in 1908 for two consecutive terms, he sponsored laws on coastal water rights, irrigation, sugar, finance, colonization and immigration, and he helped preserve Argentina's arbitration treaty with Italy during a crisis of 1907 and 1908. Many saw him as a conservative patrician who favoured British intervention, particularly in railway building. As minister of Justice and Public Instruction from 1915 he reorganised public education and developed vocational and technical training.

President Agustín P. Justo appointed him foreign minister in 1932. He brought Argentina back into the League of Nations after a thirteen-year absence. In 1932 he initiated the Declaration of August 3 in Washington, by which American states agreed not to recognise territorial changes made by force. He drafted the Treaty of Nonaggression and Conciliation, signed by six South American countries in October 1933 and two months later by all American states at the Seventh Pan-American Conference in Montevideo.

A scholar of labour legislation and international law, he supported the founding of the International Labour Organization in 1919 and in 1928 presided over its Geneva conference while leading the Argentine delegation. His publications include the three-volume Código nacional del trabajo (1933) and La Crise de la codification et de la doctrine argentine de droit international (1931). In 1935 he arranged mediation by six neutral American countries that ended the Chaco War between Paraguay and Bolivia. He was elected president of the Assembly of the League of Nations in 1936.

After leaving the ministry in 1938 he was rector of the University of Buenos Aires from 1941 to 1943 and taught there until 1946. He died in Buenos Aires in 1959 and was buried at La Recoleta Cemetery.
carmelites: Historical records of the order's origin are uncertain. Berthold of Calabria and Albert of Vercelli are traditionally associated with its founding, but few clear records survive. Tradition gives 1185, but that rests on a pilgrim's story whose interpretation is questionable; the oldest reliable written accounts of Latin hermits on Mount Carmel date from 1220 and 1263. The Carmelites look back not to a founder but to the prophet Elijah and his disciple Elisha, whom they regard as their spiritual fathers. A written rule of life for the hermits, centred on prayer, is dated 1209 and was requested, tradition says, from the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, Albert of Vercelli.

In Europe the hermits met difficulties. Their solitary life did not suit their new settlements, and they competed with other mendicant orders. In 1274 the Second Council of Lyon disestablished all mendicant orders founded after 1215; only the Franciscans, the Order of Preachers, the Carmelites and the Augustinians remained. The Carmelites, barely spared, had to change from hermits to friars. They settled across Europe, among other places at Aylesford in Kent in 1242 and in Paris in 1259.

After the Black Death had reduced the number of members, a majority of Carmelites asked Pope Eugene IV in 1432 to mitigate the rule because of its severity. John Soreth, Prior General from 1451 to 1471, worked to restore a stricter life. The Teresian reform of the 1560s created the Discalced Carmelites, who faced opposition from unreformed houses: Carmelites at Toledo imprisoned John of the Cross. The French Revolution suppressed the order, and the Compiègne Carmelites were guillotined.

The Carmelites are a mendicant order for men and women. The order of Carmelite nuns was formalised in 1452, and John Soreth had a leading part in founding the Third Order for lay members. Their distinctive garment is a scapular of two strips of dark cloth worn on the breast and back. Tradition holds that the Virgin Mary gave it to Simon Stock and promised that those who die wearing it with faith and piety would be saved.
carnation-revolution: The Estado Novo grew out of the coup of 28 May 1926 and was renamed in 1933; António de Oliveira Salazar was prime minister until 1968. Elections were mostly shams, and the political police, the PIDE, persecuted opponents, who were often tortured, imprisoned or killed. After Salazar's stroke in 1968 Marcelo Caetano promised reform, but censorship stayed until 25 April 1974. Independence movements had begun in Mozambique, Angola and Portuguese Guinea, and the colonial war of 1961 to 1974 took up to 40 per cent of the budget. The war became unpopular, and many young men avoided conscription by emigrating.

By December 1973 officers including Vasco Lourenço, Vítor Alves and Otelo Saraiva de Carvalho were preparing a coup, and the Armed Forces Movement, the MFA, took shape. The coup, code-named Operation Historic Turn, had two signals: the song E Depois do Adeus, broadcast at 22:55 on 24 April, and Grândola, Vila Morena, by the banned singer Zeca Afonso, broadcast at 00:20 on 25 April.

Within six hours the government gave way. Though the MFA urged civilians to stay home, thousands filled the streets. Celeste Caeiro, a restaurant worker, offered carnations to soldiers, and others put them in gun barrels, which gave the revolution its name. Caetano took refuge in the barracks at Largo do Carmo and ceded power to General António de Spínola. The siege of the security police's headquarters lasted until the next morning, and four civilians were killed by its warning shots.

Power passed to the National Salvation Junta and then the Revolutionary Council, in a turbulent period that culminated in the Hot Summer of 1975. Portugal's first free election was held on 25 April 1975 to write a new constitution, and the first constitutional government, led by the socialist Mário Soares, took office after a further election in 1976.

Portuguese troops were withdrawn from Guinea in 1974, and in 1975 Cape Verde, Mozambique, São Tomé and Príncipe and Angola became independent, and East Timor declared independence. More than one million Portuguese, the retornados, left the African territories. 25 April, Freedom Day, is a national holiday.
carol-i-of-romania: Carol was born Karl Eitel Friedrich Zephyrinus Ludwig on 20 April 1839 at Sigmaringen in southern Germany, the second son of Prince Karl Anton of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen and Princess Josephine of Baden. His family belonged to the Catholic Swabian branch of the House of Hohenzollern, was related to the Prussian royal family and, through both grandmothers, to the Bonaparte family. He trained at the cadet school in Münster and the artillery school in Berlin and served as a Prussian officer until 1866, taking part in the Second Schleswig War.

In 1866 a coup removed Alexandru Ioan Cuza, the prince of the united Moldavia and Wallachia, and the country risked disintegration. Philip of Flanders refused the throne. Napoleon III then suggested Karl, and the politician Ion Constantin Brătianu went to negotiate with his family. Karl travelled incognito through Switzerland under a Swiss passport, was elected Domnitor on 20 April 1866 and entered Bucharest in May, swearing his oath in French because he did not yet speak Romanian.

On 29 June 1866 parliament adopted a constitution modelled closely on that of Belgium, which guaranteed freedom of speech and the press and separated powers. It also barred non-Christians from citizenship, which heavily affected the Jewish population. In 1869 Carol married Princess Elisabeth of Wied.
