Their only child, Maria, born in 1870, died in 1874, and the throne later passed to his nephew Ferdinand.

In the Russo-Turkish War Romania declared independence on 10 May 1877. After the Russian advance stalled at Pleven, Carol took command of the combined Russian and Romanian forces there, and Osman Nuri Pasha surrendered the town on 28 November 1877. The Treaty of Berlin recognised Romanian independence on 13 July 1878 and gave Romania Northern Dobruja. The constitution was amended in March 1881 and Carol was crowned king on 10 May, wearing a crown made from steel of a captured Ottoman cannon.

He built Peleș Castle in the Carpathian mountains and ordered the engineer Anghel Saligny to build a bridge over the Danube between Fetești and Cernavodă. In 1883 he arranged a secret alliance with the Central Powers, unknown to parliament and the public until the First World War. A peasant revolt in 1907 was bloodily suppressed. Romania gained Southern Dobruja in 1913. Carol died on 10 October 1914 (27 September, Old Style), and Romania, neutral at first, joined the Allies in 1916.
caroline-islands: The Caroline Islands form a widely scattered archipelago of about 500 small islands in the western Pacific Ocean, north of New Guinea and east of the Philippines. They stretch for approximately 3,540 kilometres, from Tobi in Palau in the west to Kosrae in the east. Most are low, flat coral atolls, though some rise high above sea level. Yap lies 1,900 kilometres from Manila, and the group was once called Nuevas Filipinas, or New Philippines, because it formed part of the Spanish East Indies and was governed from Manila.

Different islands tell different stories of their origins. On Pohnpei, the people divide their pre-colonial history into three eras: building or peopling before 1100, the reigns of the Saudeleur from 1100 to around 1628, and the era of the tribal chiefs, the nahnmwarki, from around 1628 to 1885. According to Pohnpeian legend, the Saudeleur came from beyond the islands and imposed an increasingly oppressive centralised rule. A foreigner named Isokelekel invaded, overthrew them and set up the more decentralised nahnmwarki system.

The Portuguese navigators Diogo da Rocha and Gomes de Sequeira, carried east by a storm in 1525, were the first Europeans to reach the islands. In 1528 Álvaro de Saavedra Cerón claimed the Ulithi Islands for the king of Spain. Francisco de Lezcano, arriving at Yap in 1686, named the group Las Carolinas in honour of Charles II of Spain. A missionary, Juan Antonio Cantova, was killed in 1731, and Spain broke off relations until 1787. Whaling ships from Britain, the United States and Australia called there through the 19th century, the first known being the London whaler Britannia at Ngatik in December 1793.

In 1885 a Spanish representative signed an agreement with the chiefs of Koror and Artingal establishing Spanish sovereignty. When Germany and the United Kingdom disputed Spain's right to collect customs duties, Pope Leo XIII arbitrated and decided in Spain's favour west of the 164th meridian east. After the Spanish-American War, Spain sold the Carolines and the Northern Marianas to Germany in 1899 for 25 million pesetas. Japan occupied the islands in 1914, received a League of Nations mandate over them in 1920, and kept a large base at Truk Lagoon in World War II. The islands then became a United States trust territory.

The group is divided between the Federated States of Micronesia in its central and eastern parts, which became independent in 1986, and Palau at its western end, independent from 1994. Pohnpeian, Chuukese, Carolinian, Kosraean, Palauan and Yapese are among the languages spoken. Yap is known for its huge stone discs quarried in Palau, which serve as tokens of wealth.
carolingian-empire: The Carolingian dynasty had ruled as kings of the Franks since 751 and as kings of the Lombards in Italy from 774. Its rise rested on Charles Martel, who took neither the title of king nor of emperor but was the absolute ruler of virtually all of continental Western Europe north of the Pyrenees. He earned his surname, Martel, meaning the Hammer, through his defence of Christian Europe against a Muslim army at the Battle of Tours in 732. In 800 Pope Leo III crowned his grandson Charlemagne as Roman emperor in return for political protection, disregarding the universalist claims of the weakened Byzantine Empire.

Under Charlemagne the empire covered most of Western Europe, as the Roman Empire once had. His son Louis the Pious, originally crowned king of Aquitaine at the age of three, became emperor unexpectedly after the deaths of his older siblings. His reign was overshadowed by a dynastic struggle that ended in a civil war from 840 to 843. In 843 his three sons settled the partition in the Treaty of Verdun. Lothar received the imperial title, the kingship of Italy and the lands between the Rhine and the Rhone. Louis took the lands east of the Rhine, and Charles those west of the Rhone.

After the death of Charles the Bald in 877 the empire was attacked by the Vikings in the north and west and faced internal struggles from Italy to the Baltic. In 884 Charles the Fat reunited all the Carolingian kingdoms for the last time, but the Frankish nobility deposed him in 887, and the empire dissolved when he died in 888. The legitimate line was restored in the western kingdom in 898 and ruled until 987, with an interruption from 922 to 936.

The empire had no permanent capital, since the court moved from place to place, as in other Western European kingdoms. Charlemagne began building the Palace of Aachen in the 780s, and its chapel, completed in 796, later became Aachen Cathedral. Aachen was meant as a meeting place for aristocrats and churchmen, where patronage was distributed, assemblies were held and laws written. The language of official acts was Latin. Carolingian Empire is a modern term, not used by contemporaries.

Frankish forces campaigned almost every year. Charlemagne gathered an assembly around Easter and launched a campaign through the summer,. The population is estimated at between 10 and 20 million, and the empire held Franks, Alemanni, Bavarians, Frisians, Lombards, Romans, Celts, Basques and Slavs, whose ethnic identities helped decide which law codes applied to them.
carpentras: Carpentras is a commune in the Vaucluse department of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur in south-eastern France. It stands on the banks of the river Auzon, a tributary of the Sorgue, 23 kilometres south-west of Mont Ventoux and 23 kilometres north-east of Avignon. Its climate is borderline between humid subtropical and hot-summer Mediterranean, with cool winters and hot summers. Its Provençal Occitan name is Carpentràs, and its Latin name was Carpentoracte.

Greek merchants used the site as a commercial centre in ancient times. The Romans knew it at first as Carpentoracte Meminorum, a name mentioned by Pliny, and then renamed it Forum Neronis, the Forum of Nero. A Roman triumphal arch survives, enclosed by the bishops' palace, which was rebuilt in 1640 and is now a law court, along with a machicolated city gate, the Porte d'Orange.

At the beginning of the Avignon Papacy, Pope Clement V took up residence in Carpentras with the Roman Curia in 1313. His successor, Pope John XXII, settled definitively at Avignon. As capital of the Comtat Venaissin, the town was frequently the residence of the Avignon popes, and the Papal States kept the Venaissin until the French Revolution. Until 1791 Carpentras belonged to the Papal States, not to the Kingdom of France. After the coup of 18 Fructidor on 4 September 1797, counter-revolutionaries attacked its Hôtel de Ville on 22 October.

In the 18th century the Hôtel-Dieu was built between 1750 and 1760 at the commission of Joseph-Dominique d'Inguimbert. It now houses the Bibliothèque Inguimbertine. Carpentras has long been an important centre of French Judaism, and its synagogue, opened in 1367, is the oldest in France. In May 1990 the Jewish cemetery was desecrated, which caused a public uproar and a demonstration in Paris attended by 200,000 people, including President François Mitterrand.

Carpentras is a commercial centre for the Comtat Venaissin and is known for its black truffle market, held every Friday morning in the winter months. Its traditional confectionery is the berlingot, a small hard candy with thin white stripes, originally made from the syrup left over from preserving fruit. The Renaissance composer known as Carpentras, Elzéar Genet (c. 1470 to 1548), and the politician Édouard Daladier, prime minister of France at the start of the Second World War, were born there.
carrara: Carrara is a town in Tuscany on the Carrione River, some 100 kilometres west-northwest of Florence, notable for the white or blue-grey marble quarried there. Its name likely comes from a pre-Roman element, kar, meaning stone, through the Latin carrariae, quarries. Its motto, Fortitudo mea in rota, or My strength is in the wheel, refers to the wheel of the cart that carried marble blocks from the quarry. The Pantheon and Trajan's Column in Rome are built of Carrara marble, and many sculptures of the Renaissance were carved from it.

The Apuan Ligures lived in the region as early as the ninth century BCE. The present town grew from a borough built for workers in the marble quarries that the Romans opened after conquering Liguria in the early second century BCE. In the early Middle Ages it was a Byzantine and then a Lombard possession, and then it fell to the bishops of Luni, to whom Emperor Otto I gave it. It became a city-state in the early 13th century. The bishops regained it in 1230, and their rule ended in 1313, after which it passed to the republics of Pisa, Lucca and Florence, and later to Gian Galeazzo Visconti of Milan.

After the death of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1447 the Malaspina family fought for Carrara, and moved the seat of their lordship there in the second half of the 15th century. Carrara and Massa formed the Duchy of Massa and Carrara, which passed to the Duchy of Modena through the last Malaspina, Maria Teresa, who married Ercole III d'Este. At the end of the 19th century Carrara became the cradle of Italian anarchism, above all among the quarry workers and stone carvers, who led the Lunigiana revolt of January 1894. The Congress of Carrara in 1968 founded the International of Anarchist Federations.

The town lies in the province of Massa and Carrara. Its sights include the 12th-century cathedral and the Ducal Palace, also called the Palazzo Cybo Malaspina, which now houses the Fine Arts Academy and combines a 13th-century castle with a Renaissance palace begun in the late 16th century.
cartography: What counts as the earliest known map is debated, partly because the term map is not well defined and some artifacts that might be maps may be something else. A wall painting that might depict the ancient Anatolian city of Çatalhöyük has been dated to the late 7th millennium BCE, and prehistoric alpine rock carvings at Mount Bego in France and Valcamonica in Italy, dated to the 4th millennium BCE, are widely interpreted as showing cultivated plots.

Other maps of the ancient world include the Minoan House of the Admiral wall painting of about 1600 BCE, showing a seaside community in oblique perspective, and an engraved map of the Babylonian city of Nippur from the Kassite period. The oldest surviving world maps are from Babylonia of the 9th century BCE; one shows Babylon on the Euphrates, surrounded by Assyria, Urartu and several cities, all encircled by a bitter river.

Cartography is the study and practice of making and using maps, combining science, aesthetics and technique. Its traditional objectives are to select the traits to be mapped, to represent terrain on flat media through map projections, to remove irrelevant characteristics through generalization, and to arrange the elements of the map to convey its message.

Maps are divided into general maps, made for a general audience, and thematic maps, which concern specific geographic themes, such as a map of corn production. A topographic map describes a place, with contour lines showing elevation, while a topological map disregards scale and detail to communicate route information; Beck's London Underground map is the usual example.

About 1,100 medieval European mappae mundi survive, of which some 900 illustrate manuscripts. In 1154 the Arab geographer Muhammad al-Idrisi produced his atlas Tabula Rogeriana, and his world map, mostly Ptolemaic in conception, remained the most accurate for the next three centuries. In 1492 Martin Behaim, advisor to King John II of Portugal, made the oldest extant globe, and Hartmann Schedel was among the first to use the printing press for maps.

The Selden map, made by a Chinese cartographer around 1620, though historians debate the date, shows trading routes, a compass rose and a scale bar. Enlightenment maps used copper plate intaglio rather than woodcut, and mapmakers often plagiarized: Herman Moll's Beaver Map of 1715 closely reproduces Nicolas de Fer's work of 1698. Some scholars argue that maps are inherently biased, and that cartography served imperial power in the conquest of Africa.
casale-monferrato: Casale Monferrato lies in the province of Alessandria in Piedmont, about 60 kilometres east of Turin, on the right bank of the Po, where the river runs at the foot of the Montferrat hills. An ancient Roman municipium, it has been the most important trade and manufacturing centre of the area for centuries. Its origins are fairly obscure. A Gaulish settlement called Vardacate stood on the Po here, and by the beginning of the 8th century a small town under Lombard rule, probably called Sedula or Sedulia, occupied the site.

The cult of Saint Evasius, said by late and unreliable accounts to have been beheaded here with 146 followers, flourished, and by 988 the town was known as Casale di Sant'Evasio. In the time of Charlemagne it came under the bishops of Vercelli, and Frederick Barbarossa freed it from their power. Troops from Vercelli, Alessandria and Milan sacked it in 1215, and it was rebuilt and fortified in 1220. It fell under the Marquess of Montferrat in 1292 and later became the capital of the marquessate. The Visconti of Milan held it from 1370 to 1404. The condottiere Facino Cane was born there.

In the 15th and early 16th centuries Casale was the capital of the House of Palaiologos, and in 1471 William VIII, Marquess of Montferrat, made it the permanent seat of his court. In 1536 it passed to the Gonzagas of Mantua, who fortified it strongly. It was besieged during the War of the Mantuan Succession. In 1745, after the Piedmontese defeat at the Battle of Bassignano, French and Spanish troops occupied it and damaged many buildings; the Baroque rebuilding that followed shaped the town's appearance. During the Wars of Italian Independence it resisted the Austrians in 1849 and was strengthened in 1852. Its Jewish ghetto lasted until the emancipation of the Jews in Piedmont after Charles Albert granted a constitution in 1848.

Limestone deposits in the nearby hills led to the opening of several cement factories in the late 19th and early 20th centuries, and Casale became known as the cement capital of Italy. An Eternit asbestos-cement factory operated there from 1907 to 1986, and some 1,800 deaths from mesothelioma and other asbestos-related diseases in the area have been linked to it.

The historic centre is built around Piazza Mazzini, the site of the Roman forum. Nearby are the Lombard Romanesque cathedral of Sant'Evasio, founded in 742 and consecrated in 1107, and the 11th-century Torre Civica. The castle of the Paleologi is a 15th-century hexagonal fortress with four round towers and a moat. The synagogue, built in 1595, is recognised as one of the most beautiful in Europe and its women's galleries hold a Jewish museum. Casale is also known for krumiri biscuits.
casimir-iii-the-great: Casimir was born on 30 April 1310 in Kowal in Kuyavia, the third son of Władysław I Łokietek and Jadwiga of Kalisz. His father was crowned king in Kraków on 20 January 1320, and in 1325 Casimir married Aldona of Lithuania, daughter of Grand Duke Gediminas, an alliance sought against the Teutonic Order. The war against Bohemia, Brandenburg and the Teutonic Order went badly for Poland, and when his father died on 2 March 1333 Casimir inherited a small, weakened realm of two ravaged provinces, Lesser Poland and Greater Poland.

Casimir was crowned at Wawel Cathedral on 25 April 1333. John of Bohemia was still widely regarded as the rightful king of Poland, and Casimir's main strength was his alliance with Hungary. An arbitration at Visegrád in November 1335 returned Dobrzyń Land and Kuyavia to Poland, while Casimir renounced Pomerania and the Chełmno Land to the Teutonic Order. He accepted the loss of Silesia to Bohemia and turned east, conquering Galicia-Volhynia, known as Red Ruthenia, which roughly doubled the kingdom and opened access to Black Sea trade.

At the Sejm in Wiślica on 11 March 1347 he sanctioned civil and criminal codes for Greater and Lesser Poland, which earned him the title the Polish Justinian. About thirty towns received walls and some fifty castles were built, and towns grew under Magdeburg rights. In 1364, with the permission of Pope Urban V, he founded the University of Kraków. On 9 October 1334 he confirmed the privileges granted to Jews in 1264 and allowed them to settle in large numbers.

Casimir left no legitimate son. In 1355, at Buda, he named his nephew Louis I of Hungary as heir should he have no male child. After Casimir died in 1370, Louis travelled quickly to Kraków, had a will that adopted another heir set aside by bribing the nobles with future privileges, and was proclaimed king. Casimir was the last Piast king of Poland.
caspar-david-friedrich: Friedrich was the sixth of ten children, raised in the strict Lutheran creed of his father Adolf Gottlieb Friedrich, a candle-maker and soap boiler. Records of the family's finances are contradictory; some sources say the children were privately tutored, others that they lived in relative poverty. He knew death early: his mother Sophie died in 1781, a sister a year later, and another sister in 1791. In 1787 he witnessed his younger brother Johann Christoffer, aged thirteen, fall through the ice of a frozen lake and drown.

He studied in Copenhagen from 1794 to 1798, then settled permanently in Dresden. There he made etchings and designs for woodcuts, but he worked mainly in ink, watercolour and sepia, and did not work extensively in oils until his reputation was more established.

His landscapes, mostly of northern Germany, were inspired by trips from 1801 to the Baltic coast, Bohemia, the Krkonoše and the Harz Mountains. He made pencil studies of places such as the cliffs on Rügen and the Elbe, but rendered the atmospheric effects of mist, sun and moon from memory. His key innovation was to treat landscape not as a backdrop subordinated to human drama but as a self-contained emotive subject. He often used the Rückenfigur, a person seen from behind, to draw the viewer into sharing the contemplation of nature.

Resentment of the French occupation of Pomerania in 1813 led him to put motifs from German folklore in his work. In Old Heroes' Graves (1812) and Fir Forest with the French Dragoon and the Raven (c. 1813) he conveyed political symbols by means of the landscape alone, a first in the history of art. He suffered depressive episodes, and after 1826 vultures, owls, graveyards and ruins became permanent motifs, while his colours grew darker.

Friedrich married Caroline Bommer on 21 January 1818, and found patrons in Russia: Grand Duke Nikolai Pavlovich visited his studio in 1820, and the poet Vasily Zhukovsky helped him for decades. His reputation nevertheless fell over his last fifteen years, and he lived as a recluse in relative poverty. A first stroke in June 1835 greatly reduced his ability to paint. He died in Dresden on 7 May 1840, little noticed by the artistic community.

A Berlin exhibition of thirty-two of his works in 1906 began a renewed appreciation. He influenced Expressionist artists and the Surrealists, among them Max Ernst. The Nazis used his work to promote their ideology in the 1930s, and the association damaged his reputation for decades. Scholars later placed him in a purely art-historical context, and since the 1970s he has been regarded as one of the most important artists of German Romanticism.
caspian-sea: The Caspian Sea is an endorheic basin lying east of the Caucasus, west of the steppe of Central Asia, south of the plains of Southern Russia and north of the Iranian Plateau. It covers 371,000 square kilometres, stretches 1,200 kilometres from north to south with an average width of 320 kilometres, and lies about 27 metres below sea level. Its salinity is about a third of that of average seawater. The Volga, Europe's longest river, is its main freshwater inflow, entering at the shallow north end.

Like the Black Sea, it is a remnant of the ancient Paratethys Sea, and it became landlocked in the Late Miocene, about 5.5 million years ago, through tectonic uplift and a fall in sea level. The Caspian seal is the only aquatic mammal endemic to it, and the sea is known for its caviar and oil industries.

The earliest hominid remains found around the Caspian are from Dmanisi, about 1.8 million years old, and finds in the Hotu and Kamarband caves in Iran suggest human habitation south of the sea as early as 11,000 years ago. The sea's name derives from the ancient Caspi people, who lived to its southwest. Strabo wrote that the territory called Caspiane was named after the Caspian tribe, as was the sea, but that the tribe had disappeared. Greeks and Persians in antiquity called it the Hyrcanian Sea.

Other names reflect later powers. Arabic writers called it the sea of the Khazars, and Turkish, Azerbaijani and Turkmen still call it the Khazar sea after the Khazar Khaganate, a large empire based north of the sea between the 7th and 10th centuries. Since the medieval period traders reached it by portages linking the Volga with the Don and with rivers flowing into the Baltic, and canals followed from the early 18th century. Its shores were bordered in turn by Safavid, Afsharid, Zand, Qajar and Pahlavi Iran, and by the Tsardom of Russia, the Russian Empire and the Soviet Union.

Five states border the sea along about 4,800 kilometres of coastline: Kazakhstan, Russia, Azerbaijan, Iran and Turkmenistan. A treaty of 1931 between Iran and the Soviet Union stated that the sea belonged to both. Whether it is in law a sea or a lake was long debated among the five, because the answer decides access to oil and natural gas, fishing and international waters.
cassiodorus: Magnus Aurelius Cassiodorus Senator was born at Scylletium, near present-day Catanzaro in Calabria, into a family of Syrian origin. Senator was part of his surname, not his rank. His family had served the state for generations: his great-grandfather held a command defending the coasts of southern Italy against Vandal sea-raiders, his grandfather appears in a Roman embassy to Attila the Hun, and his father of the same name served Odovacer and then Theoderic the Great, finally as Praetorian Prefect. Cassiodorus began his career about his twentieth year as his father's consiliarius, a legal adviser in complex cases.

He was quaestor sacri palatii from about 507 to 511, consul in 514 and later magister officiorum under Theoderic and under the regency for Theoderic's young successor Athalaric. At Ravenna his rhetorical skill led to his drafting important public documents. He rose to praetorian prefect for Italy, effectively the head of the Ostrogothic civil government. James O'Donnell considers it almost indisputable that in 523 he accepted advancement as the immediate successor of Boethius, who was imprisoned and later executed, and notes that Cassiodorus's letters never mention it.

Athalaric died in early 534, and the rest of Cassiodorus's public career was dominated by the Byzantine reconquest and Ostrogothic dynastic intrigue. His last letters were drafted in the name of Vitiges. Around 537–38 he left Italy for Constantinople, where he stayed for almost two decades, concentrating on religious questions. He had earlier worked with Pope Agapetus I on a plan for a library of Greek and Latin texts to support a Christian school in Rome. In retirement he founded the monastery of Vivarium on his family estates on the shore of the Ionian Sea.

His writings include the Chronica, ending at 519, a Gothic History of 526 to 533 known only through the abridgment by Jordanes, the Variae epistolae, Theoderic's state papers, and an Exposition of the Psalms. The Institutiones divinarum et saecularium litterarum, written between 543 and 555, guided the monks' studies in place of the school he had planned in Rome. Its first book treats Christian texts and its second the liberal arts, which he valued mainly as aids to the study of divinity. His last known work, De orthographia of about 580, was completed when he was 93.

Vivarium had a communal monastery and a retreat for hermits, apparently without a strict rule. Cassiodorus had a complete Bible in a single volume, the Codex Grandior, made for his monks. Ceolfrith bought it in 679–80 and took it to Wearmouth Jarrow, where it served as the model for the Codex Amiatinus. The library was later dispersed, but his promotion of regular manuscript copying in monasteries helped preserve classical and Christian literature.
cassius-dio: Lucius Cassius Dio was the son of Cassius Apronianus, a Roman senator of the Cassia gens who was born and raised at Nicaea in Bithynia. Byzantine tradition holds that his mother was the daughter or sister of the Greek orator and philosopher Dio Chrysostom, though this has been disputed. Although Dio was a Roman citizen he wrote in Greek. He kept a love for Nicaea, which he called my home, while he described his villa at Capua as the place where he spent his time whenever he was in Italy.

For most of his life Dio served the state. He was a senator under Commodus and became a suffect consul in about 205. After the death of Septimius Severus he was governor of Smyrna, and he was also proconsul in Africa and in Pannonia. Severus Alexander held him in the highest esteem and made him consul a second time in 229. In his later years Dio went back to Bithynia, where he died. He was either the grandfather or the great-grandfather of another Cassius Dio, consul in 291.

Dio's Roman History, written in Greek in 80 books, began with the arrival of Aeneas in Italy and the founding of Rome by his descendant Romulus, and ran through the Republic and Empire to 229 CE. By his own account he spent ten years collecting the achievements of the Romans down to the death of Severus in 211, and twelve more composing the work. Until the first century BCE he gives only a summary of events; after that his accounts become more detailed. It is one of only three written Roman sources for the revolt of Boudica in 60 to 61 CE.

The work survives unevenly. The first 21 books are partly reconstructed from fragments and from the 12th-century epitome of Joannes Zonaras, and books 22 to 35 were already lost by his time. Books 36 to 54, covering 65 to 12 BCE, are nearly complete, as are books 56 to 60, from 9 to 54 CE. For the last twenty books only fragments and the abridgement by the 11th-century monk John Xiphilinus remain. Dio has often been dismissed as unreliable, but some recent scholars have stressed the sophistication of his political and historical interpretation.
caste: A caste is a fixed social group into which an individual is born within a system of social stratification. Members are expected to marry only within the same caste, to follow lifestyles often linked to a particular occupation, and to hold a ritual status within a hierarchy. Interaction between castes follows cultural notions of exclusion, with some castes considered more pure and others more polluted. The standard ethnographic example is the division of India's Hindu society into rigid groups, whose roots lie in South Asia's ancient history. Scholars have used it as a model for studying caste-like divisions elsewhere.

The English word comes from the Spanish and Portuguese casta, which a Spanish dictionary of 1569 defined as race, lineage, tribe or breed, and which derives from a Gothic word for a group of animals. The Portuguese, the first Europeans to reach India by sea in 1498, were the first to use casta in its modern sense, applying it to the thousands of endogamous, hereditary Indian groups they met. The spelling caste with this meaning is first attested in English in 1613.

In India the system rests on an old four-fold theoretical classification called varna, Brahmin, Kshatriya, Vaishya and Shudra, laid over the social groups called jāti. One 2016 genetic study concluded that endogamous jatis originated during the Gupta Empire. From 1901 British census authorities sorted all jatis into the four varna categories. Today there are around 3,000 castes and 25,000 sub-castes in India.

Writers have reported caste systems in many regions. In Nigeria the osu caste among the Igbo is determined by birth and brings ostracism. In Rwanda and Burundi the Maquet study of 1961 described the Tutsi, Hutu and Twa as ranked by birth. The Songhai economy was based on a caste system, with metalworkers, fishermen and carpenters among the most common groups. In Bali, ethnographers described three or four castes modelled on the Indian pattern. For centuries the Cagots of the Pyrenees and the Basque provinces were treated as an inferior caste and obliged to use separate church doors.

In colonial Spanish America, mixed-race groups were called castas, but the social order was otherwise fluid, and scholars dispute how far the Latin American and South Asian systems can be compared. The term is also used in biology for groups of ants and bees, which early observers named after the Indian system. Some scholars, such as Heidi Fjeld for pre-1950s Tibet, argue that other societies were functionally caste systems, while others reject the label.
castel-santangelo: The tomb of the Roman emperor Hadrian was erected on the right bank of the Tiber between 134 and 139. Originally it was a decorated cylinder with a garden on top and a golden quadriga. Hadrian's ashes were placed there a year after his death at Baiae in 138, together with those of his wife Sabina and of his first adopted son, Lucius Aelius, who died in 138. The remains of later emperors were also deposited there, the last recorded being Caracalla in 217. Hadrian also built the Pons Aelius, which faces the mausoleum and still gives an approach from the centre of Rome.

The building became a military fortress in 401 and was included in the Aurelian Walls under Flavius Honorius Augustus. Visigoth looters scattered the urns and ashes during Alaric's sack of Rome in 410. When the Goths besieged Rome in 537, the defenders threw the original bronze and stone statuary down upon them, as Procopius recounts. Stone from the tomb was later reused: Giorgio Vasari writes that columns were taken from it for Saint Peter's. The capstone of a funerary urn, probably Hadrian's, ended up in Saint Peter's Basilica, covered the tomb of Otto II and was later built into a Renaissance baptistery.

The popes turned the structure into a castle, beginning in the 14th century, and linked it to Saint Peter's Basilica by a covered fortified corridor, the Passetto di Borgo. Pope Clement VII took refuge there from the Landsknechte of Charles V during the Sack of Rome in 1527. Leo X built a chapel, and Paul III added a rich apartment so that a pope would have a fitting place to stay in any later siege. The Papal State also used it as a prison, and Giordano Bruno, held there for six years, and Benvenuto Cellini were among its prisoners.

According to legend, the Archangel Michael appeared on top of the mausoleum and sheathed his sword to mark the end of the plague of 590, which gave the castle its present name. In 1536 Raffaello da Montelupo made a marble statue of Saint Michael to stand on the roof. Peter Anton von Verschaffelt's bronze statue of the same subject replaced it in 1753, and Montelupo's can be seen in a courtyard inside. The castle is the setting for the third act of Giacomo Puccini's opera Tosca of 1900. It was decommissioned in 1901 and is now the Museo Nazionale di Castel Sant'Angelo.
castor-and-pollux: Castor and Pollux, or Polydeuces, are twin half-brothers whose mother was Leda. The sources disagree about their parentage. In the Homeric Odyssey they are sons of Tyndareus alone, the king of Sparta, and in the Hesiodic Catalogue of Women sons of Zeus. Pindar's Nemean Odes gives the conventional account, in which only Pollux was fathered by Zeus, which explains why Pollux was granted immortality and Castor was mortal. In the Iliad, Helen says that her brothers are dead and buried at home in Lacedaemon, which suggests that in some early traditions both were mortal. Scholars connect them with the Indo-European horse twins, such as the Vedic Ashvins.

Both brothers were excellent horsemen and hunters. They took part in the hunt of the Calydonian Boar and joined the crew of the Argo, on which Pollux defeated King Amycus of the Bebryces in a boxing contest. When Theseus abducted their sister Helen, they invaded Attica to rescue her and took Theseus's mother Aethra to Sparta as her slave.

They then carried off the Leucippides, Phoebe and Hilaeira, who were betrothed to their cousins Idas and Lynceus. A cattle raid ended in a quarrel, and Idas fatally wounded Castor with a spear. Pollux killed Lynceus, and Zeus struck Idas dead with a thunderbolt. Zeus then offered Pollux a choice between all of Olympus and sharing his immortality with his dying brother. Pollux chose to share it, so the twins alternate between Olympus and Hades. They became the two brightest stars of the constellation Gemini, and were said to appear to sailors as St. Elmo's fire. They were regarded as patrons of travellers, sailors, horsemen and athletes, intervening at moments of crisis.

The twins were important at Sparta. A symbol of them was two upright posts joined by crossbars, called dokana, and it was carried before the army in the field. Their grave-shrine was at Therapne, across the Eurotas from Sparta. The Etruscans venerated them as Kastur and Pultuce.

The Romans revered them from the 5th century BCE, probably through the Greek colonies of Magna Graecia. According to legend the twins fought at the head of the Roman army at the Battle of Lake Regillus and brought the news of victory to Rome, and the temple of Castor and Pollux was built in the Roman Forum to fulfil a vow made after that battle. On 15 July, their feast day, 1,800 equestrians paraded through Rome. After the rise of Christianity, Pope Gelasius I in the 5th century still attested a cult of the Castores that people did not want to abandon, and the church adopted Saints Peter and Paul in place of the twins as patrons of travellers.
catamarca-province: Catamarca lies in the northwest of Argentina and covers 102,602 square kilometres. It borders Salta, Tucumán, Santiago del Estero, Córdoba and La Rioja, and to the west the country of Chile. Eighty percent of the territory is covered by mountains, which fall into four systems: the Pampean sierras in the east and centre, the Narváez-Cerro Negro-Famatina system in the west, a cordilleran transition area at the western extreme, and the Puna, an elevated portion in the northwest.

The province is semi-arid, and the scarce water determines where people live: agriculture is concentrated in pockets and valleys between the mountains, and in the east the population gathers around watercourses from which canals and ditches carry the water. The Puna in the extreme west has a desert climate with very low precipitation, and snow cover is permanent at the highest peaks of the Sierra del Aconquija.

Before the Spanish conquest most of what is now Catamarca was inhabited by the Diaguita people, among them the fierce Calchaquí. In 1558 Juan Pérez de Zurita founded Londres de la Nueva Inglaterra, but it was constantly attacked by indigenous people, its population stayed small, and it was re-founded several times at new sites with new names. The sixth foundation, by Fernando de Mendoza Mate de Luna on 5 July 1683, bore the name San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca. The name of the province is believed to come either from Quechua cata, slope, and marca, fortress, or from Aymara catán, small, and marca, town.

When the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata was created in 1776, Catamarca became a subintendencia under the Salta intendency. In 1821 the province claimed its autonomy and elected Nicolás Avellaneda y Tula as its first governor. The mountains kept it isolated from the rest of Argentina until 1888, when the railways first reached it. Its valleys and dry climate attracted immigrants from Lebanon and Iran, who found it reminiscent of the orchard-lined mountain valleys they had left.

Catamarca is a province of Argentina with its capital at San Fernando del Valle de Catamarca, usually shortened to Catamarca. Its population was 429,556 at the 2022 census, and other important cities are Andalgalá, Tinogasta and Belén. The province is divided into sixteen departments.

Mining is important in its economy, notably the Bajo de la Alumbrera copper and gold mine. Among its sights are Antofagasta de la Sierra, the San Francisco Pass, the archaeological park Las Huellas del Inca and prehistoric petroglyphs.
catapult: The word catapult comes from the Latin catapulta, from the Greek katapeltēs, formed from kata, downwards, and pallō, to toss or hurl. A catapult launches a projectile at a great distance without gunpowder, by the sudden release of stored energy: tension or torsion built up slowly in springs, bows, twisted rope or elastic. King Uzziah of Judah is recorded as equipping the walls of Jerusalem with machines that shot great stones, and Jaina texts record that Ajatashatru of Magadha used catapults against the Licchavis in the 5th century BCE. In China the mangonel appeared in the same century.

Greek catapults were invented in the early 4th century BCE. Diodorus Siculus describes a mechanical arrow-firing catapult devised by a Greek task force in 399 BCE and used at the siege of Motya in 397 BCE. It developed from the gastraphetes, or belly-bow, a foot-held crossbow that stored more energy than ordinary bows.

An Athenian arsenal inscription dated between 338 and 326 BCE is the first clear evidence for torsion catapults, which were more powerful than crossbow types and came to dominate Greek and Roman artillery. The change was probably spurred by the engineers of Philip II of Macedonia, who used arrow-firing machines at the siege of Perinth in 340 BCE. Alexander the Great used catapults at the Battle of Jaxartes and in sieges. The Romans began to use them in their wars against Syracuse, Macedon, Sparta and Aetolia, and later fitted ballistae to warships.

Medieval armies used ballistae, springalds, mangonels and trebuchets against castles and walled cities, throwing stones, incendiary missiles, and sometimes carcasses or garbage over the walls. The trebuchet was probably the most powerful, in a traction form worked by people and a counterpoise form worked by a counterweight. At the siege of Stirling Castle in 1304 the army of Edward I built a giant trebuchet called Warwolf, which levelled a section of wall.

Defences improved until catapults were largely ineffective, and the Viking siege of Paris in 885–6 used nearly every siege instrument known to the classical world to little effect. Leonardo da Vinci designed a catapult powered by a leaf spring and winding drum, which enthusiasts have since built. The last large-scale army use was in the trench warfare of the First World War, when catapults threw hand grenades into enemy trenches until small mortars replaced them. Catapults also launched aircraft from ships, from British experiments in 1917 to common fittings on major warships by the 1930s.
catharism: Few Cathar texts survive, and much of what is known of Cathar thought comes from Catholic denunciations of the movement. Most historians of the 20th century agreed that its beliefs came from the East, from the weakening Byzantine Empire, along the trade routes, and spread from the First Bulgarian Empire towards the Netherlands. The movement appears to have been strongly influenced by the Bogomils of the First Bulgarian Empire, and may have begun among followers of the Paulician movement in Armenia and eastern Anatolia who were resettled in Thrace. The name Cathar, from the Greek for the pure ones, was coined by Catholic theologians; in their own texts the believers called themselves Good Men, Good Women or Good Christians.

According to Catholic sources, Cathars held that there were two Gods, a good God of the spiritual realm and an evil god who made the physical world and whom they identified with Satan. Some communities held a mitigated dualism, in which Satan had once been the true God's servant before he rebelled; others, probably a majority over time, held an absolute dualism of two equal principles. Human souls were thought to be sexless spirits trapped in matter, reincarnated until they were freed through the consolamentum, a rite that removed sin and made the believer a Perfect. The Cathars honoured Jesus but denied his physical incarnation and resurrection.

The Perfecti lived in austerity, avoided animal food and anything produced by sexual reproduction, and travelled in pairs to minister to the people. Ordinary believers were called credentes. Women could be Perfect and administer the consolamentum. By about 1140 a liturgy and doctrine had been set, and bishoprics were created, first at Albi around 1165, then at Toulouse, Carcassonne and Agen after the council of 1167 at Saint-Félix-Lauragais.

Papal missions from 1147 onwards had little lasting effect. In January 1208 the papal legate Pierre de Castelnau was murdered after excommunicating Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse. The crusade that followed besieged Béziers on 22 July 1209, and the Treaty of Paris of 1229 ended the official war, leaving the princes of Languedoc dispossessed of much of their lands. Persecution by the Inquisition continued: Peire Autier, leader of a revival in the Pyrenean foothills, was executed at Toulouse in April 1310, and the last known Perfect in Languedoc, Guillaume Bélibaste, in 1321.

Since the 1990s some historians, notably R. I. Moore, have questioned whether Catharism existed as an organised religion at all, arguing that churchmen largely constructed it from a broader spiritual revival. The region of Cathar castles such as Montségur and Carcassonne is now called Pays cathare. The Cathars have also been tied, without sound basis, to the Holy Grail and the Knights Templar.
catherine-de-medici: Catherine was born Caterina Maria Romula de' Medici in Florence, the only child of Lorenzo de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, and Madeleine de la Tour d'Auvergne, countess of Boulogne. Her parents had married the year before at Amboise as part of an alliance between Francis I of France and Lorenzo's uncle Pope Leo X. Within a month of her birth both parents were dead. She was raised first by her grandmother Alfonsina Orsini and then by her aunt Clarice de' Medici, and from 1523 lived under the protection of her cousin Pope Clement VII. In Florence she was called duchessina, the little duchess.

Clement arranged her marriage to Henry, second son of Francis I. The wedding took place in Marseille on 28 October 1533, when both were fourteen. When Henry's elder brother died in 1536 Catherine became dauphine, and with no child for years she was told that divorce was being discussed.

As queen from 1547 she had almost no political influence: Henry gave the Château of Chenonceau, which she had wanted, to his mistress Diane de Poitiers, who stood at the centre of power. Henry's accidental death in 1559 left her the mother of the fifteen-year-old Francis II, whose reign the Guise brothers dominated. When Francis died in 1560 she became regent for the ten-year-old Charles IX and presided over his council. She summoned church leaders to the Colloquy of Poissy, which failed in October 1561, and in January 1562 issued the tolerant Edict of Saint-Germain.

On 1 March 1562 the Duke of Guise and his men attacked Huguenots worshipping at Vassy, killing 74; the massacre lit the fuse of the French Wars of Religion, and for thirty years France was in civil war or armed truce. Catherine at first made concessions to the Huguenots but failed to grasp the theology that drove them, and later turned to hardline policies. She was blamed for the persecutions under her sons, above all the St Bartholomew's Day massacre of 1572. After Charles IX died in 1574 she supported Henry III, her favourite son, until the last few weeks of her life.

Catherine believed in the humanist ideal of the learned prince and, once she controlled the royal purse, ran a programme of artistic patronage for three decades. An inventory after her death shows tapestries, maps, sculptures and hundreds of portraits, many by Jean Clouet and his son François Clouet.

Some historians excuse her from blame for the worst decisions of the crown, though her letters show ruthlessness. Without her, it is unlikely that her sons would have remained in power, and she has been called the most important woman in Europe in the 16th century.
catholicism: The word catholic comes from the Greek katholikos, meaning universal, and is first attested as a description of the church in the early second century. The first known use of the phrase the catholic church is in a letter written around 100 CE by Ignatius of Antioch to the Smyrnaeans. In 380 Theodosius I issued the edict De fide catolica when he established the state church of the Roman Empire.

The Catholic Church teaches that its public ministry began at Pentecost, and that the pope, the bishop of Rome, is the successor of Saint Peter. Scholars differ on the origin of the office. Some hold that Peter was the first bishop of Rome; others argue that the papacy does not depend on that view. Bart D. Ehrman and Raymond E. Brown note that a structure with a single bishop and several presbyters was adopted in Rome only in the mid-2nd century.

The church follows an episcopal polity with three levels of clergy: bishops, who hold jurisdiction over a diocese or eparchy; priests; and deacons. The pope's jurisdiction is called the Holy See, which governs through the Roman Curia. The church consists of 24 autonomous churches, of which the largest is the Latin Church and the other 23 are Eastern Catholic Churches, whose differing rites reflect historical and cultural diversity rather than differences in belief.

Catholic doctrine is rooted in the Nicene Creed. The church holds that revelation has two modes of transmission, Sacred Scripture and Sacred Tradition, authentically interpreted by the Magisterium, its teaching authority. It teaches that Christ instituted seven sacraments. The Eucharist, offered in the Mass, is seen as the source and summit of Christian life: Catholics believe that through consecration by a priest the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.

Divisions shaped the church's relations with other Christians. The Church of the East separated after the Council of Ephesus in 431 and the Oriental Orthodox Churches after the Council of Chalcedon in 451. The separation from the Eastern Orthodox churches developed gradually, in disputes especially over papal authority, and was solidified by the Fourth Crusade. The Protestant Reformation of the 16th century led to new Christian traditions and prompted the Catholic Counter‑Reformation.

Catholic social teaching, whose foundations are widely held to have been laid by Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum in 1891, stresses care for the poor and the sick. The church is the largest non-government provider of education and medical services in the world.
catiline: Catiline belonged to the patrician gens Sergia, which claimed descent from a Trojan companion of Aeneas, though no Sergius had been consul since 429 BCE. His father was poor by aristocratic standards. He served under Gnaeus Pompeius Strabo in the Social War and joined Sulla in 82 BCE. Ancient sources say he grew rich in Sulla's proscriptions, and Cicero accused him of killing his brother and two brothers-in-law, among them Marcus Marius Gratidianus. Some modern historians doubt his part in Gratidianus's death and see Cicero's story as political slander. He certainly profited by buying estates cheaply, and by the end of Sulla's dictatorship he was rich.

Catiline was praetor by 68 BCE and governed Africa in 67–66. On his return he was refused as a candidate for the consulship, and embassies from Africa protested his maladministration. A trial for corruption in 65 BCE ended in acquittal, with former consuls speaking for him. In the elections for 64 BCE, bankrolled by Caesar and Crassus, he lost to Cicero and Gaius Antonius Hybrida. A second prosecution for murder in the proscriptions also ended in acquittal. He stood again for 62 BCE and lost to Decimus Junius Silanus and Lucius Licinius Murena, after Cicero had presided at the elections in a cuirass and with a bodyguard.

Defeated, Catiline gathered dispossessed farmers, ruined Sullan veterans and senators whose careers had stalled, and a rising in Etruria began under Gaius Manlius. In October 63 BCE Crassus gave Cicero anonymous letters warning of a massacre, and the senate passed its emergency decree. Cicero denounced Catiline in the senate on 7 November, and Catiline left Rome, proclaimed himself consul at Faesulae, and was declared a public enemy. Cicero, with the aid of Gallic envoys, caught the conspirators who had stayed in Rome, and they were executed without trial on 5 December.

After the executions much of Catiline's army melted away, leaving perhaps just over three thousand men, and the Apennine passes to Gaul were blocked. He turned to fight at Pistoria, possibly on 3 January 62 BCE, where Marcus Petreius broke his centre. Sallust wrote that Catiline's men fell where they had stood and that he was found far ahead of them among the slain, still breathing. His name became a byword for villainy, and Sallust made him a symbol of the Republic's moral decline. The evidence is overwhelmingly Ciceronean, and some modern historians have argued that Cicero exaggerated or helped to create the conspiracy, though such defences are largely speculative.
cato-the-elder: Marcus Porcius Cato was born in the municipal town of Tusculum, like some generations of his ancestors. His family was plebeian and noted for military service, but the Tusculan Porcii had never held Roman magistracy, so at the start of his career in Rome he was regarded as a novus homo, a new man. After his father's death he inherited a small property in Sabine territory and spent his childhood overseeing the farm. Nearby stood the hut of Manius Curius Dentatus, whose simple character he admired and sought to imitate. The surname Cato comes from the Latin catus, indicating common sense that results from natural wisdom combined with experience.

Cato served in the Second Punic War, at Capua in 214, at the siege of Tarentum in 209, and, it is recorded, at the Battle of the Metaurus, where Hasdrubal Barca was slain. He was quaestor under Scipio Africanus in Sicily, where the two quarrelled over Scipio's alleged extravagance. Elected consul in 195 with his patron Lucius Valerius Flaccus, he enacted the first two of the Porcian Laws, which expanded the protection of Roman citizens against degrading or capricious punishment. In the debate over repealing the Oppian Law, which restricted women's luxury, he made an inflexible speech against repeal, but the law was repealed. In 191 he served as a legate at the Battle of Thermopylae against Antiochus III.

As censor from 184 he revised the lists of senators and knights with unsparing severity, expelling men he judged unworthy. He repaired the aqueducts, extended the sewage system and prevented private persons from drawing off public water. He also raised the amount paid by the publicani for tax collection and reduced contract prices for public works, which created controversy. He opposed Hellenistic influence, and urged the dismissal of the philosophers Carneades, Diogenes and Critolaus when they came to Rome as ambassadors from Athens. He often ended his speeches by saying Carthago delenda est, Carthage must be destroyed.

Cato was the first to write history in Latin, in his Origines, a now fragmentary work on the history of Rome. His manual on running a farm, De agri cultura, written about 160, is his only work that survives complete and is the oldest extant prose in Latin. It is a miscellaneous collection of rules of husbandry and management, with sidelights on country life in the 2nd century BCE, and it assumes a farm run and staffed by slaves. Some have argued that without the impact of his writing Latin might have been supplanted by Greek as the literary language of Rome. His date of birth is deduced from conflicting reports of his age at death in 149 BCE; Cicero and Pliny give 234 BCE.
cato-the-younger: Cato was born in 95 BCE, the son of a father of the same name and of Livia, and was descended from Cato the Elder, his great-grandfather, the first of the family to be elected consul. He and his sister Porcia were orphaned, probably before he was four, and were taken in by their maternal uncle Marcus Livius Drusus. Stories of his childhood are broadly unreliable and were told to suggest that his adult character was formed early. Plutarch reports that he studied Stoicism under Antipater of Tyre. He also adopted an austere, deliberately old-fashioned public manner: he walked rather than rode, went barefoot and wore a toga without a tunic, in imitation of statues of Rome's early founders and heroes.

As an urban quaestor at the state treasury he prosecuted and dismissed a number of its clerks and was praised for his honesty. As plebeian tribune in 62 BCE he passed laws to expand the grain dole and to force generals to give up their armies before standing in elections, and he blocked a bill of Pompey's allies. In 61 BCE he refused Pompey's offer of a marriage alliance with one of his nieces. He opposed, with varying success, the legislation of Caesar's first consulship in 59 BCE. He was praised for his honest administration in Cyprus and was elected praetor for 54 BCE.

The First Triumvirate was formed to get around his obstruction. From about 52 BCE he tried to separate Pompey from Caesar and spread the view that Caesar was a tyrant in the making. Cato seems never to have advocated civil war, but he was criticised for being too uncompromising, and many scholars hold that his strategy contributed to the war that began in January 49 BCE.

In the civil war Cato joined Pompey and tried to limit the deaths of fellow citizens. In Africa he commanded Utica and strengthened its defences. Metellus Scipio rejected his advice of attrition, fought at Thapsus and was annihilated. Cato evacuated the Roman citizens who wished to flee, sent his family and allies to seek pardon and took his own life rather than accept what he saw as Caesar's tyrannical pardon.

His death produced eulogies by Cicero and Brutus; Caesar replied with an Anticato, which has not survived. Kit Morell argues that the ancient portrait of a Stoic martyr has distorted the historical Cato.
caucasian-war: The war was fought by the Russian Imperial Army and Cossack settlers against peoples of the North Caucasus, among them the Adyghe, Abazins, Ubykhs, Chechens and Dagestanis, who resisted subjugation as the tsars sought to expand. Other parts of the Caucasus were incorporated into the Russian Empire in the 19th century through Russian wars with Persia, and in 1801 Russia annexed the Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti. Russian control of the Georgian Military Road divided the conflict into the Russo-Circassian War in the west and the conquest of Chechnya and Dagestan in the east.

The war ran through the reigns of Alexander I, Nicholas I and Alexander II. The first period of the invasion achieved surprisingly little and ended around 1825 with the death of Alexander I and the Decembrist Revolt. Wars with Persia and Turkey then took the empire's attention until 1833. When fighting resumed it marked the beginning of what is now referred to as the Circassian genocide. Resistance was led by Ghazi Mollah, Hamzat Bek and Hadji Murad, and then by Imam Shamil, who led the mountaineers from 1834 until his capture in 1859.

In August 1843 Shamil's men converged on a Russian column at Untsukul, killing 486, and within four weeks took every Russian outpost in Avaria but one. In 1845 they withstood a major offensive led by Prince Vorontsov. A truce during the Crimean War ended in 1855. Between 1856 and 1859 an army of 250,000 under General Baryatinsky broke the mountaineers' resistance in the east, and Shamil surrendered and was exiled to central Russia. Fighting went on with the Circassians in the west until a manifesto of Alexander II declared hostilities at an end on 2 June 1864.

One of the war's most dramatic consequences was the mass forced emigration of mainly Muslim mountain peoples to the Ottoman Empire and, less so, to Persia. Land was confiscated and Cossack and Russian military colonists were settled in it. Circassians made up 40 per cent of the North Caucasus population in 1795, 30 per cent in 1835 and 25 per cent in 1858.

Exiles landed at Black Sea ports such as Trabzon, Samsun and Varna and were held in camps in conditions of overcrowding, disease and hunger. At Samsun up to 110,000 refugees were gathered, and in some phases more than 200 died each day. The Ottoman state sometimes settled the newcomers as militia on its borders. A few thousand applied to return in 1861-67.
caucasus: The Caucasus lies between the Black Sea and the Caspian Sea. The Greater Caucasus range in the north has conventionally been taken as a natural barrier between Europe and Asia, and Mount Elbrus, at 5,642 metres, stands in its western part. The Lesser Caucasus in the south includes the Armenian highlands. The region is divided into the North Caucasus and the South Caucasus. More than 50 ethnic groups live here. Three language families, the Kartvelian, Northwest Caucasian and Northeast Caucasian, are indigenous to the area, alongside Indo-European and Turkic languages.

Fossils found at Dmanisi in Georgia, dated to 1.8 million years ago, are the earliest clear evidence of early humans outside Africa. The Kura–Araxes culture, from about 4000 BCE to about 2000 BCE, spread over the southern Caucasus and beyond. The first Bronze Age states, among them Urartu, formed between the 15th and 10th centuries BCE. After the conquests of Alexander the Great, Colchis, Iberia, Armenia and Caucasian Albania were states strongly marked by Greek culture.

Rome and Parthia contested the region from the 1st century BCE, and later Rome and the Sasanian Empire. The Arsacid dynasty of Armenia adopted Christianity as a state religion in 301 CE, and Georgia and Caucasian Albania also became Christian. After the Muslim conquest of Persia large parts of the region came under Arab rule. In the 12th century the Georgian king David the Builder drove Muslim rulers out of the Caucasus, and under Queen Tamar, in 1194–1204, Georgia defeated Seljuk invasions and became the strongest Christian state in the Near East.

Russia expanded south after the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca of 1774, annexed the Georgian Kingdom of Kartli-Kakheti in 1801 and conquered the North Caucasus in the second half of the 19th century. In the Caucasian Wars the Russian military expelled the Circassians from their homeland. Georgia, Azerbaijan and Armenia became independent after the Soviet Union dissolved in 1991.

The Caucasus is shared today by Georgia, Armenia, Azerbaijan and the Russian Federation, whose republics there include Dagestan, Chechnya and North Ossetia–Alania. Georgia is predominantly Orthodox Christian, Armenia Armenian Apostolic and Azerbaijan Shia Muslim. The region is a biodiversity hotspot and holds oil, natural gas and many minerals.
cavalry-warfare: Cavalry are soldiers or warriors who fight mounted on horseback. Forces that used other animals or platforms, such as chariots, camels or elephants, were not usually given the name. Before the Iron Age the role of cavalry on the battlefield was largely performed by light chariots, which originated with the Sintashta-Petrovka culture in Central Asia, spread through nomadic or semi-nomadic Indo-Iranians, and were adopted by settled peoples, among them the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt from 1550 BCE and the Assyrian army.

A mounted soldier had the advantages of greater height, speed and inertial mass over an opponent on foot, which were greatly valued in the ancient and medieval eras. Cavalry served as light cavalry in reconnaissance, screening and skirmishing, or as heavy cavalry for shock attacks. Some hosts were mostly cavalry, particularly in the nomadic societies of Asia, such as the Huns of Attila and the later Mongol armies. The Xiongnu, Avars, Khitans, Mongols and other Turkic peoples won substantial successes against settled agrarian and urban societies through strategic and tactical mobility.

In Europe, as heavy infantry declined with the fall of the Roman Empire, heavy cavalry became more effective and rose to dominate the battlefield; it evolved into the mounted knights of the medieval period. The Mamluks, who originated in the 9th century as Central Asian captives used as mounted auxiliaries by Arab armies, were trained as cavalry and followed al-furusiyya, a code that included tactics, horsemanship and archery. Cavalry formed the core of the Ottoman armies from the 14th to the 17th centuries, and in India it played a major role from the Gupta period onwards. India also has the oldest evidence for toe-stirrups.

Ownership of heavy cavalry horses was a mark of wealth among settled peoples from the beginning of civilization to the 20th century, since a horse involved considerable expense in breeding, training and equipment and had little productive use except transport. In the 17th century European cavalry discarded most of its armour, ineffective against muskets and cannon.

Cavalry was important at Blenheim in 1704, Rossbach in 1757 and Marengo in 1800. Barbed wire, machine guns and rapid-fire rifles proved deadly to horse-mounted troops on the Western Front in World War I, and by early 1915 most cavalry units no longer saw front-line action. In the interwar period many cavalry units were converted into motorized or mechanized infantry or into tank troops, and some cavalry still served in World War II. Most horse-mounted units in modern armies now serve in ceremonial roles.
cebu: Cebu lies east of Negros and west of Leyte and Bohol in the Central Visayas. The province consists of Cebu Island and 167 smaller islands and islets, among them Mactan, Bantayan, Malapascua, Olango and the Camotes Islands. The main island is long and narrow, stretching 196 km from north to south and 32 km across at its widest, with limestone plateaus, coastal plains and rugged mountain ranges. The climate is tropical, and little forest remains. The name is possibly derived from a hypothetical Proto-Philippine word meaning to bathe or to wade into the water.

Cebu was a native kingdom before the arrival of the Spaniards. Visayan folklore relates that it was founded by Sri Lumay, a half-Malay, half-Tamil from Sumatra, and that its capital was Singhapala, Tamil-Sanskrit for Lion City. Ferdinand Magellan left Sanlúcar de Barrameda with five ships and 250 people on 20 September 1519 and reached the Philippines on 16 March 1521. Rajah Kolambu of Mazaua told the crews to sail to Cebu, where they could trade and obtain provisions. In 1898 the island was ceded to the United States, and Cebu became a chartered city on 24 February 1937.

In April 1942 Japanese soldiers landed, and Cebu served as a Japanese base during the occupation. Cebuano guerrillas fought the Japanese, and the guerrilla leader James M. Cushing is credited with the Koga Papers, said to have changed American plans for retaking the Philippines. Combined Filipino and American forces landed in March 1945. Cebu later became a centre of resistance to the Marcos government, and from Fuente Osmeña circle in Cebu City the opposition relaunched its civil disobedience campaign on 22 February 1986, in the days leading up to the People Power revolution.

Cebu City, nicknamed the Queen City of the South, is the capital and largest city, and with Lapu-Lapu and Mandaue it is governed independently of the province. The province counts 53 cities and municipalities. Its population was 3,400,522 at the 2024 census, or 5,151,274 with the three independent cities. About 95 per cent of Cebuanos are Roman Catholic, and Cebuano is the main language. The Sinulog Festival is the best known of the many festivals that have earned Cebu the name Festival Island.
cecil-rhodes: Cecil John Rhodes was born on 5 July 1853 at Bishop's Stortford in Hertfordshire, the fourth son and sixth child of the Reverend Francis William Rhodes, vicar of the town. His family sent him to Natal as a teenager in the hope that the climate would improve his poor health, and he arrived in Durban on 1 September 1870. He worked on his brother's cotton farm, and in 1871 entered the diamond trade at Kimberley. In 1873 he entered Oriel College, Oxford, but stayed one term before illness sent him back to Kimberley, and he returned to Oxford in 1876. His admiration for the Oxford tutorial system later shaped his plans for a scholarship.

With funding from Rothschild and Company, Rhodes began to buy out and consolidate diamond mines, and gained a near-complete monopoly of the world diamond market. He founded De Beers in 1888. He entered the Cape Parliament in 1881 and became prime minister of the Cape Colony in 1890. Through the Glen Grey Act he took land from black Africans, saying that they had to be driven off their land to stimulate them to labour, and the Franchise and Ballot Act tripled the wealth requirement for voting, which in effect barred black voters.

Rhodes used his wealth and that of his partner Alfred Beit to obtain mineral concessions from indigenous chiefs. The Rudd Concession, signed by Lobengula, king of the Ndebele, left out the promise that no more than ten white men would mine in Matabeleland, and when Lobengula tried to renounce it the British government ignored him. Settlers and the company's police committed widespread rape of Ndebele women in the early 1890s. The company named Rhodesia after him in 1895. He was forced to resign as prime minister in 1896 after the Jameson Raid, an unauthorised attack on Paul Kruger's South African Republic.

Rhodes died of heart failure on 26 March 1902, aged 48, at his cottage in Muizenberg. At his request he was buried at Malindidzimu in the Matopos hills, a site of great importance to Shona traditional religion, a choice interpreted as a gesture of colonial conquest. His will founded the Rhodes Scholarship at Oxford, which his estate funds, with the aim of promoting leadership and of rendering war impossible through friendship between the great powers. Critics cite his seizure of land and his promotion of false claims that Great Zimbabwe was built by European civilisations, and some historians attack him as a ruthless imperialist and white supremacist.
celje: Celje lies below Upper Celje Castle at the confluence of the Savinja, Hudinja, Ložnica and Voglajna rivers in the lower Savinja Valley, at the crossing of the roads connecting Ljubljana, Maribor, Velenje and the Central Sava Valley. It is a regional centre of the traditional region of Styria and is known in German as Cilli. Its name derives from the Roman Celeia; the name is of pre-Roman origin and its further etymology is unclear.

The first settlement dates from the Hallstatt era, and findings suggest that Celts coined Noric money in the region. The area was incorporated into the Roman Empire in 15 BCE as Civitas Celeia, and in 45 CE it received municipal rights as municipium Claudia Celeia under Emperor Claudius. The town was rich and densely populated, with walls, towers and multi-storied marble palaces, and a temple of Mars known across the empire. Slavic tribes razed the city in the 5th and 6th centuries, and it was rebuilt in the Early Middle Ages.

The Counts of Celje had their seat in the town from 1341 to 1456, with princely status from 1436. It received town privileges from Count Frederick II on 11 April 1451. After the counts died out in 1456 the region passed to the Habsburgs and was administered by the Duchy of Styria. The city walls and moat were built in 1473, and the town defended itself against the Turks and against peasants who had taken the Old Castle in 1515.

At the end of the 19th century Celje was a centre of German nationalism, and the 1910 census showed 66.8 percent of the population as German. In 1918 it became part of the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes. Nazi Germany occupied it in April 1941. The city lost 575 people during the war, and more than 1,500 were deported. After the war the remaining German-speaking population was expelled or executed. Celje became part of independent Slovenia after the Ten-Day War in 1991.

Celje is the third-largest city in Slovenia. Its sights include a Grayfriars' monastery founded in 1241, a 16th-century palace and the 14th-century parish church with a Gothic chapel, which keeps the throne and tombs of the counts of Cilli.
cell-theory: The discovery of cells depended on the microscope. Compound microscopes first appeared in Europe around 1620. In 1665 Robert Hooke published Micrographia, whose observations included thin slices of bottle cork. He saw a multitude of tiny pores and named them cells, from the Latin cella, a small room such as monks lived in, and cellulae, the six-sided cells of a honeycomb. What he saw were the empty walls of plant tissue, and he did not think the cells alive. Soon afterwards Anton van Leeuwenhoek, using single-lens microscopes of up to 270-fold magnification, found moving organisms, which he called animalcules, and described red blood cells and bacteria.

Credit for the theory goes usually to Matthias Jakob Schleiden and Theodor Schwann. In 1839 Schleiden proposed that every structural part of a plant was made of cells or their products, and Schwann stated that animals were too. Two tenets followed: all living organisms are composed of one or more cells, and the cell is the most basic unit of life. Schleiden also held that cells formed by a crystallisation process, an idea refuted in the 1850s by Robert Remak, Rudolf Virchow and Albert Kolliker.

In 1855 Virchow added the third tenet, Omnis cellula e cellula: all cells arise only from pre-existing cells. Remak had proposed this already, and it has been suggested that Virchow plagiarised him. In 1852 Remak had published observations of cell division, holding that new animal cells arose by binary fission. With the third tenet, classical cell theory was complete.

Modern cell theory states that all known living things consist of one or more cells, that all living cells arise from pre-existing cells by division, and that the cell is the fundamental unit of structure and function. It has traditionally governed the study of life, although some biologists who count viruses as living organisms dispute its universal application. Later work on how cells control what passes in and out set a membrane theory against bulk-phase theories of protoplasm; the plasma membrane is now described as a fluid lipid bilayer with embedded proteins, following the model of Singer and Nicolson of 1972.
celle: Celle lies in the glacial valley of the river Aller, about 40 kilometres north-east of Hanover and 120 kilometres south of Hamburg. The Lachte and the Fuhse both flow into the Aller within the town. Celle is the southern gateway to the Lüneburg Heath and, apart from Lüneburg, the largest town of Lower Saxony between Hanover and Hamburg.

Celle is first mentioned in a document of 985 as Kiellu, meaning fishing bay. In the 11th century it was granted the right to mint coins, some of which were found in the Sandur hoard in the Faroes. In 1292 Duke Otto II the Strict, a Welf who ruled the Principality of Lüneburg from 1277 to 1330, left Altencelle and founded a rectangular settlement beside the existing castle, 4 kilometres to the north-west. He granted Celle town privileges in 1301 and began its town church in 1308.

From 1378 to 1705 Celle was the official residence of the Lüneburg branch of the dukes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, of the House of Welf, who had been banished from their original ducal seat by its townsfolk. The Reformation came in 1524, and the castle chapel, built in 1570, was consecrated in 1585. George William, the last Heath Duke, ruled from 1665 until he died in Celle Castle in 1705. In the Middle Ages the town had only a few thousand inhabitants, and growth quickened only with industrialisation: 8,800 in 1818, 20,000 by 1900. Celle was an important garrison town in Nazi Germany, and during the pogrom of 9 and 10 November 1938 its synagogue escaped destruction only because of the risk to neighbouring buildings.

Celle is the capital of its district in Lower Saxony and has about 71,000 inhabitants. Its old town has more than 400 timber-framed houses, among them the Hoppenerhaus of 1532, and the Old City Hall of 1561 to 1579 is known for its sandstone carvings. Schloss Celle, begun in 1530 and enlarged in baroque style in the 17th century, has a theatre founded in 1674, the oldest still working in Germany. The Bergen-Belsen concentration camp, where Anne Frank died in 1945, lay in the district of Celle, and a memorial marks the site.
central-african-republic: The Central African Republic is a landlocked country in the interior of Africa, bordered by Cameroon, Chad, Sudan, South Sudan, the Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo. Much of it is a flat or rolling plateau savanna about 500 metres above sea level. Two-thirds of the country lies within the basin of the Ubangi River, a tributary of the Congo, and the remaining third within the basin of the Chari River, which flows into Lake Chad. About 36 per cent of the country is forest, with the densest forest in the south.

The name comes from the country's location in Central Africa and its republican government. During the colonial era it was called Ubangi-Shari, after the Ubangi and Chari rivers. Barthélemy Boganda, the first prime minister, favoured the name Central African Republic, reportedly because he envisioned a larger union of countries in Central Africa. From 1976 to 1979 the country was known as the Central African Empire.

The region has been inhabited since at least 8000 BCE. About 10,000 years ago desertification forced hunter-gatherer societies south into the Sahel, where some settled and began farming. Before 3000 BCE the domestication of the African oil palm improved nutrition and allowed populations to expand. The Bouar Megaliths in the west indicate an advanced level of habitation in the late Neolithic, c. 3500 to 2700 BCE, and ironwork developed in the region around 1000 BCE. The Ubangian people settled along the Ubangi River, and some Bantu people migrated from southwest Cameroon.

In the 16th and 17th centuries slave traders raided the region as part of the expansion of the Saharan and Nile slave routes, and captives were shipped to the Mediterranean coast, Europe, Arabia and the Western Hemisphere. In the 18th century the Bandia-Nzakara Azande peoples established the Bangassou Kingdom along the Ubangi. In the mid 19th century the Bobangi people became major slave traders. The borders were established by France, which began annexing portions to the French Congo in the late 19th century and in 1903 created the separate colony of Ubangi-Shari, part of French Equatorial Africa.

The Central African Republic became independent from France in 1960. Its capital and largest city is Bangui, on the southern border with the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Its people belong to about 80 ethnic groups, the largest being the Gbaya and the Banda. French and Sango, a creole based on the Ngbandi language, are the official languages. The Aka of the south-west have a vocal tradition of contrapuntal polyphony in four voices.
central-america: Central America is a subregion of North America, a tapering isthmus running from the southern extent of Mexico to the northwestern portion of South America. It has the Gulf of Mexico to the north, the Caribbean Sea to the northeast and the Pacific Ocean to the southwest. It is usually defined as consisting of seven countries: Belize, Costa Rica, El Salvador, Guatemala, Honduras, Nicaragua and Panama. The term is defined differently in different contexts. In Spanish-speaking countries the Americas are considered a single continent, América, of which Central America is a subregion.

The region has over 70 active volcanoes, and several active geological faults and the Central America Volcanic Arc make seismic activity high. The longest of its many mountain ranges are the Sierra Madre de Chiapas, the Cordillera Isabelia and the Cordillera de Talamanca. At 4,220 metres, Volcán Tajumulco is the highest peak.

Central America was formed more than 3 million years ago as part of the Isthmus of Panama. In the pre-Columbian era the northern areas were inhabited by the indigenous peoples of Mesoamerica, most notably the Maya, who built numerous cities. The cultures of eastern Honduras, Caribbean Nicaragua, most of Costa Rica and Panama were predominantly speakers of Chibchan languages at the time of European contact, and are grouped by some in the Isthmo-Colombian cultural area.

Spain began its colonisation from 1502 onward. Pedro de Alvarado began the conquest of Maya territory in 1523, arriving in Soconusco, and his forces systematically conquered most of the major Maya kingdoms, including the K'iche', Tz'utujil, Pipil and Kaqchikel. By 1528 the conquest of Guatemala was nearly complete. The last independent Maya kingdoms, the Kowoj and the Itza, were defeated in 1697. In 1609 the area became the Captaincy General of Guatemala, which encompassed most of Central America except present-day Belize and Panama.

On 24 August 1821 the Spanish viceroy Juan de O'Donojú signed the Treaty of Córdoba, which established the independence of New Spain. In 1838 Costa Rica, Guatemala, Honduras and Nicaragua became the first of the region's states to become independent countries after the dissolution of the Federal Republic of Central America, followed by El Salvador in 1841, Panama in 1903 and Belize in 1981.

Despite the dissolution of the federation, its former members preserved a Central American identity. In Spanish, Centroamérica refers to the former members of the federation, emphasising their shared culture and history, while América Central refers to the geographical area of the seven countries between Mexico and Colombia.
central-asia: Central Asia has no single definition.
