Alexander von Humboldt, one of the first geographers to treat it as a distinct region, defined it by latitude, while the Russian geographer Nikolaĭ Khanykov preferred a physical definition that took in all landlocked lands, including Afghanistan, Khorasan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan, East Turkestan, Mongolia and Uzbekistan. The countries most commonly included are Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan.

The land is varied: high passes and mountains such as the Tian Shan, deserts such as the Kyzyl Kum and the Taklamakan, and vast treeless steppes that form, with those of Eastern Europe, the Eurasian Steppe. Much of it is too dry or too rugged for farming. Dense population and cities are found where irrigation is possible, along the eastern mountains, the Oxus and Jaxartes rivers and the north flank of the Kopet Dagh, and at oases such as Merv, Herat and Balkh.

Aridity and distance from the sea limited agriculture and trade, so few major cities developed, and for millennia the region was dominated by nomadic horse peoples of the steppe. Before about 1000 it was inhabited chiefly by Iranian peoples, among them the Bactrians, Sogdians and Chorasmians and the semi-nomadic Scythians and Dahae. Turkic migration then made it the homeland of the Kazakhs, Kyrgyz, Tatars, Turkmens, Uyghurs and Uzbeks, and Turkic languages largely replaced Iranian ones except in Tajikistan and where Tajik is spoken. The Silk Road crossed the region and gave rise to prosperous trading cities.

The Tang dynasty of China expanded west and controlled large parts of the region, directly and through Turkic vassals, until the Abbasid Caliphate defeated it at the Battle of Talas in 751. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Mongols conquered most of Central Asia, which fell largely under the Chagatai Khanate. From the mid-19th century the region was incorporated into the Russian Empire and later the Soviet Union, and Russians and other Slavs settled in it. During the Stalinist period Koreans were forcibly deported there. Historians stress that Central Asia has rarely been the seat of an empire of its own and has more often been a battleground for outside powers.

With the collapse of the Soviet Union, Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan became independent. Most inhabitants speak Turkic languages, among them Kazakh, Kyrgyz, Turkmen and Uzbek, and Russian remains a lingua franca. Islam is the most common religion, mostly Sunni, and Nowruz, with Zoroastrian roots, is observed in all five states. The Aral Sea and Lake Balkhash have shrunk significantly through the diversion of the rivers that feed them.
central-bank: Government control of money is documented in the ancient Egyptian economy, 2750–2150 BCE, where goods were measured against a central unit called shat, linked to gold. Issuing paper currency is not the same as central banking: government-issued money, as in China during the Yuan dynasty, is typically not freely convertible and was occasionally followed by hyperinflation. From the twelfth century professional banks emerged, primarily in Southern Europe, which could use book money to create deposits without direct control from political authorities.

The Taula de canvi de Barcelona, established in 1401, is the first example of municipal, mostly public banks that pioneered central banking on a limited scale. The Bank of Saint George in the Republic of Genoa followed in 1407, then the Bank of Amsterdam in 1609 and the Hamburger Bank in 1619.

The Swedish central bank, known since 1866 as Sveriges Riksbank, was founded in Stockholm from the remains of the failed Stockholms Banco and answered to the Riksdag of the Estates. The Bank of England received a royal charter on 27 July 1694 through the Tonnage Act, following a 1691 proposal by William Paterson. It held the government's balances and was the only limited-liability corporation allowed to issue banknotes, though it lacked several functions of today's central banks.

Napoleon created the Banque de France in 1800 to stabilise the French economy and improve the financing of his wars, and the Bank of Finland was founded in 1812. At the start of the twentieth century about two-thirds of sovereign states had no central bank; waves of adoption followed in the interwar period and after the Second World War, and the European Central Bank was established in 1998.

A central bank manages the monetary policy of a country or monetary union. In contrast to a commercial bank, it has a monopoly on increasing the monetary base, and many also supervise commercial banks. The notion of a central bank as a separate category only fully coalesced in the twentieth century, when Montagu Norman of the United Kingdom and Benjamin Strong of the United States agreed a definition after the First World War. The expression itself appeared in the early nineteenth century, when it referred to the head office of a multi-branched bank, as in Walter Bagehot's 1873 book Lombard Street. Its primary role is usually to maintain price stability.
central-europe: Central Europe has no agreed boundaries, and which countries belong to it often depends on the nationality and historical outlook of the author. The concept appeared in the 19th century, when it was understood as a contact zone between the southern and northern areas of Europe and later between the eastern and western. Geography fixes its borders most clearly to the north, across the Baltic Sea, and to the south, across the Alps and the Soča–Krka–Sava–Danube line, while the borders with Western and Eastern Europe are less defined.

After Roman rule fell in the 5th century, Germanic tribes, among them the Franks, Alemans and Bavarians, conquered parts of the west, while Slavic tribes lived mainly in the east. After the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved around 1800, power was consolidated in the Habsburgs and the Hohenzollerns, who cooperated at times but more often competed. At the Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 Austria proposed merging the smaller German-speaking states with the multi-ethnic Habsburg monarchy, which Prussia and others opposed. The idea of Mitteleuropa later became popular in the German Empire, founded in 1871.

After 1918 the concept shifted to the east and the countries that had reappeared on the map. Central Europe became a field for integration movements, such as the Little Entente, formed in 1921 by Czechoslovakia, Romania and the Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes, and the Intermarium idea, neither of which succeeded. In the Second World War Nazi Germany occupied most of the region, and the mass murder of the Jews emptied settlements that had existed for centuries. After the war much of it came under Soviet control, and the Iron Curtain divided it, although Austria, Switzerland and Yugoslavia declared neutrality.

The states most often counted as Central European are Austria, the Czech Republic, Germany, Hungary, Liechtenstein, Poland, Slovakia, Slovenia and Switzerland, and many sources add Croatia and Lithuania. The region is mostly Catholic or historically both Catholic and Protestant. The first university east of France and north of the Alps was founded in Prague in 1348 by Charles IV, Holy Roman Emperor.
central-java: Central Java lies in the middle of the island of Java. It is bordered by West Java in the west, the Indian Ocean and the Special Region of Yogyakarta in the south, East Java in the east and the Java Sea in the north. It also includes offshore islands, among them Nusakambangan in the south and the Karimun Jawa Islands in the Java Sea. The northern coastal lowland is narrow, only 4 kilometres wide at Semarang, and Mount Muria, an island at the end of the Ice Age, was fused to Java by alluvial deposits. The Bengawan Solo, at 572 kilometres the longest river on Java, rises in the Sewu Mountains and flows north through Surakarta.

Central Java is also a cultural concept that includes the Yogyakarta Special Region, administered separately since Indonesian independence. It is known as the heart of Javanese culture, and about 98 percent of its people are Javanese.

Remains of Homo erectus, known as Java Man, were found in Central Java and adjacent East Java in the 1890s by the Dutch anatomist and geologist Eugène Dubois, and are believed to be about 1.7 million years old; Sangiran is an important prehistoric site. Around 40,000 years ago peoples related to modern Australian Aboriginals and Melanesians settled there, and by about 3,000 BCE Austronesians had assimilated or replaced them, bringing pottery, outrigger canoes, domesticated animals and cultivated rice and millet.

Recorded history began in the 7th century, when writing, Hinduism and Buddhism were brought by Indians from South Asia. In 664 the Chinese monk Hui-neng visited a Javanese port he called Hēlíng, where he translated Buddhist scriptures with the Javanese monk Jñānabhadra; it is thought to lie between Semarang and Jepara.

From the late 16th century European traders frequented the ports and the Dutch established a presence through the East India Company. After Demak fell to Mataram under Sultan Agung, Mataram conquered almost all of Java by the 17th century but, through internal disputes and Dutch intervention, was partitioned: the Treaty of Giyanti of 1755 divided it into the Sultanates of Surakarta and Yogyakarta, and the Treaty of Salatiga of 1757 created the Mangkunegaran.

Central Java is a province of Indonesia with its administrative capital at Semarang and a population of 36,516,035 at the 2020 census, the third largest of any province. The standard Javanese is the Solo-Jogja or Mataram dialect, while Indonesian is the official language.

The province holds the temple of Borobudur in Magelang Regency, a UNESCO World Heritage Site, with Mendut and Pawon nearby, as well as temples of the Dieng Plateau, the Sangiran museum and the palaces of Surakarta.
central-powers: The Central Powers, also called the Central Empires or the Quadruple Alliance, were one of the two main coalitions of the First World War. The name comes from the position of the members, all four lying between the Russian Empire in the east and France and the United Kingdom in the west. The alliance began with the pact between Germany and Austria-Hungary of 1879. Italy had nominally joined that bloc in the Triple Alliance but did not fight on its side and later joined the Allies. Germany also planned a Mitteleuropa economic association with Austria-Hungary and others.

Austria-Hungary, supported by Germany, declared war on Serbia on 28 July 1914. Germany declared war on Russia and, on 3 August, on France. The Ottoman Empire, bound to Germany by a secret alliance signed on 2 August 1914, stayed formally neutral for nearly two months. It entered the war on 29 October 1914 after a raid on Russian ports by cruisers that had been transferred from Germany. Bulgaria, defeated by Serbia, Greece and Romania in July 1913, signed a treaty of defensive alliance with the Ottomans on 19 August 1914 and in October 1915 declared war on Serbia.

Other groups cooperated with the coalition. The Senussi Order, led by Ahmed Sharif as-Senussi, attacked the Italians in Libya and the British in Egypt, the Sultanate of Darfur sided with the Ottomans in 1915, and Irish nationalists launched the Easter Rising in 1916. Germany lost its colonies to the Allies; German East Africa, resisted until November 1918 by Paul von Lettow-Vorbeck, was the only one not fully conquered.

As the war lengthened, solidarity weakened. After the death of Franz Joseph, his successor Charles sought to distance Austria-Hungary from Germany, and from 1916 its leaders wanted to leave the conflict. In September 1918 a Franco-Serbian offensive under Louis Franchet d'Espèrey broke the Bulgarian front, and Bulgaria signed an armistice on 29 September 1918. The Ottoman Empire followed on 30 October, Austria and Hungary made ceasefires in the first week of November after the disintegration of the Habsburg Empire, and Germany signed on 11 November 1918. No single treaty ended the war: each of the Central Powers was dealt with in a separate treaty. The alliance dissolved in 1918.
cern: The acronym CERN originally stood for the French Conseil Européen pour la Recherche Nucléaire, European Council for Nuclear Research, a provisional council established by 12 European governments in 1952 to build the laboratory. In these early years the council worked at the University of Copenhagen under the direction of Niels Bohr before moving to its present site near Geneva. At the sixth session of the council in Paris, from 29 June to 1 July 1953, the convention establishing the organisation was signed, subject to ratification, by 12 states, and it was ratified on 29 September 1954. The founding member states were Belgium, Denmark, France, the Federal Republic of Germany, Greece, Italy, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden, Switzerland, the United Kingdom and Yugoslavia.

The name changed in 1954 to Organisation européenne pour la recherche nucléaire, European Organization for Nuclear Research, but the acronym was kept. According to Lew Kowarski, a former director, the abbreviation could have become the awkward OERN, and Werner Heisenberg said that this could still be CERN even if the name was not. CERN's first president was Sir Benjamin Lockspeiser. Edoardo Amaldi was general secretary in the early stages, when operations were still provisional, and the first Director-General, in 1954, was Felix Bloch.

The organisation is based in Meyrin, a western suburb of Geneva, on the border between France and Switzerland. Its main function is to provide the particle accelerators and other infrastructure needed for high-energy physics research, and many experiments have been built there through international collaborations. Each machine in its chain of accelerators raises the energy of particle beams before passing them to experiments or to the next, more powerful accelerator. Its original linear accelerator, LINAC 1, operated from 1959 to 1992.

Several major achievements in particle physics came from experiments at CERN: the discovery of neutral currents in the Gargamelle bubble chamber in 1973, of the W and Z bosons in 1983, and of direct CP violation in 1999. In 1995 the first atoms of antihydrogen were created, and in 2000 its Heavy Ion Programme discovered a new state of matter, quark–gluon plasma. In 2012 experiments at the Large Hadron Collider, the world's largest and highest-energy particle collider, discovered a boson with a mass around 125 GeV/c2 consistent with the long-sought Higgs boson. CERN is also the birthplace of the World Wide Web. Its large computing facility at Meyrin stores and analyses experimental data, and the laboratory has historically been a major wide area network hub.
cesar-milstein: César Milstein was born on 8 October 1927 in Bahía Blanca, Argentina. His parents were Máxima Vanarks and Lázaro Milstein, a Jewish Ukrainian immigrant. He graduated from the University of Buenos Aires. In 1958, funded by the British Council, he joined the Biochemistry Department at the University of Cambridge to work for a doctorate under Malcolm Dixon, and during this work he collaborated with Frederick Sanger. He later became a member of the Medical Research Council Laboratory of Molecular Biology at Cambridge and acquired British citizenship, holding dual British and Argentinian nationality.

Most of Milstein's research concerned the structure of antibodies and the way their diversity arises. In 1975 he worked with Georges Köhler, a postdoctoral fellow in his laboratory, to develop the hybridoma technique for producing monoclonal antibodies. The technique led to a great expansion in the use of antibodies in science and medicine. Milstein himself improved monoclonal antibody technology, particularly in providing markers that distinguish different cell types, and with Claudio Cuello he helped lay the foundation for using monoclonal antibodies to investigate neurological disorders. He foresaw that recombinant DNA technology could be applied to them and inspired the field of antibody engineering. He patented the production of monoclonal antibodies.

Later he used the hybridoma technique with nucleic acid sequencing to chart the changes in antibodies after an encounter with an antigen, and he showed the importance of somatic hypermutation of immunoglobulin V genes in antibody affinity maturation.

Milstein shared the 1984 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine with Niels Kaj Jerne and Georges Köhler. He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1975, won the Wolf Prize in Medicine in 1980 and the Copley Medal in 1989, and became a Companion of Honour in 1995. He gave time to assisting science and scientists in less developed countries. He died on 24 March 2002 in Cambridge, aged 74, of a heart condition he had had for many years.
cesar-vallejo: César Abraham Vallejo Mendoza was born on 16 March 1892 in Santiago de Chuco, a remote village in the Peruvian Andes, the youngest of eleven children. Both his grandfathers were Spanish priests and both his grandmothers were indigenous Peruvians. Lack of money forced him to work for a time at a sugar plantation, the Roma Hacienda, where he saw the exploitation of farm workers, an experience that shaped his politics and his writing. He studied at the National University of San Marcos in Lima from 1911, worked as a schoolteacher, and took a degree in Spanish literature in 1915.

In 1920 Vallejo was accused, unjustly according to the account, of taking part in the burning of a house in Santiago de Chuco. He was held in a jail in Trujillo for 112 days, from 6 November 1920 to 26 February 1921. The lawyer Eduardo González Viaña, who studied the court papers, argues that the testimony was fabricated. The process was never closed, and in 2007 the Peruvian judiciary honoured his memory. Under threat of further imprisonment he went to Europe after publishing Trilce in 1922, and lived in poverty in Paris, apart from three trips to the USSR and about two years in Spain in the early 1930s.

He joined the Peruvian Communist Party in 1931, and wrote journalism, reportage on the USSR, plays that were not performed in his lifetime, the novel El tungsteno about a foreign-owned tungsten mine, and the children's story Paco Yunque.

Trilce, published in 1922, takes language to an extreme by inventing words, stretching syntax and using automatic writing, techniques later called surrealist, though he used them before the Surrealist movement began. It remains one of the most radically avant-garde poetry collections in Spanish.

After becoming deeply involved in the Spanish Civil War, he wrote a last burst of poems in the late 1930s. They were published after his death as Poemas humanos and España, aparta de mí este cáliz, though their titles and arrangement are still debated. He died in Paris on 15 April 1938, after an illness later understood to be a return of malaria he had had as a child.
cesare-beccaria: Cesare Beccaria was born in Milan on 15 March 1738 to an aristocrat of moderate standing. He was educated at the Jesuit college in Parma and graduated in law from the University of Pavia in 1758. Reading Montesquieu turned his attention to economics, and in 1762 he published a tract on the disorder of the currency in the Milanese states. In his mid-twenties he became close friends with Pietro and Alessandro Verri, and with other young Milanese aristocrats they formed a literary society, the Academy of Fists. Much of its talk concerned reform of criminal justice.

In 1764, encouraged by Pietro Verri, Beccaria published On Crimes and Punishments, a brief treatise that marked the high point of the Milan Enlightenment. Alessandro Verri, a Milan prison official, knew the prison's appalling conditions at first hand. The treatise protested against torture to obtain confessions, secret accusations, the arbitrary discretion of judges and capital punishment for serious and even minor offences. It was the first full work of penology. Beccaria published it anonymously, fearing a backlash, and acknowledged it only once the government's approval was clear.

He argued from the social contract and from utility. Punishment, he held, should prevent crime rather than avenge it, should be proportionate to the crime, and should be prompt. A high probability of punishment, not its severity, achieves prevention, and laws should be clear so that judges decide only whether a law has been broken. He condemned the death penalty because the state has no right to take lives and because it is neither useful nor necessary.

The treatise was translated into French and English almost at once, and Catherine the Great publicly endorsed it. Many penal reforms in the principal European nations can be traced to it, but few contemporaries accepted its argument against the death penalty. The Grand Duchy of Tuscany, the first state to abolish capital punishment, followed Beccaria's argument about its lack of utility, not about the state's lack of right. His thinking also shaped Jeremy Bentham's utilitarianism. In 1768 a chair of law and economy was founded for him in Milan. He died there on 28 November 1794, and his grandson was the novelist Alessandro Manzoni.
cesare-borgia: Cesare Borgia was born at Subiaco in the Papal States, the illegitimate son of Cardinal Rodrigo Borgia, later Pope Alexander VI, and his Italian mistress Vannozza dei Cattanei. His family came from the Kingdom of Valencia, and his great-uncle Alphonso Borgia became Pope Callixtus III in 1455. He studied law at Rome and was groomed for the Church, becoming bishop of Pamplona and archbishop of Valencia while still a youth, and a cardinal when his father was elected pope. In 1497 his brother Giovanni, the captain-general of the papal forces, was murdered in unclear circumstances. A contemporary suggested that Cesare was the killer, but his part has never been established, and he had no certain motive.

On 17 August 1498 Cesare resigned as cardinal to follow a military career, and Louis XII of France named him Duke of Valentinois. In 1499 he married Charlotte d'Albret, a sister of John III of Navarre, and accompanied Louis into Milan. With French troops and papal money, he took Imola and Forlì, which were ruled by Caterina Sforza, and then drove Giovanni Sforza from Pesaro. Rimini and Faenza followed, whose young lord Astorre III Manfredi was later drowned in the Tiber on Cesare's order. In May 1501 he was created Duke of Romagna. In 1502 he took Urbino and Camerino by treason.

His condottieri, among them Vitellozzo Vitelli and the Orsini, feared his cruelty and plotted against him. On 31 December 1502 he called for reconciliation, then imprisoned them at Senigallia and had them strangled, a deed the historian Paolo Giovio called a wonderful deceiving. In 1503 he took the Republic of San Marino. Niccolò Machiavelli, who was at his court from October 1502 to January 1503, wrote dispatches on him, and The Prince treats him as an example of the danger of gaining a principality through another's power. Leonardo da Vinci served him as military engineer in 1502 and 1503.

Machiavelli named Cesare's dependence on the goodwill of the papacy as the chief weakness of his rule. His father died in 1503, while Cesare lay ill with malarial fever. Pius III, who supported him, reigned only twenty-six days, and Giuliano Della Rovere, his deadly enemy, won his support with promises he broke once elected Pope Julius II. Cesare was captured at Naples and held in Spain, escaped from the Castle of La Mota, and reached Pamplona on 3 December 1506, where King John III welcomed him. During the siege of the castle of Viana he chased fleeing knights alone and was killed in an ambush on 12 March 1507. His remains lie outside the Church of Santa María at Viana.
cesena: Cesena was originally an Umbrian or Etruscan town, later known as Caesena. After a brief spell under Gaulish rule it was taken over by the Romans in the 3rd century BCE, and it was destroyed in the wars between Gaius Marius and Sulla. It lay on the border that the Exarchate of Ravenna shared with the Lombards, and it was presented to the Papacy by its Frankish conqueror in 754, in the Donation of Pepin. It then passed back and forth between the popes and the archbishops of Ravenna, was briefly a communal republic from 1183 to 1198, and was long contested between popes and Holy Roman Emperors.

The brief rule of the Forlì family of the Ordelaffi was crushed in 1357 by papal troops led by Cardinal Gil de Albornoz, after a long siege endured by Cia degli Ordelaffi. The town revolted again in 1377 and was recaptured by Breton troops under the condottiere John Hawkwood and the command of Robert, Cardinal of Geneva, later the antipope Clement VII. Acting as legate of Pope Gregory XI, he directed the murder of between 2,500 and 5,000 civilians, an atrocity even by the laws of war of the time, called the Cesena Bloodbath. The following year what remained of Cesena was assigned to Galeotto I Malatesta.

From 1379 to 1465 the city recovered and prospered under the Malatesta, who rebuilt the castle, the Rocca Malatestiana. The fortress was begun by Cardinal Albornoz in 1380 and completed by the papal governor Lorenzo Zane in 1480. It is octagonal, with two main towers, the taller maschio and the shorter foemina, and Cesare Borgia later used it to imprison Caterina Sforza. Near the castle, Malatesta Novello built the Malatestiana Library, a fine example of a Renaissance library that holds many valuable manuscripts and is a UNESCO Memory of the World site.

After Novello's death in 1465 Cesena returned to the Papal States, but Cesare Borgia seized it and made it the capital of his short-lived duchy. Pope Pius VI and Pope Pius VII were born in the city and Pope Pius VIII was its bishop, which earned it the title of city of the three popes. During the Napoleonic Wars it lost numerous monasteries and churches, and some of its citizens played notable roles in the unification of Italy. In the Second World War it lay near the Gothic Line and suffered heavily from bombing.
cesis: Cēsis, in German Wenden, is a town in the Vidzeme region of Latvia, about 90 km north-east of Riga, on ridges above the valley of the Gauja. Its historic centre keeps its medieval street plan, sections of the town wall, St. John's Church of the late 13th century and the ruins of Cēsis Castle.

The earliest known fortified settlement stood on Riekstu Hill, where the Vends lived in the 11th and 12th centuries. The area came under the Livonian Brothers of the Sword in 1207, and a stone castle was begun on the neighbouring plateau, probably around 1214. Cēsis was first named as a town in 1323 and joined the Hanseatic League in the early 15th century. After the destruction of the Order's castle in Riga in 1484, Cēsis became the main residence of the Livonian Order's masters. Lutheran preaching began in 1524.

The town and castle were heavily damaged in the Livonian War, and during the siege of 1577 several hundred people sheltering in the castle killed themselves by igniting gunpowder rather than surrender to the army of Ivan the Terrible. The castle never regained its earlier importance. Swedish forces completed their conquest of the town in 1626, Russian troops occupied it in 1703, and it became a district town in 1785. The Riga-Pskov railway reached it in 1889.

After Latvia declared independence in November 1918, the Battles of Cēsis in June 1919 ended in an Estonian and Latvian victory over German forces, a major turning point in the Latvian War of Independence. In 1988 Cēsis was the first town to raise the red-white-red flag over a major public building during the national revival.

Latvians were a majority in Cēsis by the 1897 census, in a town with a substantial Baltic German community. The New Castle, converted into a manor residence in 1762, has housed the town's history museum since 1949, and a Victory Monument commemorates the battles of 1919.
cesky-krumlov: Český Krumlov lies on both banks of the Vltava in the Bohemian Forest Foothills, about 20 kilometres south-west of České Budějovice and 134 kilometres south of Prague. The area was settled from the Older Stone Age, with mass settlement in the Bronze Age, Celtic settlements about 400 BCE and the first Slavic settlement from the 6th century CE.

The castle was founded shortly before 1250 by a local branch of the noble Vítkovci family, and the town was first mentioned in a deed of 1253 as Chrumbenowe. It grew in two stages: Latrán, built spontaneously below the castle by people connected with its administration, and a newly founded Old Town. Both Czech and German nationalities were present from the start, and a Jewish community is documented from 1334.

When the Vítkovci line died out in 1302, King Wenceslaus II ceded the estate to the Rosenberg family, who made it their main residence. Peter I of Rosenberg had the upper castle built in the early 14th century, and the town reached its highest prosperity in the 15th century under Oldřich II of Rosenberg. Gold found near the town in the late 15th century brought German miners, shifting the ethnic balance further.

In 1555 William of Rosenberg joined Latrán and the Old Town into one, and later rebuilt the castle in Renaissance style. Peter Vok of Rosenberg sold Krumlov in 1602 to Emperor Rudolf II, who gave it to his illegitimate son Julius d'Austria. After the Battle of White Mountain in 1620 Emperor Ferdinand II gave it to the Eggenberg family, and it became the seat of the Duchy of Krumlov. The Schwarzenberg family held the castle from 1719 to 1947.

In 1910 the town had 8,662 inhabitants, 85 per cent of them German and 15 per cent Czech. It passed to Czechoslovakia under the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye in 1919, was annexed by Nazi Germany under the Munich Agreement in 1938, and after the Second World War its German majority was expelled. The historic centre fell into disrepair under communist rule and has been largely restored since 1989. The castle complex, about 7 hectares with forty buildings around five courts, is one of the largest in central Europe, and the town and castle have been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1992. The town has about 13,000 inhabitants.
cetinje: Cetinje lies in a small karst plain of about 7 square kilometres, at an average height of 671 metres, surrounded by limestone mountains that include Mount Lovćen, a mountain prominent in Montenegrin historiography. It is 12 kilometres in a straight line from the Adriatic and 15 from Skadar Lake. The town is named after the Cetina river that, according to written data, flowed down the plain until the end of the 17th century. Cetinje is first mentioned in historical documents in 1440, and rainfall there is very heavy, though the karst leaves few water sources on the surface.

Cetinje was founded in 1482, when Ivan Crnojević moved his capital from Obod, above the Crnojević River, to a more easily defended field at the foot of Mount Lovćen. He had his court built there that year and founded a monastery as a personal endowment, and the court and monastery are the first recorded Renaissance buildings in Montenegro. Because of the Ottoman invasions he also moved the seat of the Eparchy of Zeta from Vranjina to Cetinje in 1485. A printing house of the Crnojević family worked there from 1492 to 1496, and its books spread Cyrillic type among the Orthodox peoples of south-eastern Europe.

For the next two centuries Cetinje stagnated and was often attacked by Venice and the Ottomans. The court and monastery of the Crnojević dynasty were destroyed. The town began to flourish again from 1697, under the Petrović dynasty refounded by Danilo Petrović. His successors were occupied with wars of liberation and the unity of the country, and greater progress came only under Petar II Petrović Njegoš, who built his residence, the Biljarda, in 1838. New houses led to genuine urbanisation, and foreign consulates, French, Russian, British, Italian and Austro-Hungarian, put up buildings after relations with European states were established.

Podgorica is the capital of Montenegro, but Cetinje is the seat of several national institutions, among them the National Museum of Montenegro, the national library and the State Archives. The official residence of the president, the Blue Palace, is there. Its main sights include the monastery, Biljarda, the Vlaška church and the old foreign embassies. It is the seat of the Eparchy of Montenegro and the Littoral of the Serbian Orthodox Church, and the Montenegrin Orthodox Church also has its seat there. The 2023 census counted 12,460 people in the town.
ceuta: Ceuta lies on the North African coast, 17 kilometres across the Strait of Gibraltar from the Spanish mainland, and shares a land border of 6.4 kilometres with Morocco. It has an area of 18.5 square kilometres. Monte Hacho, on the La Almina Peninsula above the port, is one of the possible sites of the southern Pillar of Hercules of Greek legend; the other is Jebel Musa. The Strait of Gibraltar is an important military and commercial chokepoint, and the narrow isthmus joining the La Almina Peninsula to the African mainland made the site easy to defend.

Phoenicians established an outpost there early in the 1st millennium BCE, which continued under Roman rule as Septem Fratres. The Vandals crossed the strait around 425 CE, but lost Tingis and Septem in a series of Berber revolts. Around 533 the Byzantine general Belisarius made Septem the westernmost outpost of the Byzantine Empire, and the empire, which did not push far inland, made it their regional capital in place of Tingis. It was annexed by the early caliphates in the Islamic conquest of the Maghreb, destroyed in the Berber Revolt, and rebuilt in the ninth century. For much of the Middle Ages powers north and south of the strait vied for control of it as a key port in the so-called Battle of the Strait.

On the morning of 21 August 1415 King John I of Portugal led his sons and their forces in a surprise assault known as the Conquest of Ceuta. About 45,000 Portuguese arrived on 200 ships, caught the defenders off guard and took the town by nightfall, with only eight casualties. After the death of King Sebastian of Portugal at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir in 1578 and a succession war, Philip II of Spain was crowned Philip I of Portugal in April 1581, and Ceuta passed to the Hispanic Monarchy. On 1 January 1668 King Afonso VI of Portugal ceded it to King Carlos II of Spain by the Treaty of Lisbon.

Moroccan forces under Moulay Ismail besieged the city from 1694 to 1727, the longest siege in history, and the city lost its Portuguese character. It was besieged unsuccessfully again in 1790 and 1791, and British forces occupied it from 1810 to 1815. A dispute over the border led to the war between Spain and Morocco of 1859 to 1860, ended by the Treaty of Wad Ras.

Ceuta is an autonomous city of Spain, a status it gained through its Statute of Autonomy in March 1995; before then it was a municipality of the province of Cádiz. Spanish is its official language, and Moroccan Arabic is also widely spoken. Its population is mainly Spanish Christians and Arab Muslims, with small Sephardic Jewish and Sindhi Hindu minorities.
cfa-franc: The CFA franc was created on 26 December 1945, together with the CFP franc, because the French franc was weak after World War II. When France ratified the Bretton Woods Agreement in December 1945, the French franc was devalued to set a fixed rate against the US dollar. New currencies were created in the colonies to spare them the strong devaluation, which made it easier for them to import goods from France and harder to export to France. French officials presented the decision as generosity. Between 1945 and 1958 CFA stood for Colonies françaises d'Afrique, and from 1958 until independence for Communauté française d'Afrique.

The name covers two currencies that have the same value but are not interchangeable. The West African CFA franc is issued by the Central Bank of the West African States at Dakar for eight countries: Benin, Burkina Faso, Guinea-Bissau, Ivory Coast, Mali, Niger, Senegal and Togo. The Central African CFA franc is issued by the Bank of the Central African States at Yaoundé for Cameroon, the Central African Republic, Chad, Equatorial Guinea, Gabon and the Republic of the Congo. Both are guaranteed by the French Treasury.

The rate against the French franc was changed only twice. From 1945 one CFA franc was worth 1.70 French francs; from 17 October 1948 it was worth 2. On 12 January 1994 an overnight devaluation of 50 per cent halved its value. When the euro replaced the French franc on 1 January 1999 the rate became 655.957 CFA francs to the euro.

The zone has changed since independence. Guinea left in 1960 and Mali in 1962, rejoining in 1984; Madagascar and Mauritania left in 1973, and Guinea-Bissau, a former Portuguese colony, joined in 1997. Critics hold that the currency restricts the sovereignty of the member states and makes national monetary policy all but impossible, and some object that the notes are printed in France. Defenders argue that it stabilises the national currencies and eases trade with France.
chad: Chad is a landlocked country of 1,284,000 square kilometres, bordered by Libya, Sudan, Niger, Nigeria, Cameroon and the Central African Republic. Its capital is 1,060 kilometres from the nearest seaport, Douala in Cameroon, and the distance and desert climate have led to the nickname Dead Heart of Africa. A wide basin is bounded by the Ennedi Plateau and the Tibesti Mountains, which include the dormant volcano Emi Koussi, at 3,414 metres. Lake Chad is the remains of an immense lake of 330,000 square kilometres that existed 7,000 years ago. The Sahara covers the northern third, a Sahelian belt lies in the centre, and savanna in the south.

From the 7th millennium BCE ecological conditions favoured settlement in the north, and some of Africa's most important archaeological sites are in the Borkou-Ennedi-Tibesti Region. The earliest civilisation of the Chad Basin was the Sao, known from artefacts and oral histories, which fell to the Kanem Empire. Kanem became the first and longest-lasting of the states in the Sahelian strip, its power based on the trans-Saharan trade routes. Islamisation increased from the 11th century, and by the 12th century its scribes had developed an original script style, the barnāwī.

Kanem's expansion peaked under Mai Dunama Dabbalemi, who reigned c. 1221 to 1259. Around 1396 Bulala invaders forced Mai Umar Idrismi to move the imperial centre to Bornu. The Sultanate of Bagirmi and the Wadai Sultanate arose in the 16th and 17th centuries, and Wadai's Muhammad Sharif, who reigned from 1843 to 1858, subjugated Bagirmi and resisted French colonisation. The Territoire Militaire des Pays et Protectorats du Tchad was created in 1900, and by 1920 France had secured full control and made Chad part of French Equatorial Africa.

Chad became independent in 1960 under François Tombalbaye. Resentment of his policies in the Muslim north led to a civil war that began in 1965, and rebels took the capital in 1979. Hissène Habré defeated rival commanders, and a Chadian–Libyan conflict that began in 1978 ended in 1987 with French military intervention. Idriss Déby overthrew Habré in 1990. Chad has over 200 ethnic and linguistic groups, and its official languages are French and Arabic. Islam is practised by 55.1 per cent and Christianity by 41.1 per cent.
chagatai-khan: Chagatai was born in late 1183 or 1184 to Börte, of the Onggirat tribe, and Temüjin, the later Genghis Khan. Because Börte had been kidnapped by the Merkit tribe before the birth of her elder son Jochi, whose paternity was never known, Chagatai was the first son definitively fathered by Temüjin. When Genghis divided his new nation after the assembly of 1206, Chagatai received territories near the Altai Mountains and either 4,000 or 8,000 subjects. He was known for his knowledge of Mongol law and custom, and chroniclers such as Juzjani noted the harshness of his temperament.

With his brothers Jochi and Ögedei he commanded the right wing in the invasion of the Jin dynasty in 1211. In the invasion of the Khwarazmian Empire in 1219 he was charged with building bridges and maintaining roads. He and Ögedei besieged Otrar, which fell in February 1220; the Mongols killed or enslaved its entire population. At the Siege of Gurganj, which fell in April 1221, the usual narrative has Chagatai and Jochi quarrel over how to conduct it until Genghis placed Ögedei over both; the historian Christopher Atwood argues that this account was a later invention meant to support Ögedei's right to rule.

Genghis thought Chagatai too strict and narrow-minded for a ruler and was troubled by his hatred of Jochi, and excluded him from the succession. After Genghis died in 1227, Chagatai held to his father's will, prevented any usurpation before the accession of Ögedei in 1229, and presided over the coronation with Tolui and their uncle Temüge. In Central Asia his capital and summer pastures were at Almaliq. He disputed jurisdiction with the imperial official Mahmud Yalavach, and when Bukhara revolted against tax demands in 1238 he left its suppression to Ögedei's armies.

After Ögedei died in December 1241, Chagatai's support made Töregene regent. He died in 1242; his wife Yesülün accused a steward named Vajir of poisoning him and had him executed. His grandson Qara Hülegü succeeded him but was displaced by Chagatai's son Yesü-Möngke between 1246 and 1250.

Chagatai upheld traditional Mongol law, which forbade elements of Islamic practice, and gained a reputation for being anti-Muslim; one contemporary Muslim writer claimed that he urged Ögedei to kill every Muslim in the empire. The historians Michael Hope and Peter Jackson think this far from the truth, pointing to the powerful Muslim officials at his court. His descendants were nonetheless far slower to convert to Islam than the rulers of the Golden Horde and the Ilkhanate.
chagatai-khanate: When Genghis Khan died in 1227, his son Chagatai Khan inherited lands that roughly matched the defunct Qara Khitai empire: the Issyk-Kul, Ili, Chu and Talas regions, Transoxania and the Tarim Basin. Chagatai was not fully independent and still received orders from Karakorum. After his death in 1242 the throne passed between young khans, regents and appointees of rival Great Khans. With the division of the Mongol Empire after 1259 the khanate became functionally separate, and at its height in the late 13th century it stretched from the Amu Darya to the Altai Mountains. It was also called the Dumdadu Mongγol Ulus, the Middle Mongolian Empire.

Under Kaidu, who dominated the khanate from 1266 to 1301, it fought both the Yuan dynasty and the Ilkhanate. After Kaidu's death Duwa recognised Yuan authority in 1303. Chagatai armies raided the Delhi Sultanate several times, with little lasting result. Tarmashirin, khan from 1326 to 1334, converted to Islam and reached Delhi, but an anti-Muslim rising of the eastern tribes brought him down.

In the 1340s the khanate split in two. In Transoxania the khans became puppets of local emirs and later of Timur, who ruled from 1369. In the east, the Dughlats enthroned Tughlugh Timur as khan of Moghulistan in 1347, and he converted to Islam in 1350. Moghulistan lasted until the late 15th century, when it divided into the Yarkent and Turpan Khanates. The last Chagatai domains lost their independence to the Dzungar Khanate in 1680.

The Chagatai Mongols remained mostly nomadic in their mode of government and did not settle in towns until the late 15th century. They treated the townspeople of Transoxiana and the Tarim Basin as dependants. The Mongol ruling groups underwent a gradual and uneven Turkification and Islamization, though Mongolian political and administrative traditions stayed important, and Mongolian was still used for official documents into the 14th century. The Kumul Khanate, governed by descendants of Chagatai Khan, was abolished in 1930, which ended the dynasty.
chagatai-language: Chagatai, also called Turki, Eastern Turkic or Chagatai Turkic, belongs to the Karluk branch of the Turkic languages and descends from Middle Turkic, which served as a lingua franca in Central Asia, with a strong infusion of Arabic and Persian words and turns of phrase. Its name relates to the Chagatai Khanate, a descendant empire of the Mongol Empire left to Genghis Khan's second son, Chagatai Khan, and many of the Turkic peoples who spoke the language claimed political descent from it.

Mehmet Fuat Köprülü divides its history into early Chagatai in the 13th and 14th centuries, a pre-classical period in the first half of the 15th, a classical one in the second half of the 15th, its continuation in the 16th and a decline from the 17th to the 19th.

Chagatai was widely spoken across Central Asia and remained the shared literary language of the region until the early 20th century, when it died out. It was used in western or Russian Turkestan, Eastern Turkestan, Crimea and the Volga–Ural region. It is written in a variant of the Perso-Arabic alphabet known as Kona Yëziq, the old script. Its basic word order is subject–object–verb, it has vowel harmony and six cases, and it has complex syntax copied from Persian. Central Asian Turkic authors regarded Persian literature as superior and deliberately imitated it in creating Chagatai literature.

The second phase of Chagatai literature began with the publication of Ali-Shir Nava'i's first divan and was its highpoint. According to Geoffrey Lewis, his writings raised Chagatai to the status of literary language of Central Asia, and the language is sometimes called Nava'i's language. In his Muhakamat al-Lughatayn he compared Chagatai with New Persian and argued for its superiority for literary purposes. The biography of Timur and the Baburnama of Babur, the Timurid founder of the Mughal Empire, are in Chagatai, as is the prose work of Muhammad Shaybani of 1507.

The 17th and 18th centuries are often seen as a period of decay, when it lost ground to Persian; Abu al-Ghazi Bahadur wrote his genealogies in it, and Magtymguly Pyragy introduced it into Turkmen literature in the second half of the 18th century.

Chagatai is the direct ancestor of Uzbek and Uyghur, and Kazakh and Turkmen were heavily influenced by it for centuries. In 1921 it was first intended as the national language of the Uzbek SSR, but it proved too archaic and a new literary language based on Uzbek dialects replaced it. In preparing the Soviet republic of Uzbekistan in 1924 it was renamed Old Uzbek, a step Edward A. Allworth argued distorted the literary history of the region.
chagos-archipelago: The Chagos Archipelago is a group of coral atolls, reefs and submerged banks in the central Indian Ocean, at the southern end of the Chagos–Laccadive Ridge. It lies about 2,200 km north-east of Mauritius and 500 km south of the Maldives. Five atolls carry islands: Diego Garcia, Peros Banhos, the Salomon Islands, the Egmont Islands and the Great Chagos Bank, described as the world's largest atoll by area. The 55 to 59 islands are small and low, with a total land area of about 53 km2, more than half of it on Diego Garcia. The reefs are largely free of local pollution, so they serve as a scientific reference site.

Portuguese navigators probably sighted and named the islands early in the 16th century, and they appear on Portuguese charts from 1538. From the 1740s ships from Île de France, as Mauritius was then called, explored the islands, and concessions for coconut plantations followed, leading to permanent settlement. Accounts of the date differ: one dates it to a concession of February 1783, the territory's British administration dates the first French copra plantations to 1793. The plantations were worked by enslaved people brought mainly from Madagascar and Mozambique.

The United Kingdom administered the archipelago as a dependency of Mauritius until 1965, when it detached the islands to form the British Indian Ocean Territory. Between 1967 and 1973 the whole population, the Chagossians, was either prevented from returning or removed, most of them to Mauritius, and construction of a joint British–American military base on Diego Garcia began in March 1971. Mauritius says that the detachment was unlawful. In May 2025 the two governments signed a treaty on the transfer of sovereignty.

The archipelago has no permanent inhabitants. About 2,000 people, mostly military personnel and contractors, are ordinarily present on Diego Garcia. The Chagossians, also called Ilois, descend mainly from the enslaved Africans and Malagasy brought to the plantations and from labourers recruited later in Mauritius and Seychelles. By the end of the 19th century they had formed a distinct island society, mostly Roman Catholic. Their music and dance, Sega tambour Chagos, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2019 as intangible cultural heritage in need of urgent safeguarding. Their language, Chagos Kreol, is a French-lexified creole related to those of Mauritius and Seychelles.
chaitanya-mahaprabhu: Chaitanya was born Vishvambhara Mishra at Nabadwip, in present-day West Bengal, on the evening of 18 February 1486, although some accounts give 27 February. His father, Jagannatha Mishra, was a Brahmin from Sylhet. The only sources for his life are the hagiographies of the Gaudiya tradition, which regard him as an avatar of Krishna, and the canonical account was established in the early 1600s by the Chaitanya Charitamrita of Krishnadasa Kaviraja. He began his schooling at five and mastered Sanskrit grammar and logic with great speed. At sixteen he opened a school of his own and became known as Nimai Pandit.

Around 1508 or 1509 he went to Gaya to perform funeral rites for his father and there met the ascetic Īśvara Purī, who initiated him. On returning to Nabadwip he closed his school and devoted himself to sankirtan, congregational chanting, with his associates Nityananda and Advaita Ācārya. The local Muslim ruler, the Chand Kazi, banned the chanting, and Chaitanya led thousands in a peaceful protest to his house, after which, according to the account, the ruler was won over.

In 1510, aged twenty-four, he took the vows of renunciation at Katwa and was given the name Sri Krishna Chaitanya. He made Jagannatha Puri in Odisha his headquarters, spent about two years travelling in southern India and returned in 1512. King Prataparudra arranged for him to live in a secluded room, the Gambhira, in Puri, where he spent most of his remaining years. In 1514 he set out for Vrindavan, and on the way accepted two ministers of Sultan Husain Shah as disciples, renaming them Rupa and Sanatana.

The Shikshashtaka, eight devotional verses, is the only work accepted as composed by Chaitanya. According to his associate Murari Gupta, he taught that kirtan, the chanting of God's name, is the most effective practice in the Kali Age, and he presented bhakti as the primary means of approaching Krishna. Dinesh Chandra Sen reads his teaching as centred on divine love and placing devotion above social distinction. He appointed the Goswamis to compose texts explaining this devotion, and the movement produced a large body of philosophical and literary work.
chalcidice: Chalcidice, in Greek Chalkidiki, is a peninsula in the north-western Aegean Sea in coastal Macedonia, shaped like a hand with three fingers, which in Greek are often called legs. From west to east they are Kassandra, whose highest peak is 350 metres, Sithonia, whose highest peak, Mount Itamos, is 817 metres, and Athos, whose peak reaches 2,033 metres. The Toronean Gulf and the Singitic Gulf separate them. The Cholomontas mountains lie in the north-centre, and the climate is mainly Mediterranean, with cool, wet winters and hot, relatively dry summers. The peninsula is named after the Greek city of Chalcis in Euboea, which colonised it in the 8th century BCE.

The first Greek settlers came from Chalcis and Eretria, cities of Euboea, around the 8th century BCE and founded cities such as Mende, Toroni and Scione. A second wave from Andros in the 6th century BCE founded cities including Akanthos. The peninsula became an important theatre of the Peloponnesian War between Athens and Sparta. Aristotle was born at Stageira. Philip II annexed the whole peninsula to Macedon, and after the Roman conquest of Macedon a Roman colony was settled at Cassandreia in 43 BCE and resettled by Augustus in 30 BCE.

In the Byzantine period Chalkidiki belonged to the theme of Thessalonica. A chrysobull of Emperor Basil I, dated 885, proclaimed Mount Athos a place of monks, with no laymen, farmers or cattle-breeders allowed to settle there. The Great Lavra monastery was founded soon afterwards with the support of Nikephoros II Phokas, and Athos has been self-governing ever since. After a short rule by the Latin Kingdom of Thessalonica the area became Byzantine again until the Ottomans conquered it in 1430, and under them it was important for gold mining.

In 1821 the Greeks of Chalkidiki rose in the Greek War of Independence under Emmanouel Pappas, a member of the Filiki Eteria. The revolt, confined to Athos and Kassandra, ended in a decisive Ottoman victory at Kassandra, after which many villages were burnt. The peninsula joined the Greek Kingdom in 1912 to 1913, and after the exchange of populations between Greece and Turkey of 1923 refugees from East Thrace and Anatolia settled in parts of it.

The capital is Polygyros, in the centre of the peninsula, and the largest town is Nea Moudania. Athos forms an autonomous monastic region in the east, home to Orthodox monks from Greece and many other countries. The peninsula produces olive oil, honey and wine, and its beaches have made tourism the main industry.
chalcis: Chalcis, also called Chalkida, is the chief city of the island of Euboea in Greece, on the Euripus Strait at its narrowest point. The name derives from the Greek word for copper or bronze, although there is no trace of any mines in the area. In the Late Middle Ages it was known as Negroponte, an Italian name that came from the Greek phrase meaning to the Euripos, altered by folk etymology so that ponte, bridge, was read as the bridge of Chalcis to Boeotia.

Chalcis is first mentioned in the Iliad, in the same line as its rival Eretria. In the 8th and 7th centuries BCE its colonists founded thirty townships on the peninsula of Chalcidice and important cities in Magna Graecia and Sicily, among them Naxos, Rhegion, Zankle and Cumae. Pithecusae on the island of Ischia, founded around 770 BCE by Chalcidians and Eretrians, is the first recorded settlement in the West. Chalcidian trade carried its alphabet to Italy, where the Etruscans took it up.

In the late 8th century BCE Chalcis and Eretria fought the Lelantine War, one of the first major wars between Greek cities. Late in the 6th century BCE a war with Athens broke its prosperity, and the Athenians settled a cleruchy there. Aristotle came to Chalcis in 323 BCE and died there the next year.

Venice had a trading station in the 12th century and seized the town in 1209, after the Fourth Crusade. Negroponte was shared between Venice and the Veronese barons of the rest of Euboea, known as the triarchs, and became a Latin Church diocese. It was attacked by the Principality of Achaea in 1257–58, by the Catalan Company in 1317 and by the Turks in 1350–51, until the Ottoman Empire captured it in 1470 after a long siege. The Ottomans held it against a Venetian attack in 1688.

Chalkida became part of the Greek state after the Greek War of Independence, and a railway link to Athens opened in 1904. Surviving sights include the Church of Saint Paraskevi, begun about 1250 as a Dominican priory church, the Roman aqueduct, the Ottoman Karababa Fortress of 1684, and a modern cable-stayed bridge over the strait, opened in 1993.
chaldean-empire: Babylonia had been an independent state since about 1894 BCE, and under Hammurabi it briefly became a major power. It later fell to the Hittite king Mursili I, was ruled by the Kassites for almost five centuries and then by native rulers of a small rump state, before coming under Assyrian rule. Early in the reign of the Assyrian king Sinsharishkun, Nabopolassar, a southern official or general, revolted amid political instability in Assyria. In 626 BCE he seized Babylon and Nippur, and he withstood the Assyrian siege of Uruk. In November of that year he was crowned King of Babylon.

The fall of the Assyrian Empire in 612 to 609 BCE firmly established the new kingdom, the first time southern Mesopotamia had dominated the Near East since Hammurabi. Nebuchadnezzar II succeeded Nabopolassar in 605 BCE, and his reign of 43 years is described in Babylonian sources as a golden age. The biblical account tells of his campaign against the Kingdom of Judah and the siege of Jerusalem in 587 BCE, which destroyed Solomon's Temple. There is evidence that he destroyed Ashkelon in 604 BCE.

After Nebuchadnezzar the empire fell into turmoil. His son Amel-Marduk reigned two years before the courtier Neriglissar killed him in a coup. Neriglissar died in 556 BCE, and his underage son Labashi-Marduk was assassinated after nine months. The last king, Nabonidus, favoured the moon god Sîn over Babylon's patron Marduk, a policy that later served Cyrus the Great as a pretext. Cyrus defeated the Babylonian forces at the Battle of Opis, and on 12 October his soldiers entered Babylon without a battle after his engineers diverted the Euphrates. Nabonidus surrendered and was deported.

The king, called šar, took an oath of loyalty from his subjects and used the titles King of Babylon and King of Sumer and Akkad. He was the largest landowner, and other domains belonged to the royal family and high officials. Rulers followed a traditionalist policy: Akkadian remained the language of administration and culture even though Aramaic was the everyday tongue, and old artworks were preserved with near-religious care.

Local assemblies called puhru acted as courts, and slaves, mostly foreigners taken in war or trade, were costly property that owners often trained or rented out. Tribute flowed into Babylonia for the first time since the Assyrian conquest, and building projects, chiefly in Babylon, fostered growth. Under Achaemenid rule Babylonia supplied as much as a third of the empire's tribute, and at least five rebels proclaimed themselves King of Babylon, but Babylon never regained its independence.
chalon-sur-saone: Chalon-sur-Saône lies on the Saône in the south of the region of Bourgogne-Franche-Comté, about 55 kilometres north of Mâcon. It is the largest city of the Saône-et-Loire department, though the department's capital is the smaller Mâcon. It was once a busy port and distribution point for local wines, which were sent up and down the Saône and along the Canal du Centre, opened in 1792.

The site, ancient Cabillonum, was a capital of the Aedui, and objects of the La Tène culture have been recovered from the river bed there. Its first mention is in the Commentarii de Bello Gallico. The Roman city was already a river port and a hub of road communications, including the Via Agrippa.

In 354 CE the emperor Constantius II stationed the Roman 7th Army there for an invasion of the lands of the brother kings Gundomadus and Vadomarius, but the troops, not receiving supplies, revolted and were pacified with money by the grand chamberlain Eusebius. By Late Antiquity the city had shrunk so far that its wall enclosed fifteen hectares.

Saint Marcel is said to have been martyred there in 179. Chalon became one of the de facto capitals of the kingdom of Burgundy under Guntram, king from 561 to 592, who died there and promoted the cult of Marcel. The city was frequently attacked until the 10th century. A diocese, a suffragan of Lyon, was established in the 6th century, and a church council met there from 644 to 655. After the Concordat of 1801 the diocese was merged with that of Autun.

In the 19th century Nicéphore Niépce, born in the city in 1765, made the earliest surviving photograph; his 1807 Pyréolophore is probably the world's first internal combustion engine, and in 1818 he built a dandy horse, for which he coined the word vélocipède. Dominique Vivant Denon, who helped convert the royal palace into the Louvre museum, also lived there.

The Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1845, and in the late 19th century copper and iron works were the main industry, among them the Petit-Creusot engineering works. Saint Vincent's Cathedral dates mainly from the 12th to the 15th centuries, with elements from the eighth century and a neo-Gothic façade of the 19th. The city has a museum of photography on the Quai des Messageries, with more than two million photographs.
chalons-en-champagne: The city was a Gallic and later a Gallo-Roman settlement, named for the Catalauni, a Belgic tribe living in the region of modern Champagne. It is conjectured to have been the site of several battles, among them the Battle of Châlons in 274, fought between the Roman emperor Aurelian and Tetricus I of the Gallic Empire, and the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains in 451, which turned back Attila's westward advance.

Among its natives was Jean Talon, born in 1626, the first Intendant of New France. Nicolas Appert, born in 1749, was the inventor of appertisation, a method of preserving food. The town hall was completed in 1776, and the Porte Sainte-Croix, formerly the Porte Dauphine, was dedicated to Marie Antoinette when she passed through on her way to Paris to marry the future Louis XVI. In 1806 a national engineering school, now Arts et Métiers ParisTech, was established there.

Châlons lies in the Grand Est region and is the prefecture of the Marne department, although it has only about a quarter of the population of Reims. Formerly called Châlons-sur-Marne, it was officially renamed Châlons-en-Champagne in 1995, and should not be confused with the Burgundian city of Chalon-sur-Saône. About 22 kilometres to the north, near Mourmelon-le-Grand, lies the Camp de Mourmelon, formerly the Camp de Châlons. Napoleon III had it created, and it opened on 30 August 1857. It began as a ground for manoeuvres but quickly became a showcase of the Imperial Army, where citizens could watch parades,.

The cathedral of Saint Étienne keeps parts of a first Romanesque cathedral of the 12th century but was mainly rebuilt in the Gothic style, with a Baroque west façade added in the 17th century. The collegiate church of Notre-Dame-en-Vaux, built between 1157 and 1217 and a place of pilgrimage in the 12th century, is part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing. Saint-Alpin, possibly the oldest church in the city, was rebuilt around 1170. The old circus of 1899 houses the Centre National des Arts du Cirque.
chambery: Chambéry was founded at a crossroads of ancient routes between the Dauphiné, Switzerland and Italy, in a wide valley between the Bauges and Chartreuse massifs on the Leysse River. It lies 214 kilometres from Turin, 100 from Lyon and 85 from Geneva, and is a railway and road junction. Its surroundings run from the vineyard slopes of the Combe de Savoie almost to the shores of the Lac du Bourget, the largest natural lake in France.

The history of Chambéry is closely linked to the House of Savoy. It was the Savoyard capital from 1295 to 1563, when Savoy stretched from Bourg-en-Bresse across the Alps to Turin, north to Geneva and south to Nice. The Château des ducs de Savoie, a fortified castle dating from the 11th century, was settled by the first counts of Savoy in 1285 and expanded in the early 14th century as residence, seat of administration and stronghold. It soon became obsolete as a defence against a siege, and constant French hostilities led Duke Emmanuel Philibert to move his capital to Turin in 1563.

The château remained an administrative centre until Christine Marie of France, Duchess of Savoy, returned to hold court there in 1640. In 1684 it saw the marriage of Victor Amadeus II and Anne Marie d'Orléans, a niece of Louis XIV. Victor Amadeus III added a Royal Wing in 1786. France annexed the lands of the duchy west of the Alps in 1792, but returned them to the House of Savoy in Turin in 1815 after Napoleon's defeat. Chambéry was ceded to France by Piedmont in 1860, under Napoleon III, and its Hôtel de Ville opened in 1867.

Chambéry is the prefecture and largest city of the Savoie department, with 60,251 inhabitants in 2022. The château now houses the departmental administration. The Fontaine des Éléphants, built in 1838 to honour Benoît de Boigne's feats in India, is its best-known landmark. The Cistercian Abbey of Hautecombe, founded in 1135, is one of the burial places of the rulers of Savoy, and the cathedral of Saint Francis of Sales has the largest trompe-l'oeil paintings in Europe. The Sisters of St Joseph, an order founded at Chambéry in 1812, work in teaching and charity.
champa: Champa was a collection of independent Cham polities along the coast of what is now central and southern Vietnam, from about the 2nd century CE until 1832. According to the earliest sources the first Cham polities arose in the 2nd and 3rd centuries, after Khu Liên's rebellion against the Eastern Han. They grew out of the seafaring Austronesian Sa Huỳnh culture. Scholars disagree about how far Champa was ever united: older writers saw one kingdom, while others argue that it was mostly a confederation of kingdoms and city-states.

Wars with the neighbouring kingdom of Funan in the 4th century brought Indian culture into Cham society, and Hinduism became the state religion. The Đông Yên Châu inscription, of about 350, is the oldest known text in a native Southeast Asian language. King Vikrantavarman I, who reigned from 653 to 686, had many sanctuaries built at Mỹ Sơn and sent regular embassies to the Tang court. Champa reached its height in the 9th and 10th centuries, and its trade linked the Indian Ocean and East Asia until the 17th century.

In 1471 Champa suffered serious defeats by the Vietnamese state of Đại Việt, in which 120,000 people were captured or killed, among them the king, Tra Toan, who died in captivity on the way north. What remained was a small enclave near Nha Trang and Phan Rang, and many Chams fled to Cambodia. In 1832 the emperor Minh Mạng annexed the last Cham territory. Islam began to spread among the Chams after the 10th century, and by the 17th century the royal families had adopted it.

The Cham, Rade and Jarai peoples of Vietnam and Cambodia speak Chamic languages, and many Cham today are Muslim, while the Bacam keep a form of Hinduism. Cham red brick temples survive in many places. Mỹ Sơn, a former religious centre, and Hội An are World Heritage Sites, and the largest collection of Cham sculpture is in the museum at Da Nang, founded in 1915.
chan-chan: Chan Chan lies at the mouth of the Moche Valley in La Libertad, about five kilometres west of Trujillo, in a particularly arid part of the northern Peruvian coastal desert. With no rain, the main fresh water came from rivers carrying runoff from the Andes, which allowed the control of land and water by irrigation. The city first relied on wells about 15 metres deep. A network of canals diverting water from the Moche River, some reported as running up to 20 miles, later extended the farmland around it. The name Chan Chan is unexplained: linguists agree it is not Mochica, but they dispute whether it comes from Quingnam or from a Quechua word meaning fenced place.

Chan Chan was the capital of Chimor, a conquest state that developed from the Chimú culture of the Peruvian coast. It is believed to have held 40,000 to 60,000 people. Its society was strongly stratified, with rulers and deities at the top and servants at the bottom, and its craftsmen were known for pottery and textiles. The Chimú are said to have held that the sun made three eggs, of gold for the ruler and elite, of silver for the rulers' spouses and of copper for everyone else. Many canals to the north were destroyed by a catastrophic flood around 1100, which turned the Chimú towards an economy based on outside resources.

The Incas conquered the Chimú around 1470 and dispersed Chimú civilians to lands they had recently conquered. It is reported that they cut off the irrigation system. Chan Chan declined, and after Francisco Pizarro founded Trujillo in 1535 the Spaniards looted its tombs, one sixteenth-century list recording a treasure equal to 80,000 pesos of gold.

The site covers about 20 square kilometres, with a dense urban centre of six, and is considered the largest adobe city in the Americas. It has ten walled compounds, called ciudadelas, which contained courts, storerooms, temples, reservoirs and burial platforms for rulers, with high walls carved in relief with fish, birds, waves and nets.

The walls of the Tschudi compound rise up to twelve metres and are wider at the base, which suits an earthquake zone. Ordinary housing took the form of small irregular rooms that doubled as workshops. UNESCO designated Chan Chan a World Heritage Site on 28 November 1986. Excavations by Michael Moseley and Carol J. Mackey began in 1969, and rain and floods from El Niño threaten the adobe walls.
chand-dynasty: The traditional genealogical lists of the Chand kings, the vamshavalis, were compiled in the mid-19th century and are not completely reliable. They place Som Chand in the 7th century, and a British report of 1849 accordingly dated the start of Chand rule to 685 CE. Historians dispute this, because the Katyuri kingdom is known to have ruled Kumaon until the third quarter of the 10th century.

Tradition makes Som Chand an immigrant from Jhusi and a relative of the king of Kannauj. The historian Krishna Pal Singh suggests that he came to Kumaon during the upheaval of the Ghaznavid invasion of Kannauj in 1018–1019, and dates the beginning of Chand rule to 1019–1021. By the early 13th century the Chands appear to have ruled as feudatories: the Baleshwar Temple inscription of 1223, set up by Krachalla Deva, a conqueror from present-day Nepal, lists men whose names suggest that they belonged to the family.

Rudra Chand (1565–1597) seized Sira in 1581 and made the first of several attacks on the Garhwal Kingdom, all of which were repulsed. In 1587 he visited the Mughal emperor Akbar at Lahore as a mark of obeisance, and the Ain-e-Akbari lists a Sarkar of Kumaon. Baz Bahadur Chand (1638–78), one of the most powerful of the line, joined Shahjahan in an attack on Garhwal in 1655 that captured the Terai region including Dehradun, and extended his territory east to the Karnali river. In 1672 he began a poll tax whose revenue was sent to Delhi as tribute.

In 1744 the Rohilla leader Ali Mohammed Khan sent a force that took Almora against weak resistance. The Rohillas stayed seven months and left after a payment of three lakh rupees; a second attack was defeated at Barakheri. Hill troops under Dip Chand later fought beside the Rohillas at the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761. Internal strife over the following thirty years cost the kings most of the land they had held in the plains.

The Gurkhas invaded early in 1790, crossing the Kali River, and the Chands were driven to the Bhabhar and finally expelled. Nepalese rule lasted twenty-four years. During the Anglo-Nepalese War Harak Deo Joshi, minister of the last Chand raja, sided with the British, who captured Almora on 26 April 1815; with the Treaty of Sugauli, ratified on 4 March 1816, Kumaon passed to British rule. Champawat, the first capital, keeps a medieval fort and the Baleshwar and Nagnath temples, and Chand kings also built temples at Bageshwar, Bhimtal and Almora.
chandragupta-maurya: There are no historical facts about Chandragupta's origins and early life, only legends, and the narrative of his reign is deduced mainly from a few fragments in Greek and Roman sources and a few Indian religious texts, all written centuries after his death. Plutarch says that in his youth he saw Alexander the Great during the invasion of India, which led one scholar to propose a birth after 350 BCE. The Sanskrit play Mudrarakshasa calls him Vrishala, a word that one later commentator read as meaning a shudra, while the historian Radha Kumud Mukherjee argued that it means the best of kings.

He rose in the unrest after Alexander's death in 323 BCE, in Magadha, a region then ruled by the unpopular Nanda dynasty. The exact chronology remains debated. His conquest of Magadha is generally dated to about 322 to 319 BCE and his expansion into the Punjab to about 317 to 312 BCE, though some scholars think he first consolidated in the Punjab, and an alternative chronology places these events in about 311 to 305 BCE. According to Mudrarakshasa, his mentor Chanakya assisted him and later became his minister. The Roman writer Justin says Chandragupta led the people in killing Alexander's Greek governors, and then oppressed those he had freed.

Seleucus I Nicator, who had established the Seleucid Empire at Babylon, confronted him between about 305 and 303 BCE, intending to retake the former Persian satrapies along the Indus. The two formed a dynastic marriage alliance, with Seleucus receiving five hundred elephants and Chandragupta gaining control of the regions bordering the Indus. The administration was decentralised, with provinces, local governments and a council of ministers.

Digambara Jain accounts say that Chandragupta abdicated in favour of his son Bindusara and became a monk under Bhadrabahu at Shravanabelagola in Karnataka, where he fasted to death. These legends developed about 900 years later; contemporary Greek evidence says he drank wine, hunted and performed Vedic sacrifices, and no contemporary source supports his conversion to Jainism.

His reign is called the sheet anchor of Indian chronology, because in 1793 Sir William Jones identified him with the Sandracottus of Greek and Roman writers, allowing Indian and Greek history to be dated together. The empire he founded reached its peak under his grandson Ashoka. Western and Indian historians differ in their views of him, the latter often presenting him as the founder of the first Indian nation.
chandrayaan-3: Chandrayaan-3 is the third mission of the Chandrayaan programme, a series of lunar-exploration missions developed by ISRO. Its name comes from the Sanskrit chandra, Moon, and yana, craft. ISRO had earlier launched Chandrayaan-2, with an orbiter, a lander and a rover. Its lander lost contact with mission control, deviated from its intended trajectory while attempting to land near the lunar south pole, and crashed. Chandrayaan-3 consisted of a lander, Vikram, and a rover, Pragyan, as replacements for those of Chandrayaan-2, together with a propulsion module. The mission aimed to land safely and softly on the Moon, to show the rover driving there, and to carry out experiments on the lunar surface materials.

Chandrayaan-3 was launched on 14 July 2023 aboard an LVM3 M4 rocket from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre in Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh. It entered lunar orbit on 5 August, and on 17 August the Vikram lander separated from the propulsion module, which had carried it to a lunar orbit of 100 kilometres.

On 23 August 2023 the lander fired its four engines as a braking manoeuvre at 30 kilometres above the Moon. It then rotated from a horizontal to a vertical position using eight smaller thrusters. It slowed to roughly 150 metres, where it hovered for about 30 seconds to find a good landing spot, and touched down near the lunar south pole, at 69 degrees south, at 12:33 UTC.

The rover's laser-induced breakdown spectroscope reported sulfur near the south pole, and ISRO released temperature profiles from the top 10 centimetres of the lunar surface, in which a high range of 70 °C near the surface was not expected. The lander also made a short hop of about 40 centimetres. The lander and rover were built to operate for one lunar daylight period, or 14 Earth days, and not to endure the night temperatures of minus 120 °C. The rover was put into sleep mode on 3 September, and neither responded to wake-up calls later in September.

With the landing, ISRO became the fourth national space agency to land successfully on the Moon, after the Soviet space programme, NASA and CNSA, and the first to make a soft landing near the lunar south pole. The Prime Minister of India, Narendra Modi, named the touchdown point Station Shiv Shakti and declared 23 August National Space Day. The live stream of the landing on ISRO's YouTube channel had eight million concurrent viewers, the highest on YouTube for a live video. ISRO chairman S. Somanath said that the agency had learnt a lot from its failure and corrected it.
changchun: Changchun lies in the middle portion of the Northeast China Plain at a moderate elevation of 250 to 350 metres, with a small area of low mountains in the east, the highest being Laodaodong Mountain at 711 metres. It has a humid continental climate, with long, cold, windy but dry winters from November to March and hot, humid summers. Its name means long spring in Chinese. The municipality is administered as a sub-provincial city of Jilin province.

Changchun began as a small trading post and frontier village, dealing mainly in furs and other natural products. In 1800 the Jiaqing Emperor selected a village on the east bank of the Yitong River and named it Changchun Ting. At the end of the eighteenth century peasants from overpopulated provinces such as Shandong and Hebei began to settle in the region, and in 1889 the village was promoted to a city known as Changchun Fu. In May 1898 it received its first railway station, at Kuancheng, on the southern branch of the Chinese Eastern Railway built by the Russian Empire between Harbin and Lüshun.

After Russia lost the southern section of this line in the Russo-Japanese War of 1904–1905, the Kuancheng station became the last Russian station on the branch. The next station to the south, the new Japanese Changchun station, became the first of the South Manchuria Railway. The Treaty of Portsmouth transferred the railway between Changchun and Port Arthur to Japan in 1906, and the Japanese government sent planners and engineers to choose the best site for a new station.

On 10 March 1932 the capital of Manchukuo, a Japan-controlled puppet state in Manchuria, was established in Changchun, and on 13 March it was renamed Hsinking, meaning new capital. The Emperor Puyi lived in the Imperial Palace, now a museum. The region experienced harsh suppression, forced conscription and labour and brutal warfare on the civilian population, and at the same time rapid industrialisation and militarisation. On 20 August 1945 the Soviet Red Army captured the city and renamed it Changchun; Soviet forces remained until 1946.

Changchun became the capital of Jilin in 1954. Construction of the First Automobile Works began in 1953, with Soviet technical support, and production of the Jiefang CA-10 truck, based on the Soviet ZIS-150, started in 1956. In 1958 it introduced the Hongqi limousines. The city is known as China's City of Automobiles and is home to Jilin University and Northeast Normal University. Among its sights are the Badabu, the group of buildings of the former eight Manchukuo ministries, the Museum of the Manchu State Imperial Palace and the Jilin Provincial Museum.
changsha: Changsha lies in northeastern Hunan, in the lower reaches of the Xiang River and the western part of the Changliu Basin.
