Most of the rivers in the area belong to the Xiang system, and fifteen tributaries flow into the Xiang. The city has a humid subtropical climate with distinct seasons, long and very hot summers, and a mean January temperature of 5.3 °C. It forms a metropolitan region with Zhuzhou and Xiangtan, known as the Changzhutan City Cluster. The name means long sandy place and is attested as early as the eleventh century BCE, when a vassal lord sent King Cheng of Zhou a gift described as a Changsha softshell turtle.

Settlement is said to have begun around 3000 BCE with the proliferation of the Longshan culture, although there is no firm evidence of such a link; people certainly lived in the area during the Bronze Age. The name appears in the Yi Zhou Shu, written before the Qin, and the Qin set up the Changsha Commandery. In the Western Han dynasty the Changsha Kingdom was established. The historian Ying Shao wrote in the second century that the Qin use of the name for the area continued its old name. In the Tang dynasty the Tongguan Kiln in Changsha produced the world's earliest underglaze porcelain, which was exported to Western Asia, Africa and Europe.

During the period of the Five Dynasties Changsha was the capital of Southern Chu. In the Northern Song dynasty the Yuelu Academy, later Hunan University, was one of the four major private academies of the last thousand years. Under the Qing, Changsha was the capital of Hunan and prospered as one of China's chief rice markets. During the Taiping Rebellion rebels besieged the city for three months, in 1852 or 1854, but it never fell. The rebels moved on to Wuhan, and Changsha became the principal base for the government's suppression of the rebellion.

Changsha is the capital of Hunan and among the first cities designated a National Historical and Cultural City in China. It has a history of more than 2,400 years of urban construction. Its main industries include construction machinery and new materials, and it is home to the Hunan Broadcasting System. Sights include the Yuelu Academy and the statue of the young Mao Zedong on Orange Isle. Changshanese, a kind of Xiang Chinese, is spoken in the downtown area, and Hunan cuisine, hot and spicy, remains the most popular.
channel-islands: The Channel Islands are an archipelago in the English Channel, to the west of the Cotentin Peninsula and off the Normandy coast. Channel Islands is a geographical term, not a political unit, first used around 1830, possibly by the Royal Navy. The two major islands, Jersey and Guernsey, make up 99 per cent of the population and 92 per cent of the area. The highest point is Les Platons in Jersey at 143 metres.

Humans lived on what is now Jersey at least 250,000 to 200,000 years ago, as La Cotte de St Brelade shows Neanderthal occupation when the island was connected to the mainland. Rising sea levels detached the islands in the Mesolithic period. Dolmens, the burial mound of La Hougue Bie in Jersey and the statue menhirs of Guernsey show a population large and organised enough for constructions of considerable size. In the sixth century Christian missionaries visited, and saints such as Samson of Dol and Helier are associated with the islands.

In 933 Raoul, King of Western Francia, granted the islands to William Longsword, and they were annexed to the Duchy of Normandy. When King John lost mainland Normandy to King Philip II of France, he kept control of the islands, and by the Treaty of Paris of 1259 Henry III surrendered his claim to the duchy while retaining them. Since around 1290 they have been split into two bailiwicks. In the Wars of the Three Kingdoms Jersey held out for the Royalist cause and gave refuge to Charles, Prince of Wales, while Presbyterian Guernsey favoured Parliament. Charles II rewarded George Carteret, bailiff and governor of Jersey, with a grant of land in America, which he named New Jersey.

The islands form two self-governing Crown Dependencies, the Bailiwick of Jersey and the Bailiwick of Guernsey, which includes Alderney, Sark and Herm. Neither is part of the United Kingdom, which is responsible for their defence and international relations. Each has its own laws, elections and representative bodies. The capitals are Saint Helier and Saint Peter Port. German forces occupied the islands in the Second World War: the British government demilitarised them in June 1940, and 6,600 of 50,000 people left Jersey and 17,000 of 42,000 left Guernsey, among them thousands of children evacuated with their schools.
chao-phraya-river: The Chao Phraya begins at the confluence of the Ping and Nan rivers at Nakhon Sawan and flows south for 372 kilometres to Bangkok and the Gulf of Thailand. At Chai Nat it splits off the Tha Chin River, which runs parallel and reaches the gulf at Samut Sakhon. Its watershed, 157,924 square kilometres, is the largest in Thailand.

The plain falls only about 80 metres over 500 kilometres from the hills to the sea, so the rivers run sluggishly and boats could be poled or paddled upstream for most of the year, which made water the most convenient transport before the modern era. The delta took its present form late: the coast reached the site of Bangkok between 3000 and 1000 BCE and settled near its present position by 500 CE.

The basin saw the rise of some of the earliest civilisations of Southeast Asia, notably Dvaravati from the 7th to the 11th century. The river was crucial to the Lavo kingdom and to its successors, and formed the basis of the Ayodhya Kingdom, incorporated into the Ayutthaya Kingdom in the 14th century. Rice growing intensified from the 13th century under Sukhothai and Ayutthaya with the introduction of floating rice from Bengal.
During the Ayutthaya period shortcut canals were dug across river loops, the first in 1538 on the order of King Chairachathirat, and the river's course has since followed many of them.

Rattanakosin, now Bangkok, was founded in 1782 on the east bank, a position that protected it from Burmese invasions from the west. Canalisation and cultivation of the southern swamps followed, and Thailand began to export rice in 1855. The name Chao Phraya is documented in writing only from the reign of King Mongkut in the 19th century; earlier maps usually called the river the Menam. It probably comes from Bang Chao Phraya, the settlement now called Samut Prakan, recorded from about 1660.

The provinces along the river, from Nakhon Sawan to Samut Prakan, include Ayutthaya, Nonthaburi and Bangkok, among the most historically significant and densely populated in Thailand. Its many canals, called khlong, irrigate the rice paddies of the plain, and in Bangkok the river is a major transport artery for ferries and long-tail boats. The original swamp forests of the lowlands have almost entirely been cleared for farming and cities.
charcoal: Charcoal is a lightweight black residue of carbon, made by strongly heating wood or other plant and animal material in minimal oxygen so that all water and volatile constituents are driven off. In the traditional process, called charcoal burning, part of the starting material is itself burnt to supply the heat, with a limited supply of air. The properties of the product depend on the material charred and on the temperature: charcoal made at about 300 degrees Celsius is brown, soft and friable, while charcoal made at higher temperatures is hard and brittle.

Wood charcoal has been made since ancient times wherever wood was abundant. Billets of wood were stacked on end in a conical pile, with openings at the bottom to admit air and a central shaft serving as a flue. The pile was covered with turf or moistened clay and lit at the bottom of the flue, and the fire spread slowly outward and upward. In the clamp used in Britain, logs leaned against a chimney of four stakes and were covered with soil and straw, and burned into charcoal over about five days.

The skill lay in controlling the combustion, so the work was left to professional charcoal burners, or colliers, who often lived alone in small huts to tend their piles. In the Harz Mountains of Germany they lived in conical huts called Köten, which still exist.

Charcoal has served for art, medicine, pigment and as a constituent of black powder, but its most important use has been as a metallurgical fuel. It burns at more than 1,100 degrees Celsius, and its heat can be moderated by controlling the flow of air, so it remains the traditional fuel of the blacksmith's forge. It has been used to make iron and steel, where it also supplies carbon, since at least 2000 BCE, with remains found in Proto-Hittite layers at Kaman-Kalehöyük.

The demand was great enough that charcoal making became a major cause of deforestation, especially in Central Europe, where at its height it employed hundreds of thousands of people. In the 16th century England passed laws to keep the country from being stripped of trees by iron production, and many woods were managed as coppices, cut and regrown in cycles. Growing scarcity of wood helped drive the move to coal, and in the 19th century coke largely replaced charcoal in steelmaking.
charente-maritime: Charente-Maritime lies on the west coast of France, named after the river Charente, with an area of 6,864 square kilometres. It was created by a decree of the Constituent Assembly of 22 December 1789, which took effect on 4 March 1790, as one of the 83 original departments of the French Revolution. It encompasses most of the former province of Saintonge, nearly all of Aunis and the Pays d'Aulnay from Poitou. Initially named Charente-Inférieure after the lower course of the river, it was renamed on 4 September 1941, reflecting its Atlantic coast identity. Saintes, the capital of Saintonge, was the prefecture from 1790 until Napoleon decreed its transfer to La Rochelle in 1810.

Human settlement dates to the Lower Paleolithic, and a Neanderthal skeleton found at Roche à Pierrot in Saint-Césaire in 1979, dated to about 36,300 years ago, confirmed an overlap with Cro-Magnons. The Santoni made the oppidum at Pons their political and trading hub in the La Tène period, and after the Gallic War Mediolanum Santonum, now Saintes, became the first capital of the Roman province of Aquitaine under Augustus. It was burned by the Alamanni in 276. In 418 the Visigoths settled in the region, and Clovis ousted them after defeating Alaric at Vouillé in 507.

La Rochelle grew in the twelfth century under the Dukes of Aquitaine and received a communal charter from Henry II in 1175. Eleanor of Aquitaine's marriage to Henry Plantagenet in 1152 tied the region to England, and the Hundred Years' War devastated it until the French recaptured Montguyon in 1451. La Rochelle became a Protestant stronghold in the Wars of Religion. In 1627 Cardinal Richelieu began a siege of the city, with a dike blocking its access to the sea, and famine and disease reduced the population from 28,000 to 5,000 before it surrendered on 28 October 1628. Explorers Pierre Dugua de Mons and Samuel de Champlain, from Saintonge, founded Québec in 1608.

The nineteenth century brought prosperity under the Second Empire, driven by cognac, until the phylloxera crisis. German forces occupied the department in the Second World War and built sea defences, including pillboxes on Oléron. Royan was nearly destroyed by an RAF raid on 5 January 1945, and La Rochelle was freed on 9 May 1945.

The prefecture is La Rochelle, and the department lies in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine. The islands of Ré and Oléron belong to it. The Paléosite centre at Saint-Césaire, opened in 2005, presents the Neanderthal find, and Saintes keeps Roman monuments such as a votive arch and an amphitheatre.
chariot: The critical invention that allowed light, horse-drawn chariots was the spoked wheel. Chariots emerged in the early 2nd millennium BCE. The oldest known come from burials of the Sintashta culture in present-day Russia, dated to about 1950 to 1880 BCE, although some scholars classify those finds as carts rather than true chariots. Cylinder seals from Kültepe in central Anatolia of about 1900 BCE also depict them. The first certain attestation of chariots in the Hittite empire dates to the late 17th century BCE, and they reached Egypt around 1650 BCE during the Hyksos invasion. The Hittites developed a lighter design with four-spoked wheels, wide enough for a driver, an archer and a shield-bearer.

A chariot was a fast, light, open, two-wheeled vehicle drawn by two or more horses harnessed side by side, little more than a floor with a waist-high guard at the front and sides. Greek chariots had no seat and no suspension. Egyptian chariots served as mobile archery platforms with two men, and the best preserved examples are the four found in the tomb of Tutankhamun. By the 7th century BCE the Neo-Assyrian Empire used heavy chariots with a crew of four. In Roman usage a two-horse chariot was a biga, a three-horse chariot a triga and a four-horse chariot a quadriga.

Chariots played a major role in Late Bronze Age warfare, including the Battle of Kadesh, fought about 1274 BCE between the Hittites and the Egyptian Empire. The Mycenaean Greeks, who most probably adopted them from the Hittites, recorded large inventories of them on Linear B tablets. In China the earliest evidence is a burial at Hougang, Anyang, from about 1250 BCE, and their use there peaked from the 8th to the 5th centuries BCE. Massed chariot warfare became all but obsolete after the Warring States period, as crossbows, long halberds and cavalry took over.

Elsewhere cavalry likewise replaced them, though chariots remained in use for travel, processions, games and races. British chariots were described by Julius Caesar, and the last mention of chariots in battle seems to be at the Battle of Mons Graupius in 84 CE. In the Roman Empire they were used in racing at the Circus Maximus and in triumphal processions.
charites: The Charites, called the Graces in English and the Gratiae in Latin, personify beauty and grace. In Hesiod's Theogony they are the three daughters of Zeus and the Oceanid Eurynome: Aglaia, Euphrosyne and Thalia. Accounts differ, however, in names, number and parentage. Homer mentions Pasithea as one of the younger Graces, and Pausanias reports that the Athenians worshipped two Charites, Auxo and Hegemone, and the Spartans two, Cleta and Phaenna, while by Boeotian tradition Eteocles, king of Orchomenus, fixed the number at three.

They have little independent mythology and mostly attend the Olympian gods, above all Aphrodite, whom they bathed and anointed at Paphos. Pindar says they arranged feasts and dances for the Olympians and danced with Apollo and the Muses. One of them was the wife of the smith god Hephaestus: Hesiod calls her Aglaia, and in the Iliad she is called Charis.

Their cult is very old, and their name appears to be pre-Greek in origin. Its purpose seems to have resembled that of the nymphs, concerned with fertility and nature and with springs and rivers. An inscription of the sixth century BCE on Thera records a cult, and dance was strongly linked with it. At least four temples were dedicated to them alone, at Orchomenus, Hermione, Sparta and Elis. The most important was at Orchomenus in Boeotia, where the cult was thought to have begun. There the goddesses were worshipped at a very ancient site with a trio of stones and received a share of the produce of the rich plain, and Strabo says that Eteocles founded their temple.

In Greek art of the Archaic and Classical periods the Charites were dressed and shown in a line as dancers. The Roman and later pose, a nude interlaced group, developed later; Pausanias says he could not find who first showed them naked. The earliest known image is from a temple of Apollo at Thermon, of the seventh or sixth century BCE. A Classical relief of the Charites and Hermes at the entrance to the Acropolis was popularly ascribed to Socrates. In the Renaissance the nude group allowed pagan beauty to appear in art, and the Graces were painted by Botticelli in Primavera and sculpted by Antonio Canova and Bertel Thorvaldsen.
charlemagne: Charlemagne was the eldest son of Pepin the Short and Bertrada of Laon. His year of birth is uncertain, and the biographer Einhard reports him as 72 at his death. He was probably functionally bilingual in Germanic and Romance dialects from an early age, also spoke Latin and, according to Einhard, could understand and perhaps speak some Greek. After Pepin's death in 768 he and his brother Carloman I became kings of the Franks, and he became sole ruler three years later.

Charlemagne continued his father's policy of protecting the papacy and removed the Lombards from power in northern Italy in 774. His first war against the Saxons began what became over thirty years of nearly continuous warfare. After a defeat in 782 the annals record that he had 4,500 Saxon prisoners beheaded in the massacre of Verden, a figure historians think may be exaggerated although the event itself is not in doubt. The Capitulatio de partibus Saxoniae, with the death penalty for pagan practices, has been described as a programme for forced conversion. His campaigns of the 790s were more destructive still, and his court settled at Aachen, where he built a palace and a chapel. His forces also brought down the kingdom of the Avars.

Pope Leo III was attacked by his enemies in April 799 and fled to Charlemagne. After an assembly in Rome at which Leo swore an oath of innocence, Leo crowned Charlemagne emperor of the Romans at St Peter's Basilica on Christmas Day 800. He was the first reigning emperor in the west since 476, and historians debate the significance of the coronation. From 801 he ruled more from Aachen and rarely led armies in person. He sought recognition of his title from Constantinople, which Emperor Michael I finally confirmed after a peace in 810.

In September 813 Charlemagne crowned his only surviving son, Louis, as co-emperor at Aachen. He died in 814 and was buried in the Palatine Chapel at Aachen. His reign inspired the cultural revival known as the Carolingian Renaissance, for which he promoted learning to create a more effective clergy. He held 23 synods and required the Rule of St Benedict in monasteries. After Louis's death the Treaty of Verdun divided the empire among his sons, and Carolingians ruled in East Francia until 911 and in West Francia until 987. Otto the Great was crowned emperor in 962, founding or re-establishing the Holy Roman Empire, which lasted until 1806.
charles-borromeo: Charles Borromeo was born in the castle of Arona on Lake Maggiore on 2 October 1538. His father, Gilbert, was Count of Arona, and his mother, Margaret, belonged to the Milanese branch of the House of Medici. The Borromeo family was one of the oldest and wealthiest in Lombardy. Charles received the tonsure at about twelve and, when given the income of a rich Benedictine abbey, told his father that whatever exceeded the cost of his preparation for the church belonged to the poor. He studied law at the University of Pavia and took his doctorate on 6 December 1559.

When his uncle was elected Pope Pius IV on 25 December 1559, he summoned Borromeo to Rome and made him a cardinal on 31 January 1560. He organised the third and last session of the Council of Trent in 1562 and 1563 and had a large share in the Tridentine Catechism. The death of his brother Federico in November 1562, and his contacts with the Jesuits and Theatines, led him to a stricter life and to put into practice a bishop's duties as the Council set them out. He was formally appointed archbishop of Milan in 1564 and entered the city in September 1565.

Milan was the largest archdiocese in Italy, with over 3,000 clergy and 800,000 people, and no archbishop had been present for about 80 years. Borromeo found indulgences and offices sold and monasteries in disorder. He made pastoral visits and, believing that abuses arose from ignorant clergy, founded seminaries and colleges, the Oblates of St Ambrose and the first Sunday school classes. Some members of the Humiliati, an order that opposed him, plotted against his life, and a shot fired at him in his chapel missed.

In 1576 famine struck Milan, followed by plague, and the governor and many nobles fled. Borromeo stayed, tried to feed 60,000 to 70,000 people daily and went into debt to do so. In 1583, as apostolic visitor to the Swiss cantons, he repressed Protestantism in the valleys. In the Valle Mesolcina 150 people were arrested for witchcraft, and the civil authorities condemned eleven women and the provost of Roveredo to be burned alive.

Borromeo's uncompromising stance brought him into conflict with secular leaders, priests and even the pope. He fell ill in 1584 and died in Milan on 3 November, aged 46. Paul V canonised him on 1 November 1610, and he is the patron saint of bishops, catechists and seminarians.
charles-bridge: The bridge replaced the Judith Bridge, built between 1158 and 1172 and severely damaged by a flood in 1342. Czech legend holds that Charles IV himself laid the first stone at 5:31 in the morning of 9 July 1357, chosen because the figures, 1357, 9/7, 5:31, form a palindrome, a numerical bridge in the eyes of an emperor who believed in numerology. The bridge was completed in 1402. It was originally called the Stone Bridge or the Prague Bridge and has been called Charles Bridge only since 1870. Until 1841 it was the only way across the Vltava, which made Prague important on the trade route between Eastern and Western Europe.

The bridge is 516 metres long and nearly 10 metres wide. Following the example of the Stone Bridge at Regensburg, it was built as a bow bridge with 16 arches shielded by ice guards. Three towers protect it, two on the Lesser Quarter side and the Old Town Bridge Tower on the other. An avenue of 30 statues stands along the balustrade, mostly Baroque and mostly erected between 1683 and 1714, among them John of Nepomuk. Since 1965 all have been replaced by replicas, and the originals are shown in the Lapidarium of the National Museum.

The bridge has survived floods and wars. A flood in 1432 damaged three pillars, and in 1496 the third arch broke down. After the Battle of White Mountain the heads of leaders of the anti-Habsburg revolt, executed on 21 June 1621, were displayed on the Old Town Bridge Tower. In 1648 the heaviest fighting for the Old Town took place on the bridge, as the Swedes advanced from the west bank. A flood on 2-5 September 1890 tore down three arches and two pillars, and the bridge reopened on 19 November 1892. A capital repair from 1965 to 1978 secured the pillars, and all vehicles have been excluded since then.
charles-darwin: Charles Robert Darwin was born on 12 February 1809 at The Mount, his family's home in Shrewsbury, Shropshire, the fifth of six children of the wealthy doctor and financier Robert Darwin and Susannah Darwin, née Wedgwood. His grandfathers Erasmus Darwin and Josiah Wedgwood were both prominent abolitionists, and Erasmus had praised general concepts of evolution and common descent in his Zoonomia (1794). His mother died in July 1817. In October 1825 he entered the University of Edinburgh Medical School, found lectures dull and surgery distressing, and neglected his studies. He assisted Robert Edmond Grant's research on marine invertebrates, then studied at Christ's College, Cambridge, from 1828 to 1831.

His five-year voyage on HMS Beagle, from 1831 to 1836, established him as an eminent geologist, and his observations supported Charles Lyell's concept of gradual geological change. The Voyage of the Beagle (1839) made him a popular author. Puzzled by the distribution of the wildlife and fossils he had collected, he devised his theory of natural selection in 1838, but he needed time for extensive research and his geological work had priority.

In 1858 Alfred Russel Wallace sent him an essay outlining the same idea, which led to a joint submission to the Linnean Society of London. Darwin published On the Origin of Species in 1859, and later The Descent of Man (1871), on human evolution and sexual selection. His final book was The Formation of Vegetable Mould, through the Actions of Worms (1881). He and his wife and cousin Emma Wedgwood had ten children, two of whom died in infancy.

Darwin died on 19 April 1882 and was buried in Westminster Abbey. By the 1870s the scientific community and most of the educated public accepted evolution as a fact, though many favoured explanations that gave natural selection only a minor role. A broad consensus that natural selection is the basic mechanism came with the modern evolutionary synthesis of the 1930s to the 1950s. Later movements, among them eugenics and Social Darwinism, invoked his name, sometimes against his own comments; he insisted that social policy should not be guided simply by concepts of struggle and selection.
charles-de-foucauld: Charles Eugène, vicomte de Foucauld de Pontbriand, was born in Strasbourg on 15 September 1858 into an old noble family from Périgord. His parents died within months of each other in 1864, and he and his sister were brought up in Strasbourg by their maternal grandfather, Colonel Beaudet de Morlet. In 1870 the family fled the Franco-Prussian War and later settled in Nancy. At 15 he lost his faith and for twelve years believed, in his later words, nothing. He entered the Saint-Cyr Military Academy in 1876, graduating 333rd of 386, and led an extravagant life after inheriting his grandfather's fortune.

Posted to the 4th Regiment of Chasseurs d'Afrique in Algeria, he grew bored with garrison service and travelled in Morocco in 1883–84, the Sahara in 1885 and Palestine in 1888–89. His research on the geography and culture of Algeria and Morocco won the gold medal of the Société de Géographie de Paris in 1885, and he published an account of his Moroccan journey in 1888. On 14 January 1890 he entered the Trappist monastery of Notre-Dame des Neiges. He was later sent to Akbès on the Syrian-Turkish border, and left the order in 1897 after seven years, working as a servant near a convent of Poor Clares in Nazareth.

He was ordained a priest on 9 June 1901 and settled at Béni Abbès in the Algerian Sahara, building a hermitage for adoration and hospitality, though nobody joined him. He then moved to Tamanghasset among the Tuareg and spent ten years studying their language and traditions, using the Assekrem as a place of retreat. His Tuareg dictionary, published after his death in four volumes, is known to specialists for its rich and apt descriptions, and he also collected Tuareg poetry.

On 1 December 1916 a group of tribal bandits dragged de Foucauld from his bordj at Tamanrasset, intending to kidnap him. Interrupted by two soldiers of the French Camel Corps, a startled 15-year-old shot him dead, and the soldiers were also killed. The Tuareg buried him the next morning. His remains were moved in April 1929 to El Meniaa. René Bazin's biography made him widely known, and the Little Brothers of Jesus, the Little Sisters of Jesus and many other congregations and fraternities draw on his life and writings. He was beatified on 13 November 2005 and canonised on 15 May 2022.
charles-de-gaulle: Charles André Joseph Marie de Gaulle was born on 22 November 1890 in Lille, the third of five children. He was raised in a devoutly Roman Catholic, conservative and monarchist family. His father, Henri de Gaulle, was a professor of history and literature at a Jesuit college and later founded his own school.

In 1909 he won a place at the military academy of Saint-Cyr, finishing 119th out of 221. Before entering he served a year in the ranks in the 33rd Infantry Regiment at Arras. His company commander declined to make him a sergeant at first, remarking that the young man evidently thought nothing less than Constable of France good enough for him.

In the First World War he was wounded in the knee at the Battle of Dinant on 15 August 1914 and later taken prisoner by the German Empire. After the armistice he served on the French military mission to Poland and won the Polish Virtuti Militari. In the interwar years he advocated mobile armoured divisions.

When the German invasion came in May 1940 he led an armoured division in a counterattack and was appointed Undersecretary for War. Refusing his government's armistice with Germany, he went to Britain and urged the French to fight on in his Appeal of 18 June. He led the Free French Forces and in June 1944 became head of the Provisional Government of the French Republic. He resigned in 1946 and withdrew to Colombey-les-Deux-Églises to write his War Memoirs.

During the May 1958 crisis, as the Algerian War threatened the Fourth Republic, the National Assembly brought him back to power. He commissioned a new constitution and was elected President of France on 21 December 1958. He withdrew France from NATO's integrated military command and launched an independent nuclear force, and on 22 January 1963 he signed the Élysée Treaty with Chancellor Konrad Adenauer. He resigned in late April 1969 after losing a referendum on decentralisation.

De Gaulle died suddenly on 9 November 1970 from an abdominal aortic aneurysm while watching television. His successor Georges Pompidou announced his death by saying simply, "General de Gaulle is dead. France is a widow." French political parties and leaders claim a Gaullist legacy, and streets and monuments in France and elsewhere bear his name.
charles-dickens: Charles John Huffam Dickens was born on 7 February 1812 at Landport in Portsea Island (Portsmouth), the second of eight children of Elizabeth and John Dickens, a clerk in the Royal Navy Pay Office. He spent his formative years at Chatham in Kent, reading widely, including Tobias Smollett, Henry Fielding and The Arabian Nights. At 12 he left school to work in a boot-blacking factory when his father was imprisoned for debt, and after three years he returned to school.

Dickens began as a political journalist, reporting Parliamentary debates and election campaigns. His journalism in periodicals formed Sketches by Boz in 1836, Boz being a family nickname. His literary success began with the serial publication of The Pickwick Papers in 1836, and within a few years he was an international celebrity. In December 1845 he became editor of the Daily News but resigned after ten weeks.

On 9 June 1865, returning from Paris with Ellen Ternan, he was in the Staplehurst rail crash in Kent, in which ten passengers were killed. He tended the wounded until rescuers came and went back for the manuscript of Our Mutual Friend.

Dickens wrote 15 major novels, several novellas and many short stories. Most were published in weekly or monthly instalments, which became the dominant Victorian mode, and let him judge his audience's reaction and sometimes change his plot. Among his works are A Christmas Carol (1843), David Copperfield (1849 to 1850) and Bleak House (1852 to 1853), a satire on the judicial system that helped support a reformist movement leading to the legal reform of the 1870s. His works have never gone out of print.
charles-fourier: François Marie Charles Fourier was born in Besançon on 7 April 1772, the son of a small businessman. He cared more for architecture than for his father's trade and as a boy was most interested in geography. When his father died in 1781 he received two-fifths of an estate valued at more than 200,000 francs, which allowed him to travel through Europe. From 1791 to 1816 he worked in Paris, Rouen, Lyon, Marseille and Bordeaux as a travelling salesman and correspondence clerk, complaining of serving the knavery of merchants. He wrote most of his works between 1816 and 1821 and died in Paris on 10 October 1837.

His first book, the Theory of the Four Movements and the General Destinies, appeared anonymously in Lyon in 1808 and sold few copies. Fourier held that cooperation is the key to social success. People would live in communities called phalanxes, housed in phalanstères, four-storey apartment complexes where the richest had the upper floors. Jobs would be assigned by interest and desire, with higher pay for unattractive work. He counted 12 common passions and 810 types of character, so that an ideal phalanx would have 1,620 people. The phalanstères remained concepts, since he never obtained the money to build them.

Fourier argued that important jobs should be open to women by skill, and he never married. He saw poverty rather than inequality as the chief cause of disorder. He also wrote of Jews as the ruin of the body politic, called trade, which he associated with them, the source of all evil, and proposed that Jews be made to farm in the phalansteries. John K. Roth and Richard L. Rubenstein see his antisemitism as economic and religious, not the racial kind that emerged later.

Fourier's proposals inspired intentional communities in the United States, among them Utopia in Ohio, the North American Phalanx in New Jersey and Brook Farm in Massachusetts, and the Familistery of Guise in France. His follower Victor Considerant carried his ideas into the 1848 Revolution and the Paris Commune. Friedrich Engels named him one of three major utopian socialists, and Peter Kropotkin saw him as founder of the libertarian branch of socialism.
charles-i-of-anjou: Charles was the youngest child of King Louis VIII of France and Blanche of Castile, and the first Capetian to be named for Charlemagne. The late king willed that his youngest sons be prepared for a career in the Church, and Charles was destined for it until the early 1240s. He received a good education and had a documented passion for poetry, medicine and law. In December 1244 Louis IX took a vow to lead a crusade, and Charles took the cross too, despite his mother's opposition. The crusaders took Damietta in 1249, and the brothers were captured on 6 April 1250 and released for a ransom. Charles returned to France in October 1250.

Charles held Provence and Forcalquier through his wife's inheritance. After returning from Egypt he put down a rebellion in Provence: Arles surrendered in April 1251, Avignon in May, and Marseille, the last to resist, made peace in July 1252. In 1263 he accepted the Holy See's offer of the Kingdom of Sicily, called the Regno. He was crowned in Rome on 5 January 1266, annihilated Manfred's army and occupied the Regno almost without resistance. His victory over Conradin at Tagliacozzo in 1268 secured his rule. In 1272 he took the title King of Albania, in 1277 he purchased a claim to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, and in 1278 he became Prince of Achaea.

His rule in the Regno rested on heavy taxation, notably the subventio generalis, which the popes called illegal. In 1281 Pope Martin IV authorised a crusade against the Byzantine Empire. The Sicilian Vespers rebellion of 30 March 1282 ended his rule on the island, and Peter III of Aragon was declared king of Sicily at Palermo on 4 September.

Charles prepared a campaign to regain Sicily, but fell seriously ill, made his will on 6 January 1285 and died on 7 January. His body was buried in Naples, and his heart was placed at the Couvent Saint-Jacques in Paris. Two realms, each ruled by a king styled of Sicily, then coexisted for more than a century. The chroniclers Bartholomaeus of Neocastro and Saba Malaspina strongly influenced modern views of Charles, though both were biased: the first called him a tyrant to justify the Vespers. He gave estates in the kingdom to about 700 noblemen from France or Provence.
charles-ii-of-england: Charles was born on 29 May 1630 at St James's Palace, the eldest surviving son of Charles I and Henrietta Maria of France. At or around his eighth birthday he was designated Prince of Wales, though he was never formally invested. After his father's execution on 30 January 1649 the Parliament of Scotland proclaimed him king on 5 February, while England became a republic. Oliver Cromwell defeated him at the Battle of Worcester on 3 September 1651, and Charles spent the next nine years in exile in France, the Dutch Republic and the Spanish Netherlands.

After Cromwell's death in 1658 the unrest that followed his son Richard's resignation led George Monck, the Governor of Scotland, to march into London and restore the excluded members of the Long Parliament. A general election followed, and Charles was invited to return; he was received in London on 29 May 1660, his thirtieth birthday. The royalist and Anglican Cavalier Parliament passed the acts later called the Clarendon Code, which secured the position of the Church of England against nonconformists. Charles accepted them although he favoured religious tolerance.

In 1665 the Great Plague of London peaked at up to 7,000 deaths a week, and the court withdrew to Salisbury. The Great Fire of London began on 2 September 1666 in Pudding Lane and destroyed about 13,200 houses and 87 churches, including St Paul's Cathedral; Charles and his brother James helped direct the firefighting. In 1670 he made the Treaty of Dover with Louis XIV of France, and in 1672 issued a Declaration of Indulgence for Catholics and dissenters, which Parliament forced him to withdraw. The Test Act followed, and by 1674 the Third Anglo-Dutch War had gained England nothing.

The Popish Plot of 1679 and the Catholicism of his heir James, Duke of York, produced the Exclusion Crisis, from which the Whig and Tory parties took their names. Charles sided with the Tories, dissolved Parliament several times, and after 1681 ruled without it. He had a lasting interest in the navy and in science, and revived public festivities after the Puritan rule of Cromwell. His marriage to Catherine of Braganza produced no surviving children, but he acknowledged at least 12 illegitimate children.

He suffered an apoplectic fit on 2 February 1685 and died four days later at Whitehall, aged 54. Suspicion of poison arose at the time; a modern analysis points instead to symptoms resembling uraemia, though the cause remains unproven. His brother succeeded him as James II.
charles-ii-of-spain: Charles was born on 6 November 1661, the only surviving son of Philip IV of Spain and Mariana of Austria, his second wife and niece. The Spanish and Austrian Habsburgs married within the family to an unusual extent, and the causes of Charles's lifelong ill health remain disputed. He survived measles, chickenpox, rubella and smallpox in childhood, and rickets left him unable to walk unaided until he was four. The suggestion that he went uneducated is incorrect: he had tutors from the age of six, and records of his government and reports of foreign diplomats indicate that his mental capacities remained intact.

Philip IV died on 17 September 1665, and Mariana ruled as Queen Regent through a valido, first the Austrian Juan Everardo Nithard. Reform was hampered by her rivalry with Charles's illegitimate half-brother Don Juan, who took control of the government in January 1678 and made peace with France in the Treaties of Nijmegen. In 1679 Charles married Marie Louise of Orléans, a niece of Louis XIV.

The state finances were in perpetual crisis, and the Crown had declared bankruptcy nine times between 1557 and 1666. Castile's population fell from 6.5 million in 1600 to fewer than 5 million in 1680, and in the 1680s drastic deflationary decrees revalued the coinage, disrupting commerce before the currency was stabilised in 1686.

Marie Louise died in February 1689, and Charles married Maria Anna of Neuburg, who also had no children. The autopsy suggested that Charles was incapable of fathering any. The succession then dominated European diplomacy. Treaties in 1698 and 1700 tried to divide the Spanish possessions among claimants, but the Spanish government refused any division. In September 1700 he fell gravely ill, and Luis Manuel Fernández de Portocarrero persuaded him to name Philip of Anjou, Louis XIV's grandson, as heir. Charles died on 1 November 1700, aged 38.

Philip was proclaimed king on 16 November 1700, and the War of the Spanish Succession formally began on 9 July 1701. Charles's reign has traditionally been viewed as one of decline, a foreign ambassador remarking in 1691 that it was incomprehensible how the monarchy survived. More recent studies call the myth of decline and an incapable king simplistic, and argue that Bourbon propaganda shaped the older view. The monarchy remained largely intact at his death, and some of the commercial policies begun in his reign formed the basis for Bourbon reforms. Universities approved by decrees in his name, such as San Carlos in Guatemala, still exist.
charles-iii-of-spain: Charles was born on 20 January 1716, the fourth son of Philip V of Spain and the eldest son of Philip's second wife, Elisabeth Farnese. His mother, who hoped he would have a kingdom of his own, made him heir to the Italian duchies of Parma and Piacenza, and in 1731, at fifteen, he became their duke. At eighteen he led Spanish troops down Italy in an almost bloodless march to take the Kingdom of Naples and the Kingdom of Sicily, entering Naples on 10 May 1734. The Treaty of Vienna of 1738 confirmed him in both kingdoms. In Naples his chief minister, Bernardo Tanucci, pursued a regalist policy that limited the privileges of the clergy, whose lands were exempt from tax.

Charles became King of Spain on the death of his childless half-brother Ferdinand VI on 10 August 1759, and gave up the thrones of Naples and Sicily. He ruled as an enlightened absolutist and relied on capable ministers, among them the Marquess of Esquilache, the Count of Campomanes, the Count of Aranda and the Count of Floridablanca. He widened trade, modernised agriculture and land tenure, promoted science and university research, and strengthened the army and navy.

Spain joined France in the Family Compact of 15 August 1761, and the British captured Havana and Manila in 1762–63, though both were returned in the peace of 1763. To pay for a standing army and fortified ports, the sales tax, the alcabala, was raised from 2% to 5%. Bread riots in 1766, the Esquilache Riots, drove out the minister, and in 1767 Charles expelled the Jesuits from Spain and its empire, confiscating their haciendas and closing their colleges.

The Bourbon Reforms sought to bring the overseas territories under firmer control. The Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, set up in 1776, took Upper Peru and what is now Argentina from the Viceroyalty of Peru, so that the silver of Potosí flowed towards Buenos Aires. In 1780 an indigenous rising led by Túpac Amaru II broke out against colonial rule in the Viceroyalty of Peru.

Charles died on 14 December 1788, months before the French Revolution began. The historian Stanley Payne judged him probably the most successful European ruler of his generation. His reforms mostly raised revenue and extended state power, though he never gained complete control of the finances. His reign has been called the apogee of empire, which was not sustained after him: his son Charles IV continued some of his policies, but was forced to abdicate by his own son Ferdinand VII and was imprisoned by Napoleon Bonaparte, who invaded Spain in 1808.
charles-martel: Charles was a son of the Frankish statesman Pepin of Herstal and a noblewoman named Alpaida, who was his mistress and possibly his second wife. Older writing calls him illegitimate, but the line between wives and concubines was not clear-cut in 8th-century Francia, and the charge probably comes from the wish of Pepin's first wife Plectrude to see her own line as heirs. By his lifetime the Merovingian kings had ceded power to the mayors of the palace, who controlled the treasury and granted land in the name of a figurehead king.

When Pepin died in December 714, Plectrude had designated his young grandson Theudoald as sole heir and imprisoned Charles in Cologne. Charles escaped in 715 and was acclaimed mayor of the palace over Austrasia. In the civil war that followed he suffered his only defeat, near Cologne in 716, against the Neustrians and Radbod, King of the Frisians. He then won at Amblève in April 716 and at Vinchy on 21 March 717, took Cologne, and defeated Chilperic II and Odo, duke of Aquitaine, at Soissons in 718. Between 718 and 732 he campaigned against the Saxons, the Frisians, Bavaria and the Alemanni, and he appointed the Merovingian kings himself.

In 731 he crossed the Loire into Aquitaine. An army under Abd al-Rahman al-Ghafiqi then marched north and was defeated by Charles at the Battle of Tours, between Tours and Poitiers, in 732. The historian Paul Fouracre suggests the Arab campaign was a long-distance raid rather than the start of a war, and Arabic sources of the period give the battle little prominence. Charles did not gain full control of Aquitaine, and Odo remained duke until 735. After the death of King Theuderic IV in 737 he appointed no successor, and the throne stayed vacant until his own death.

Charles died on 22 October 741 at Quierzy-sur-Oise and was buried at Saint Denis. A year earlier he had divided his lands between his sons Carloman and Pepin the Younger. Many historians see him as laying the foundations for Pepin's rise to the Frankish throne in 751 and for Charlemagne's imperial acclamation in 800, although Fouracre notes that his career ended with unfinished business.

His reputation has varied. Early authors praised his victories, while a 9th-century text portrayed him suffering in hell for taking church lands. Edward Gibbon and later writers made him the saviour of Christian Europe at Tours, a view that more recent historians such as Alessandro Barbero call overstated.
charles-maurice-de-talleyrand: Charles-Maurice de Talleyrand-Périgord was born in Paris on 2 February 1754 into an ancient but not wealthy aristocratic family. From childhood he walked with a limp, which later gave him the nickname le diable boiteux, the lame devil. In his Memoirs he blamed an accident at the age of four, but recent research has shown the condition was congenital. It barred him from inheriting his father's title despite being the eldest surviving son, so his parents chose a career in the Church for him.

He studied theology at the Sorbonne, read Montesquieu and Voltaire and other writers who were beginning to question the authority of the ancien régime, was ordained a priest on 19 December 1779, and in 1780 became Agent-General of the Clergy. In 1789, just before the French Revolution, he became Bishop of Autun.

Talleyrand sat in the Estates-General of 1789 for the clergy and supported the revolutionaries' anti-clericalism. With Mirabeau he promoted the appropriation of Church property, helped write the Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen, and proposed the Civil Constitution of the Clergy. Few bishops followed him in obeying the new decree, and much of the clergy came to regard him as schismatic.

He helped bring about the coup of 18 Brumaire in 1799 and was soon made foreign minister by Napoleon, though he rarely agreed with his foreign policy. The Pope released him from excommunication in the Concordat of 1801. He worked for peace, helped complete the Treaty of Amiens in 1802. After resigning as foreign minister in 1807 he kept a seat on the Council of State, and at the Congress of Erfurt in 1808 he secretly counselled Tsar Alexander I against Napoleon's proposals.

In April 1814, as Louis XVIII succeeded Napoleon, Talleyrand was a key agent of the Bourbon Restoration. He signed the Treaty of Paris, whose terms were lenient towards France, and was the chief French negotiator at the Congress of Vienna. There he won admission for France to the inner decisions, and on 3 January 1815 signed a secret defensive treaty with Austria's Metternich and Britain's Castlereagh against Russia and Prussia. He served under Louis XVIII, Charles X and Louis Philippe I.

He died on 17 May 1838. He left no legitimate children. Opinion remains divided: some see one of the most skilled diplomats in European history with a realistic view of the French national interest, others a serial turncoat who betrayed the ancien régime, the Revolution and Napoleon in turn for his own advantage.
charles-the-bald: Charles was born on 13 June 823 in Frankfurt, the youngest son of Louis the Pious by his second wife, Judith. His elder brothers were already adults with sub-kingdoms of their own, and his father's attempts to give him one, first Alemannia and then the country between the Meuse and the Pyrenees, failed in the face of rebellions by Lothair, Pepin I of Aquitaine and Louis the German. At a diet in Aachen in 837 Louis the Pious had the nobles do homage to Charles as heir to all that was once Gaul. When Louis died in 840 war broke out between his sons.

Charles allied with Louis the German against the new Emperor Lothair I, and they defeated Lothair at Fontenoy-en-Puisaye on 25 June 841. In 842 the brothers confirmed their alliance by the Oaths of Strasbourg, and the war ended with the Treaty of Verdun in August 843, which gave Charles the western kingdom, roughly modern France as far as the Meuse, the Saône and the Rhône, with the Spanish March as far as the Ebro. His reign was troubled. The Bretons under Nomenoë and Erispoë defeated him at Ballon in 845 and Jengland in 851 and gained de facto independence.

Vikings devastated the Seine and Loire valleys, and after they sacked Paris in 845 Charles had to buy their retreat at a heavy price. By the Edict of Pistres of 864 he gave the army a cavalry element and ordered fortified bridges built across rivers; two of them saved Paris during the siege of 885 to 886. After the death of his nephew Lothair II in 869 he had himself consecrated king of Lotharingia at Metz, but under pressure from Louis he agreed in 870 to partition it.

After the death of Emperor Louis II, Charles travelled south with the support of Pope John VIII, was crowned king at Pavia, and received the imperial insignia in Rome on 25 December 875. He was beaten by Louis the German's forces at Andernach on 8 October 876, and a second expedition at the pope's call found little support among the nobles. Ill, he turned back and died at Brides-les-Bains on 6 October 877.

His son Louis succeeded him. His nickname may have been ironic, for contemporary images show him with a full head of hair; one suggestion links it to his early lack of a kingdom. His seal as emperor bore the words renovatio imperii Romani et Francorum, renewal of the empire of the Romans and Franks.
charles-the-bold: Charles Martin was born on 10 November 1433 in Dijon, the only child of Philip the Good and his third wife, Isabella of Portugal, to survive infancy. His father made him a knight of the Golden Fleece and count of Charolais. From 1454 to 1464 Philip excluded him from power. In his youth Charles was known for his chivalric ambitions and his admiration for Alexander the Great. He developed an intense rivalry with Louis XI of France, who became king on 22 July 1461, and in 1465 formed the League of the Public Weal, a coalition of French feudal lords, and led them in a war against the king.

Philip the Good died on 15 June 1467, and Charles formally became duke fourteen days later. His joyous entry into Ghent provoked unrest, and the following January he forced the mayors to ask his pardon and abolished the city's governmental rights. He inherited a vast but fragmented collection of territories from the Low Countries to the borders of Switzerland and wanted to turn them into an independent kingdom.

At Trier in October 1473 he met the Holy Roman Emperor Frederick III, hoping to be recognised as king of the Romans and to betroth his daughter Mary to the emperor's son Maximilian. He married Margaret of York to secure an English alliance. A patron of illuminated manuscripts, he kept a court noted for its chivalric culture and etiquette. Between 1468 and 1473 he issued military ordinances, creating in 1471 a standing army of 1,250 lances fournies with archers, handgunners and pikemen.

Charles fought the Burgundian Wars against an alliance of Swiss, German and Alsatian powers. His siege of Neuss lasted from July 1474 to June 1475 and cost him heavily. In 1476 he was defeated by the Swiss at Grandson and at Morat. When René II of Lorraine retook Nancy on 6 October 1476, Charles besieged it through the winter. On 5 January 1477, in the Battle of Nancy, the Count of Campobasso's Italian mercenaries having deserted to René, Charles was killed. His body was found two days later on the frozen river, and René had him buried in the Saint-George collegiate church. In Artois some refused to believe he was dead.

Three weeks later Louis XI invaded Burgundian territory, Ghent rebelled, and Liège and Guelders sought independence. His death led to the collapse of the Burgundian State, since he had no legitimate male heir, and he was succeeded by his only child, Mary. His German enemies called him the Grand Turk of the West.
charles-the-fat: Charles was the youngest of the three sons of Louis the German, first King of East Francia, and Hemma, of the House of Welf, and a great-grandson of Charlemagne. The nickname Carolus Crassus is not contemporary: it first appears with the Saxon Annalist in the twelfth century, and no contemporary source mentions his size. He was made Count of the Breisgau in 859 and, when Louis the German's lands were divided in 865, received Alemannia. After Louis died in 876, Charles ruled there. In 879 his brother Carloman, incapacitated by a stroke, divided his domains, and Italy passed to Charles, who spent most of his time there until 886.

Pope John VIII, begging his help against Guy II of Spoleto, crowned Charles emperor on 12 February 881. Charles did little against Guy, though hopes of a revival had been raised. His brother Louis the Younger died on 20 January 882, leaving him the whole of East Francia, and on the death of Carloman II on 12 December 884 the nobles of West Francia invited him to rule there too, reuniting the Carolingian Empire. He built a palace at Sélestat in Alsace on the model of Charlemagne's at Aachen. His rule in the west was distant, and he left daily business to the higher nobility.

Against the Vikings he preferred negotiation. In 882 he besieged their camp at Asselt, then made terms: Godfrid accepted Christianity and became his vassal, and Sigfred was bribed off. In 885 Charles had Godfrid executed at a conference at Spijk. When a large fleet under Sigfred besieged Paris in 885 and 886, Charles brought a large army but did not fight; he sent the attackers up the Seine to ravage rebellious Burgundy and paid the 700 pounds of silver promised, and his prestige in France was greatly diminished.

Charles had no legitimate children and failed to have his illegitimate son Bernard recognised as heir, against opposition from several bishops; he then adopted Louis of Provence. In November 887 his nephew Arnulf of Carinthia led a rising of Bavarians and Slavs, and Charles's support in East Francia collapsed within a week. By 17 November he was out of power. He was given estates at Naudingen (Donaueschingen) and died there, of natural causes, on 13 January 888, and was buried at Reichenau.

The empire then split into separate kingdoms: Arnulf took East Francia, the French elected Odo, Berengar was acclaimed in Italy, and Louis was crowned in Provence. Contemporary opinion of Charles was kinder than later accounts, and the Annales Fuldenses praise his piety. A modern suggestion is that his poor record owed much to constant illness; he is believed to have had epilepsy.
charles-the-simple: Charles was born on 17 September 879, the third and posthumous son of King Louis the Stammerer and his second wife, Adelaide of Paris. He was a child of five when his half-brother, King Carloman II, died on 6 December 884, and the Frankish nobles asked their cousin, Emperor Charles the Fat, to take the crown instead. After Charles the Fat was deposed in 887, the nobility again passed over the young prince and elected Odo, Count of Paris, the hero of the siege of Paris of 885 to 886, as king. Charles was put under the protection of Ranulf II, Duke of Aquitaine.

In 893, aged 14, Charles was crowned at Reims Cathedral by a faction opposed to Odo, aided by Archbishop Fulk of Reims. By 897 he ruled only the city of Laon. He became king of West Francia in 898, when Odo on his deathbed designated him as his successor. He soon showed ambition to conquer Lotharingia, the cradle of the Carolingian dynasty, and invaded in 898 at the call of Count Reginar of Hainaut.

In 911 a band of Vikings led by Rollo besieged Paris and Chartres. After a victory near Chartres on 26 August, Charles negotiated with Rollo, and the Treaty of Saint-Clair-sur-Epte created the Duchy of Normandy. The Vikings received the land between the river Epte and the sea, and Rollo agreed to be baptised and to marry Charles's daughter Gisela. Also in 911, Louis the Child, the last Carolingian king of East Francia, died, and the Lotharingian nobles under Reginar declared Charles their king, in preference to Conrad I, whom East Francia had elected. Charles defended Lotharingia against two attacks by Conrad.

Charles's favouritism towards Hagano, a petty nobleman and a relative of his first wife Frederuna, turned the aristocracy against him. He gave Hagano monasteries that were already the benefices of other barons. The nobles seized him in 920, and Archbishop Herveus of Reims negotiated his release. In 922 the nobles revolted again under Robert of Neustria, Odo's brother, who was crowned king, and Charles fled to Lotharingia. Returning in 923 with a Norman army, he was defeated by Robert's forces at the Battle of Soissons on 15 June, and Rudolph of Burgundy, Robert's son-in-law, was elected king. Charles was captured by Herbert II of Vermandois and imprisoned, finally at Péronne.

He died in prison on 7 October 929 and was buried in the monastery of Saint-Fursy. His son Louis by his second wife Eadgifu of Wessex was crowned in 936 as Louis IV of France, with the support of Hugh the Great.
charles-university: Holy Roman Emperor Charles IV asked his friend and ally Pope Clement VI to create a university in Prague. The papal bull, modelled on the University of Paris, established all four faculties, including theology, and Charles, as king of Bohemia and later as king of the Romans, confirmed its privileges and immunities from secular power by Golden Bull. Archbishop Arnošt of Pardubice took part in the foundation and became chancellor. The first graduate was promoted in 1359, and lectures were held in colleges, the oldest of them the Carolinum of 1366.

In 1402 Jerome of Prague copied works of John Wycliffe at Oxford, and Jan Hus, dean of the philosophical faculty, translated the Trialogus into Czech. The university forbade its members to follow Wycliffe in 1403, but his doctrine spread. In the Western Schism the Bohemian nation backed King Wenceslaus and the Council of Pisa, while the other three nations supported Pope Gregory XII. By the Decree of Kutná Hora on 18 January 1409 the king gave the Bohemian masters three votes and left one for all the other nations together. Foreign, mostly German, professors and students left and founded the University of Leipzig in May 1409. Hus became rector of the Czech-dominated university that autumn, and it became a bastion of the Hussite movement.

The faculties of theology and law disappeared by 1419, and the faculty of arts became the chief doctrinal authority of the Utraquists. In 1654 Ferdinand III merged the Carolinum and Clementinum as the Charles-Ferdinand University.

German replaced Latin as the language of instruction on 29 July 1784, and Protestants and then Jews were admitted. After disputes between Czechs and Germans, an act sanctioned by Emperor Franz Joseph on 28 February 1882 divided it into a German and a Czech university of equal status.

In 1920 a law made the Czech university the successor of the original and named it Charles University. In 1939, after German occupation, Czech universities were closed on 17 November after the funeral demonstration for the student Jan Opletal; nine student leaders were executed and about 1,200 students were interned in Sachsenhausen. The German university was dissolved at the end of the war. After the communist coup of 1948 the university suffered purges for four decades, and students and faculty played a large part in the Velvet Revolution of 1989. Today it is the largest university in the Czech Republic, with 17 faculties.
charles-vi-holy-roman-emperor: Archduke Charles was born on 1 October 1685, the second son of Emperor Leopold I and his third wife, Eleonore Magdalene of Neuburg. After the death of Charles II of Spain in 1700 without a direct heir, he declared himself King of Spain, and the War of the Spanish Succession lasted almost 14 years against Louis XIV's grandson Philip, Duke of Anjou. Portugal, England, Scotland, Ireland and most of the Holy Roman Empire backed Charles, and in Spain his supporters were concentrated in the Crown of Aragon.
He landed in Spain in 1705 and held power only in Catalonia until the death of his brother Joseph I called him to Vienna. In 1708 he married Elisabeth Christine of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel.

Britain, unwilling to see Austria and Spain united again, withdrew its support, and the Treaties of Utrecht, Rastatt and Baden recognised Philip as king of Spain while ceding Naples, Milan, the Austrian Netherlands and Sardinia to Austria. In the Austro-Turkish War of 1716 to 1718 he added the Banat to Hungary and established direct Austrian rule over Serbia and Oltenia. The War of the Polish Succession ended in 1738 with Charles giving Naples and Sicily to Don Carlos in exchange for Parma and Tuscany. His last Turkish war, begun in 1737 with Russia, ended with the Treaty of Belgrade in 1739, in which he gave up central Serbia and Oltenia.

Charles was a devout Catholic who supported the restoration of Catholic church structures in lands freed from Ottoman rule, and he confirmed older privileges of his Orthodox subjects. Having no surviving son, he issued the Pragmatic Sanction of 19 April 1713, abolishing male-only succession and declaring Habsburg lands indivisible, although the Diet of Hungary approved it only in 1723. He spent the rest of his reign seeking recognition from other powers, and agreed to close the Ostend Company, which he had founded in 1722, to win Britain's assent.

Charles fell ill after a hunting trip in October 1740 and died on 20 October in the Hofburg; Voltaire wrote that he died after eating death cap mushrooms. His daughter Maria Theresa had to defend her inheritance in the War of the Austrian Succession against a coalition of states, among them Prussia, Bavaria and France, that had all been parties to the sanction. She kept her crown and most of her lands but lost Silesia to Prussia and Parma to Spain. At his death the Habsburg lands were deeply in debt, the exchequer held only 100,000 florins, and the Habsburg male line was extinct.
charles-vi-of-france: Charles VI was born in Paris, in the Hôtel Saint-Pol, on 3 December 1368, the son of Charles V and Joanna of Bourbon. His father died on 16 September 1380, leaving a favourable military situation, and Charles was crowned at Reims on 4 November, aged eleven. His uncles ruled as regents: Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, Louis I, Duke of Anjou, John, Duke of Berry, and Louis II, Duke of Bourbon. Philip took the dominant role.

During the regency the treasury built up by Charles V was squandered for the dukes' profit, and the reimposition of unpopular taxes led to revolts known as the Harelle. In 1388 Charles stripped his uncles of their positions and restored his father's advisers, the Marmousets.

In 1392, leading an expedition against the Duchy of Brittany, Charles suffered his first attack of delirium in the forest near Le Mans, and killed several of his own men. From then until his death he alternated between mental instability and lucidity. The cause of his illness is unknown; theories include schizophrenia, manic-depressive psychosis, porphyria and typhus-induced encephalopathy. He believed at times that he was made of glass, and in one episode he claimed to be Saint George.
On 29 January 1393 the Bal des Ardents, a masked ball in which his costume was set alight by a torch, left four dancers dead. In September 1394 he ordered that no Jew should dwell in his domains.

Queen Isabeau and the grandees governed in his name. The enmity between his brother Louis I, Duke of Orléans, and Philip's son John the Fearless led to the murder of Orléans in 1407 and to the Armagnac–Burgundian Civil War, which lasted until 1435. John the Fearless was himself killed on 10 September 1419 at Montereau, in a meeting with the Dauphin, and his son Philip the Good then sided with the English.

Henry V of England invaded and defeated the French army at Agincourt on 25 October 1415. By the Treaty of Troyes of 21 May 1420 Henry was named Charles's successor, the Dauphin was disinherited, and Charles's daughter Catherine of Valois was betrothed to Henry. Charles died on 21 October 1422 at the Hôtel Saint-Pol and was buried at Saint-Denis. Henry V had died a few weeks earlier, so the infant Henry VI of England became king of France under the treaty. The disinherited Dauphin, with Joan of Arc's help, was crowned Charles VII at Reims on 17 July 1429, and the war ended in 1453 with a Valois victory.
charles-vii-holy-roman-emperor: Charles Albert was born in Brussels on 6 August 1697, the eldest son of Maximilian II Emanuel, Elector of Bavaria, and Theresa Kunegunda Sobieska, a daughter of King John III Sobieski of Poland. The family was divided by the War of the Spanish Succession. His father was defeated at Blenheim in 1704 and put under an imperial ban, his mother was forced into exile for ten years, and Charles spent many years under house arrest in Austria. The family was reconciled only in 1715. On 5 October 1722 he married Archduchess Maria Amalia, the youngest daughter of Emperor Joseph I.

Charles became elector on 26 February 1726 after his father's death. When Charles VI died, he rejected the Pragmatic Sanction of 1713 and claimed the Habsburg German lands against Maria Theresa. By the Treaty of Nymphenburg in July 1741 he allied with France and Spain. His French allies took Prague in November 1741, and he was crowned king of Bohemia on 19 December. He was elected king of Germany on 24 January 1742 and crowned emperor on 12 February 1742.

Soon after, the Austrians overran most of his lands and occupied Bavaria, and he lived for almost three years in Frankfurt. Most of Bohemia was lost in December 1742. He was mocked as an emperor who controlled neither his realm nor the empire, and a Latin saying called him et Caesar et nihil, both emperor and nothing. In October 1744 he regained Munich for good.

Suffering badly from gout, Charles died at Nymphenburg Palace on 20 January 1745 and was buried in the crypt of the Theatinerkirche in Munich. His son Maximilian III Joseph made peace with Austria, and in the Treaty of Füssen Austria recognised the legitimacy of his father's election. His reign was the height of the Bavarian rococo: Nymphenburg Palace was completed, and the architect François de Cuvilliés built the Amalienburg hunting lodge.
charles-vii-of-france: Charles was born at the Hôtel Saint-Pol in Paris on 22 February 1403, the eleventh child and fifth son of Charles VI of France and Isabeau of Bavaria. His four elder brothers each held the title of Dauphin and all died childless. After the Burgundians seized Paris in 1418 the fifteen-year-old Charles became the Armagnac leader and set up his court at Bourges. His men killed John the Fearless, Duke of Burgundy, on the bridge at Montereau during a meeting meant to reconcile them; how far Charles was involved has remained uncertain. Under the Treaty of Troyes of 1420 Charles VI recognised Henry V of England as his heir.

In October 1422 northern France, including Paris, was ruled for the infant Henry VI of England by the Duke of Bedford. Charles, mockingly called the King of Bourges, kept an itinerant court in the Loire Valley. Joan of Arc reached him at Chinon on 23 February 1429, the siege of Orléans was lifted on 8 May, the French won at Patay on 18 June, and Charles was crowned at Reims on 17 July 1429. Joan was captured by Burgundian troops in 1430 and burnt at the stake on 30 May 1431; Charles took no action to save her.

By the Treaty of Arras of 5 August 1435 Philip the Good of Burgundy abandoned the English alliance. Charles entered Paris on 13 April 1436. He took royal control of church appointments through the Pragmatic Sanction of Bourges in 1438 and, between 1445 and 1448, formed a cavalry force 12,000 strong, followed by conscripted infantry archers. After a truce at Tours in 1444 he resumed the war in 1449. The French won at Formigny on 15 April 1450 and Castillon on 17 July 1453, leaving only Calais in English hands.

Charles's last years were spoiled by conflict with his heir, the future Louis XI, whom he banished to the Dauphiné in 1446 and who fled to Philip the Good in 1456. Ill from 1458, Charles became convinced that traitors surrounded him, and died at Mehun-sur-Yèvre on 22 July 1461. His reputation has long been overshadowed by Joan of Arc, but he achieved what four generations of his predecessors had not, the expulsion of the English apart from Calais. He also founded the University of Poitiers in 1432.
charles-viii-of-france: Charles was born on 30 June 1470 at the Château d'Amboise, the only surviving son of Louis XI and Charlotte of Savoy. He succeeded on 30 August 1483 at the age of 13. His health was poor, and contemporaries thought him pleasant but unsuited to the business of state. As Louis XI wished, the regency went to his elder sister Anne, whom her father called the least foolish woman in France, and her husband Peter of Bourbon, until 1491. In the Mad War of 1485 to 1488 the great lords rebelled against royal centralisation, and the royal government won.

Charles had been betrothed in 1483 to the three-year-old Margaret of Austria, daughter of Maximilian of Austria. When Francis II, Duke of Brittany, died in 1488, his daughter Anne, aged 11, inherited the duchy and in 1490 married Maximilian by proxy. The regents refused a Habsburg on a second French border, and the French army invaded Brittany while Maximilian was preoccupied with Hungary. Anne of Brittany was forced to renounce Maximilian and marry Charles at Langeais in December 1491. Margaret went home in 1493 with her dowry, though Burgundy was retained under the Treaty of Senlis.

Charles bought the neutrality of England, Aragon and Maximilian by the treaties of Étaples, Barcelona and Senlis in 1492 and 1493, and built a large army with one of Europe's first siege trains. He invaded Italy in September 1494 with 25,000 men, 8,000 of them Swiss mercenaries, took Naples without a pitched battle on 22 February 1495 and was crowned King of Naples on 20 May. The Italian rulers, Spain and the Empire formed the League of Venice on 31 March 1495, but could not stop him at Fornovo in July from marching home, and Aragonese forces soon subdued his garrisons in Naples.

Charles died at Amboise in 1498. By the usual account he struck his head on a door lintel on the way to a game of real tennis and died nine hours later; a study of 2021 held that such a blow would cause only minor injury. All his children died before him, so he was the last of the elder branch of the House of Valois, and Louis XII succeeded him. He left France in debt, but his expedition strengthened cultural ties with Italy and energised French art and literature.
charles-x-gustav: Charles Gustav was born on 8 November 1622, the son of John Casimir, Count Palatine of Zweibrücken-Kleeburg, and Catherine of Sweden, a daughter of King Charles IX. His parents fled the Thirty Years' War and never returned to Germany, and he was raised at the Swedish court alongside his cousin Queen Christina. He learned war under Lennart Torstenson and was present at the second Battle of Breitenfeld in 1642. Christina, who refused to marry him, declared him her successor in 1649 despite the opposition of the Privy Council under Axel Oxenstierna. He became king when she abdicated in June 1654.

In 1654 Charles married Hedwig Eleonora of Holstein-Gottorp, hoping for an ally against Denmark. In 1655 he led Sweden into the Second Northern War, invading Poland-Lithuania with 50,000 men. His forces took Warsaw and Kraków, but the defence of the fortress-monastery of Częstochowa and a national rising turned opinion against him. He gained the elector of Brandenburg, Frederick William I, as an ally by the treaties of Königsberg, Marienburg and Labiau, the last of which gave Frederick William sovereignty in East Prussia.

When Denmark-Norway declared war on 1 June 1657, he attacked from the south and overran Jutland. In the winter of 1658 the Little Belt froze, and on 30 January he led his army across the ice to Funen. On the advice of his engineer Erik Dahlberg he then crossed by way of Langeland, Lolland and Falster and reached Zealand on 11 February. Denmark-Norway accepted the Treaty of Taastrup and then the Treaty of Roskilde of 26 February 1658, giving up a great part of its territory. Charles renewed the war in July and besieged Copenhagen, but a Dutch fleet defeated the Swedish fleet in the Battle of the Sound on 29 October 1658.
At the Riksdag of 1655 he began a land reduction to recover estates that Christina had granted to the nobility. It only partly eased the state's finances, and his son used the same decrees later.

In December 1659 Charles summoned the estates to Gothenburg for fresh subsidies. Soon after they opened on 4 January 1660 he fell ill, and his physician mistook his pneumonia for scurvy and treated it with bloodletting and laxatives. On 12 February he signed his testament, naming a regency of six relatives and friends for his minor son, Charles XI, and he died the next day aged 37.
charles-xi-of-sweden: Charles was born in November 1655, the only son of Charles X Gustav and Hedwig Eleonora of Holstein-Gottorp. His father died in February 1660, and a regency led by his mother governed until Charles came of age on 18 December 1672. As an adolescent he devoted himself to sport and bear-hunting and was considered poorly educated. His difficulties are now seen as signs of dyslexia, which was poorly understood then.

Sweden joined the French war against the Dutch in 1674, and after the Swedish defeat at Fehrbellin Denmark declared war in September 1675, beginning the Scanian War. Charles took command in Scania. He won the Battle of Halmstad on 17 August 1676 and fought the Battle of Lund on 4 December, one of the bloodiest battles of its time, in which about 8,000 of over 20,000 combatants died. Louis XIV dictated peace in 1679, which left the Swedish empire practically intact.

The remaining twenty years of his reign were the longest peacetime of the Swedish Empire. At the Riksdag of October 1680 he pushed through the reduction, which recovered crown lands and lordships that had been lent or given away. It ruined some nobles and readjusted the nation's finances. The Estates also told him that he was bound by no one but himself, which formally established absolute monarchy. In 1682 he proposed the army reform in which two farms supported one soldier, and in 1680 he founded the naval base at Karlskrona.

Charles married Ulrika Eleonora of Denmark on 6 May 1680. She died in July 1693, and he never fully recovered. He complained of stomach pains from 1694 and died on 5 April 1697, aged 41, of cancer that had spread through his abdomen. Opinion of him has varied, and a 2003 biography by Rystad describes a strong-willed shaper of Sweden through economic reforms and military strength. His son Charles XII used the well-trained army he left in battles throughout Europe.
charles-xiii-of-sweden: Charles was born on 7 October 1748, the second son of King Adolf Frederick of Sweden and Louisa Ulrika of Prussia, a sister of Frederick the Great, and the younger brother of the future Gustav III. He was appointed grand admiral when only a few days old. As heir after his brother he was early seen by the Caps party as a tool against Gustav, but Gustav took care to keep him from being used, and in the December Crisis of 1768 Charles did not let himself be used by the Caps.

In the Revolution of 1772 Charles helped his brother by neutralising the Caps through his connections there and securing the southern provinces with the army, and Gustav III rewarded him with the title Duke of Södermanland. In 1774 he married his cousin Hedvig Elisabeth Charlotte of Holstein-Gottorp, then 15. Their two children, born in 1797 and 1798, did not survive infancy. He took part in secret societies and Freemasonry, was interested in mysticism, and in 1811 founded the Order of Charles XIII, which was limited to 33 knights who had to be Freemasons.

In 1788 he served with distinction as admiral of the fleet in the Russo-Swedish War, notably at the battles of Hogland and Öland. When Gustav III was assassinated in 1792, Charles acted as regent for his nephew Gustav IV Adolf until 1796, after successfully contesting a will that would have restricted his powers. He left government to his favourite, Gustaf Adolf Reuterholm, and the years have been called an Age of Lead in Swedish history. In 1794 the discovery of the Armfelt Conspiracy exposed the opposition of the Gustavian party.

He is presumed to have been aware of the plans to depose Gustav IV Adolf in 1809, and he kept passive during the coup. On 13 March 1809 the victorious party appointed him regent, and the Riksdag of the Estates then elected him king. He was 60 and in poor health, and he suffered a heart attack in November 1809. The new constitution, together with his indecision, also limited his role.

A search for an heir followed. The Danish prince Christian August was adopted as Charles August but died within months of arriving in Sweden. The marshal Jean-Baptiste Bernadotte was then chosen, and on landing in 1810 he took over the government. After a stroke in 1812 Charles lost his memory and the ability to communicate, and he sat as a silent witness in councils chaired by the crown prince. By the union of Sweden and Norway on 4 November 1814 he became king of Norway, as Charles II. He died childless on 5 February 1818, and Bernadotte succeeded him as Charles XIV John.
charleston-south-carolina: Charleston lies just south of the midpoint of South Carolina's coastline on Charleston Harbor, an inlet of the Atlantic formed where the Ashley, Cooper and Wando rivers meet. Before colonial settlement the area was inhabited by the Cusabo people, including sub-tribes such as the Kiawah, and by the Ittiwan, whom the colonists called Settlement Indians. The old downtown stands on a peninsula between the Ashley and the Cooper.

Charles II granted the Province of Carolina to eight Lords Proprietors on 24 March 1663. In 1670 Governor William Sayle arranged for shiploads of settlers from Bermuda and Barbados, who founded Charles Town at Albemarle Point on the west bank of the Ashley River. It was the first comprehensively planned town in the Thirteen Colonies, laid out under a scheme called the Grand Model that John Locke prepared for the Proprietors. Because the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina were never ratified, the town was never incorporated in the colonial period. In 1680 the settlement moved to its present site, and by the 1690s it was the fifth-largest city in North America.
