Charleston was central to the Atlantic slave trade. Local merchants, among them Joseph Wragg, helped break the monopoly of the Royal African Company, and almost half of the enslaved people imported into what became the United States arrived there. The state legislature incorporated the city as Charleston on 13 August 1783. The capital moved to Columbia in 1788, yet Charleston stayed among the ten largest American cities until 1840. Cotton brought great wealth to a small part of society and funded fine architecture, but it also raised the economic importance of slavery and brought ever tighter restrictions on Black Charlestonians.

The Civil War began in Charleston Harbor in 1861, and it ended months after United States soldiers retook the city in 1865. Reconstruction followed: the African American population rose from 17,000 in 1860 to over 27,000 in 1880. Free people of color, 3,785 at the war's outset, became leaders of South Carolina's Republican Party. In the 20th century the city languished economically, helped by a large federal military presence, and tourism grew after the 1920s.

Charleston is the most populous city in South Carolina, with 150,227 people at the 2020 census, and is the seat of Charleston County. Its economy rests on tourism, the port, aerospace and information technology. It is known for preserved architecture, including the Battery and Rainbow Row, for Fort Sumter National Monument, and for Gullah heritage, and it hosts the Spoleto Festival USA, founded in 1977 by Gian Carlo Menotti.
charlotte-of-mecklenburg-strelitz: Charlotte was born on 19 May 1744, the youngest daughter of Duke Charles Louis Frederick of Mecklenburg, Prince of Mirow. Mecklenburg-Strelitz was a small north-German duchy in the Holy Roman Empire. She was taught literature, botany, natural history, French, Italian and Latin, and played the harpsichord, though diplomatic reports at the time of her engagement called her education very mediocre.

George III, unmarried when he succeeded in 1760, needed a wife, and the Hanoverian minister in London suggested Charlotte. At 17 she appealed partly because a girl raised in an insignificant duchy would probably have no interest in party politics, and George told her soon after the wedding not to meddle. They married on 8 September 1761. They had 15 children, the first of them the future George IV, born on 12 August 1762, and all but two survived to adulthood. She had a strained relationship with her mother-in-law, Augusta, and turned to German companions.

She was a music lover and an amateur botanist who enlarged the collections at Kew Gardens, and the bird of paradise flower was named Strelitzia reginae for her. The eight-year-old Mozart played before her in 1764. George III fell ill from October 1788 until March 1789, which distressed her greatly, and after his illness became permanent in 1811 she was made his guardian while her son governed as Prince Regent.

Charlotte died on 17 November 1818 at Kew Palace and was buried at St George's Chapel, Windsor Castle. She had been queen consort for 57 years and 70 days, the longest of any British queen consort. Places named for her include Charlotte in North Carolina, Charlottesville in Virginia, Charlottetown and the Queen Charlotte Islands, now Haida Gwaii. Her funding kept the General Lying-in Hospital in London open, and it is now Queen Charlotte's and Chelsea Hospital.
chavundaraya: In his own writing Chavundaraya claims descent from the Brahmakshatriya line, Brahmins who had taken Kshatriya status. The 10th-century Algodu and Arani inscriptions name him as the grandson of Govindamayya and the son of Mabalayya, a subordinate of King Marasimha II; the family's political position under that king is believed to have led to its gradual adoption of Kshatriya status. He was a devotee of the Jain teachers Nemichandra and Ajitasena Bhattaraka, and a eulogy of him is inscribed on the Tyagada Brahmadeva Pillar at Shravanabelagola, whose base shows him with his guru Nemichandra.

The Western Gangas were feudatories of the Rashtrakutas, and as their commander Chavundaraya fought many battles for those overlords, beginning in the days of the Rashtrakuta king Khottiga Amoghavarsha. In the last years of Rashtrakuta rule the Gangas were threatened by civil war and by invasions of the Chola dynasty. When civil war broke out in 975 he supported Prince Rachamalla IV and installed him on the throne.

In the same year he suppressed a rebellion by Panchaldeva Mahasamanta, and in the battle of Bageyur he killed Mudurachayya, avenging the death of his own brother Nagavarma. His exploits earned him titles such as Samara Parashurama and Vira Martanda. He remained influential into the reign of Rachamalla V, who ruled from 986 to 999.

The Chavundaraya Purana, also known as the Trishashtishalaka Mahapurana, is the second oldest existing prose work in Kannada. It is based on two Sanskrit works, the Adipurana of Jinasena and the Uttarapurana of Gunabhadra, and tells the legends of sixty-three figures of Jain tradition: twenty-four tirthankaras, twelve chakravartis, nine balabhadras, nine narayanas and nine pratinarayanas. It was meant mainly for ordinary readers and avoided the complicated elements of Jain doctrine. He also wrote the Charitrasara in Sanskrit, and he patronised the Kannada grammarians Gunavarma and Nagavarma I and the poet Ranna.

The statue of Bahubali that he commissioned stands on the Indragiri hill, also called Vindhyagiri. Carved from fine-grained white granite, it is 60 feet tall, with a face measuring 6.5 feet, and has no support up to the thighs. The Chavundaraya basadi on the Chandragiri hill is credited to him by some scholars and to his son Jinadevana by others; another view holds that it was consecrated in the 11th century in his memory.
che-guevara: Ernesto Guevara was born on 14 May 1928 in Rosario, Argentina, the eldest of five children of Ernesto Guevara Lynch and Celia de la Serna y Llosa, in an upper-class family of Spanish, Basque and Irish ancestry. The family had leftist leanings. As a medical student Guevara travelled through South America and was appalled by the poverty, hunger and disease he saw.

After completing his medical degree he set out on 7 July 1953 through Bolivia, Peru, Ecuador, Panama, Costa Rica, Nicaragua, Honduras and El Salvador. In December he arrived in Guatemala, where President Jacobo Árbenz headed a democratically elected government attempting to end the latifundia system. Árbenz's overthrow, assisted by the CIA at the behest of the United Fruit Company, solidified Guevara's political ideology.

In Mexico City Guevara met Raúl and Fidel Castro and joined the 26th of July Movement. They sailed for Cuba aboard the Granma on 25 November 1956. Batista's military attacked soon after landing, and many of the 82 men were killed or executed on capture; only 22 found each other afterwards. Guevara, who had put down his medical supplies to pick up a box of ammunition, rose to second-in-command in the two-year guerrilla campaign that deposed Fulgencio Batista.

After the revolution he reviewed appeals and death sentences of those convicted as war criminals in the revolutionary tribunals, a procedure the Cuban Ministry of Justice said most of the population supported and likened to the Nuremberg trials. He instituted agrarian land reform as minister of industries, served as president of the National Bank and travelled as a diplomat. Critics point to half-completed or empty factories left from his short tenure as minister of industries, and to the internment of people labelled anti-social in labour camps between 1965 and 1968 under the ideal of the socialist new man.

In late 1966 he went to Bolivia. He arrived in La Paz on 3 November under the false name Adolfo Mena González. His first base camp was in the remote Ñancahuazú region, where training proved hazardous and little was accomplished in building an army.

Guevara was killed in Bolivia on 9 October 1967. According to the account of his last minutes, he told the soldier guarding him that he was thinking about the immortality of the revolution, and Sergeant Terán shot him. He remains a revered and reviled figure. Admirers see a martyr and an icon of leftist movements; critics accuse him of promoting authoritarianism and endorsing violence against opponents. A photograph of him by Alberto Korda, Guerrillero Heroico, was cited by the Maryland Institute College of Art as the most widely known in the world.
chechnya: Chechnya lies in the eastern part of the North Caucasus. It borders Dagestan to the east, Ingushetia and North Ossetia-Alania to the west, Stavropol Krai to the northwest and Georgia to the south. It is divided between flatter country north of the Terek river and highlands to the south, and the Terek, Sunzha and Argun are its main rivers. Traces of human settlement dating back to 40,000 BCE have been found near Lake Kezenoyam, and cave paintings and artefacts indicate continuous habitation for some 8,000 years. Georgian tradition, in the chronicle of Leonti Mroveli, names a forefather of the Vainakhs, the ancestors of the Chechens and Ingush, as Kavkas, from whom the word Caucasus was said to derive.

In the 14th and 15th centuries the Chechens fought repeatedly with Tamerlane and Tokhtamysh. In the mid-14th century a Chechen princedom called Simsim arose under Khour II, who defeated the warlord Mamai at the Battle of Tatar-tup in 1362. Khour II later allied himself with Tokhtamysh, and Timur invaded Simsim in 1395 to punish the highlanders. Chechen tribes built fortresses, castles and defensive walls in the mountains. Peter the Great sought to extend Russian influence in the Caucasus in the Russo-Persian War of 1722–1723.

Under the Soviet Union Chechnya and Ingushetia were joined as the Checheno-Ingush Autonomous Soviet Socialist Republic. In 1944, near the end of the Second World War, the Chechens and Ingush were accused of supporting Nazi Germany, an accusation described as false, and whole nations were deported to the Kazakh SSR in Operation Lentil; over 60 percent of the Chechen and Ingush populations are said to have died.

After the dissolution of the Soviet Union the republic split into Ingushetia and the Chechen Republic, which proclaimed itself the independent Chechen Republic of Ichkeria. In the First Chechen War of 1994–1996 Russian forces failed to establish permanent control of the mountains. Its president, Dzhokhar Dudayev, was killed in April 1996, and after Aslan Maskhadov's forces retook Grozny, Boris Yeltsin declared a ceasefire and signed a peace treaty a year later. Federal control was restored in the Second Chechen War of 1999–2009. A constitution that kept Chechnya within Russia with limited autonomy was put to a referendum on 23 March 2003.

Chechnya is a republic of the Russian Federation with its capital at Grozny, and about 1.5 million inhabitants, nearly all of them Chechens. The languages in use are Chechen, which belongs to the Vainakh branch of the Caucasian languages together with Ingush, and Russian. Most of the people are Sunni Muslims who follow the Shafi'i or Hanafi schools of jurisprudence, and many belong to the Qadiri or Naqshbandi Sufi orders.
chennai: Chennai lies on the Eastern Coastal Plains, a flat stretch of clay soil on the Bay of Bengal, at an average elevation of 6.7 m. It receives most of its rain from the northeast monsoon, and cyclones are common in that season. The name derives from Chennappa Nayaka, a Nayak ruler who served as a general under Venkata Raya of the Vijayanagara Empire and from whom the East India Company took the town on lease in 1639. The first official use of the name was in August 1639, in a sale deed to Francis Day of the Company.

Stone Age implements have been found near Pallavaram. In the 2nd century CE the region was part of Tondaimandalam, ruled by the Early Cholas, and the Pallavas of Kanchi ruled it independently from the 3rd to the 9th century. The Later Cholas under Aditya I defeated the Pallavas in 879, Jatavarman Sundara Pandyan brought the region under Pandya rule in 1264, and the Vijayanagara Empire held influence over it in the 15th century.

In 1639 the East India Company obtained a grant of coastal land containing the fishing village of Madrasapattinam and built Fort St George, the first British fortress in India. The Corporation of Madras was established on 29 September 1688. In the 18th century the British and the French fought for control of the city, and by the late 18th century the British had conquered most of the region and made Madras the capital of the Madras Presidency. The idea of the Indian National Congress was conceived there after a Theosophical convention in December 1884. After 1947 Madras became capital of Madras State, the predecessor of Tamil Nadu.

Chennai is the capital and largest city of Tamil Nadu, officially renamed from Madras in 1996. The 2011 census counted 4,646,732 people within the city's 174 km2, and Tamil is the language of most residents. Its oldest surviving buildings date from the 6th to 8th centuries CE, among them the Kapaleeshwarar Temple in Mylapore and the Parthasarathy Temple in Triplicane. The Madras Music Season, begun by the Madras Music Academy in 1927, brings Carnatic music performances each December.
china: China covers 9.6 million square kilometres, the third largest country by area, with a dry and mountainous west and both mountains and wide river valleys in the east. Chinese civilization was traditionally centred in the lowlands around the two longest rivers, the Yangtze and the Yellow River, both of which originate on the Tibetan Plateau. Mount Everest, the world's highest point, lies on the border with Nepal. The climate is dominated by dry seasons and wet monsoons, and the Yellow River's perennial floods have devastated the surrounding plains throughout recorded history.

Modern Homo sapiens are attested in China from around 50,000 years ago, and pottery-making Neolithic cultures emerged after about 8,000 BCE. After 2000 BCE the Erlitou culture emerged in the Central Plain, controversially identified with the Xia, the traditionally accepted first dynasty; no written records confirm this. The Shang dynasty purportedly succeeded the Xia around 1600 BCE, and its late phase is attested by oracle bone script, the earliest known writing in China. The Zhou overthrew the Shang c. 1046 BCE, and centralised authority collapsed in 771 BCE. The Eastern Zhou saw the Spring and Autumn period and then the seven Warring States, and schools of thought such as Confucianism and Daoism.

In 221 BCE the Qin ruler Qin Shi Huang proclaimed himself the first emperor, but the dynasty lasted only fifteen years. It was followed by the Han dynasty, and two millennia of imperial rule across periods of unity and division followed. The empire was succeeded by the Republic of China after the 1911 Revolution. The Warlord Era and the Chinese Civil War followed, interrupted by the Second Sino-Japanese War. In 1949 the Chinese Communist Party proclaimed the People's Republic of China, and the Republic of China retreated to Taiwan; both sides still claim political legitimacy. The party's attempts to advance its political program faltered through famine and political turmoil, and the reform and opening-up that began in 1978 moved China towards a socialist market economy.

The 2020 census recorded a population of 1,411,778,724, and Beijing is the capital. China is a unitary state with the Chinese Communist Party as its sole ruling party. It maintained a one-child policy from 1979 to 2015.

The Han are the dominant ethnicity, and 55 minorities are recognised, including the Hui, Mongols, Tibetans, Uyghurs and Zhuang. It has 60 World Heritage Sites, including the Great Wall and the Grand Canal.
chinvat-bridge: The Avestan name, Cinvatô Peretûm, is rendered as bridge of judgement or as beam-shaped bridge; other forms of the name are Chinwad, Cinvat, Chinvar and Chinavat. How the bridge appears depends on the asha, the righteousness, of the soul that comes to it. Three divinities are thought to be its guardians: Sraosha, who stands for conscience, Mithra, for covenant, and Rashnu, for justice. Believers hold that the souls that cross successfully are united with Ahura Mazda. The Yasna describes the bridge in its 71st chapter and the Vendidad in its nineteenth fargard.

The bridge has often been identified with the rainbow or with the Milky Way, as in C. P. Tiele's History of Religion. Other scholars, among them C. F. Keary and Ferdinand Justi, reject this reading, citing descriptions of the bridge as rising straight upward and not in a curve.

Cyrus Niknam, a mobad and writer on ancient Iranian culture, denies that Zoroaster taught a bridge at all. In his reading the phrase in the hymns means a passage concerned with how to live, a questioning of the conscience, with no material crossing for the soul. He holds that the priests of the Sasanian era adapted beliefs about heaven, hell and the afterlife from other cultures that had reached Iran, and that the picture of a bridge wide for the righteous and thin as a hair for sinners belongs to that later development, as does the Book of Arda Viraf, and not to the Gathas.

The most notable of the Sogdian depictions is on the east wall of the funerary couch of the sabao Wirkak, excavated at Xi'an; a fragmentary one is on the couch in the Miho Museum. As-Sirat in Islam is a similar idea. In Yazidism the Silat Bridge at Lalish leads to the holiest Yazidi shrine, marks the passage from the profane world to the sacred, and is held to play a part at the end of times as well. In modern literature Charles Olson refers to the bridge in The Maximus Poems, and Dimitris Lyacos alludes to it in With the People from the Bridge.
chisinau: Chișinău stands on the river Bâc, a tributary of the Dniester, in the middle of Moldova, on a relatively level landscape with very fertile ground. It is roughly equidistant between the borders with Romania, 58 km away, and Ukraine, 54 km away, and very close to the geographic centre of the country. The city proper covers 120 km2 and the municipality 635 km2. Its climate is humid continental, with hot summers and cold, windy winters.

The origin of the name is unclear. One theory derives it from the archaic Romanian chișla, meaning spring or source of water, and nouă, new, because the town grew around a small spring. Another, attributed to the historian Ștefan Ciobanu, holds that it was formed like the name of Chișineu in western Romania, from the Hungarian kis, small, and Jenő, one of the seven Hungarian tribes. A third, by the linguist Kiss Lajos, derives it from a Cuman word for a grave or kurgan.

Chișinău was founded in 1436 as a monastery village and belonged to the Principality of Moldavia, which from the 16th century was a vassal state of the Ottoman Empire while retaining its autonomy. At the beginning of the 19th century it was a small town of 7,000 inhabitants. In 1812, after the Russo-Turkish War of 1806-1812, the Ottomans ceded the eastern half of Moldavia to the Russian Empire. The new territory became known as Bessarabia, and Chișinău became the capital of its oblast.

A generous development plan gave the city broad, long roads by 1834 and divided it roughly into an old part with irregular buildings and a newer centre and station. Between 1830 and 1836 the architect Avraam Melnikov built the Nativity Cathedral with a bell tower, and in 1840 the Triumphal Arch, planned by Luca Zaushkevich, was completed. The belfry was demolished in Soviet times and rebuilt in 1997. After the Russian Empire the city belonged to the Moldavian Democratic Republic in 1917-1918, to the Kingdom of Romania in 1918-1940 and 1941-1944, and to the Soviet Union in 1940-1941 and 1944-1991.

Chișinău has been the capital of Moldova since 1991. It is the country's main industrial and commercial centre and its largest transport hub, and the municipality holds nearly a third of the population. The city was significantly damaged in the Second World War and by earthquakes. The architect Alexander Bernardazzi designed many buildings, including the City Hall and the Church of Saint Theodore, and much of the city is built of limestone quarried at Cricova. The house where Alexander Pushkin lived in exile is now a museum.
christopher-columbus: Scholars agree that Columbus was born in the Republic of Genoa, between 25 August and 31 October 1451; theories placing his origin in Aragon or Portugal are discounted by most of them. His father, Domenico Colombo, was a wool weaver who worked in Genoa and Savona and owned a cheese stand where the boy worked. His mother was Susanna Fontanarossa. In 1470 the family moved to Savona, where Domenico took over a tavern. Columbus wrote that he went to sea at the age of 14, and he later settled in Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew ran a cartography workshop.

After Constantinople fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1453, the Silk Road was closed to Christian traders. In 1474 the Florentine astronomer Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli suggested to King Afonso V of Portugal that sailing west across the Atlantic would reach Asia faster than the route around Africa, but the king rejected the idea. Columbus and his brother proposed such a plan in the 1480s, and Bartolomeu Dias's rounding of the Cape of Good Hope in 1488 complicated it. After the Granada War and years of lobbying, Queen Isabella I and King Ferdinand II of Spain agreed to sponsor the voyage.

Columbus left the Port of Palos in August 1492 with three ships and made landfall on 12 October on an island in the Bahamas known to its inhabitants as Guanahani. He then visited Cuba and Hispaniola, where he founded the short-lived fort of La Navidad, and returned to Castile in early 1493 with captured American Indians. Three further voyages took him to the Lesser Antilles in 1493, to Trinidad and the northern coast of South America in 1498, and to the east coast of Central America in 1502. He never clearly renounced his belief that he had reached the Far East, and he called the people he met indios.

As colonial governor Columbus was accused by some contemporaries of significant brutality, and he was arrested and removed from Hispaniola in 1500. He afterwards demanded the tenth of the new lands' wealth promised in the Capitulations of Santa Fe, and after his death his heirs pursued the claim in the protracted lawsuits known as the pleitos colombinos. His remains were moved several times, between Valladolid, Seville, Santo Domingo and perhaps Havana, and DNA tests on those in Seville in 2003 led researchers to conclude that they are his.

His voyages began lasting contact between the two hemispheres and the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, diseases and ideas. Diseases and warfare introduced from the Old World contributed to the decline of Hispaniola's American Indians, who were also enslaved and mistreated under Columbus's government. Once idealized as a heroic discoverer, he is now examined more critically.
chutia-people: The origin of the name Chutia is not known; the chronicles written in the Ahom language called the kingdom Tiora, while those in Assamese used Chutia. The historic Chutias are thought to have had some Shan admixture, and their ruling families are estimated to have been originally matrilineal or not entirely patrilineal. They worshipped a primordial male deity and a primordial female deity, Kechaikhati, whose worship was conducted by a priestly section identified today as the Deori people. The settlement of Brahmins in the kingdom led to the Hinduisation of its rulers, and inscriptions of the late 14th century suggest that the kings then followed the Vaishnava tradition.

After the annexation the capital region became a frontier province of the Ahom kingdom under an officer called the Sadiya-khowa Gohain, and the Chutia nobles were widely dispersed in Upper Assam. Those Chutias who had not been Hinduised were initiated in the 17th century into the Ekasarana dharma under the Mayamara Satra by Aniruddhadev. After the fall of the kingdom a new Hindu lineage was constructed, tracing the Chutias to the legendary King Bhishmaka of Vidarbha.

The community divided into several groups. The Hindu Chutias were a large section. The Ahom Chutias intermarried with the Ahoms, held high offices in the Ahom administration and were mostly absorbed. The Borahi Chutias had religious rites of their own, and the Miri Chutias fled to the Miri hills and intermarried with the Mishing. According to one chronicle, the Ahom court adopted muga silk by employing a thousand producers and weavers from the Chutia community.

Most Chutias live in Upper Assam, mostly in the interior on the banks of rivers, in villages of about 60 to 140 families. They generally live in joint families headed by the father, which at times exceeded one hundred members. Their original Tibeto-Burman language has disappeared; a British colonial officer of the 19th century wrongly identified it with the Deori language, but the Deori community is not related to the Chutias ethnically or linguistically.

Their rituals have a tribal and tantric base influenced by Hinduism and Vaishnavism. Those called Kesa-ponthi accept restrictions on meat and alcohol in their rites, while the Poka-ponthi keep the older customs. The Government of India recognises the Chutias as an Other Backward Class, and there is a political movement to include them in the list of scheduled tribes.
cicero: Marcus Tullius Cicero was born on 3 January 106 BCE in Arpinum, a hill town 100 kilometres south-east of Rome, into a wealthy family of the equestrian order. His father was in poor health and could not enter public life, so he studied extensively to compensate. The cognomen Cicero comes from the Latin for chickpea, cicer. Plutarch explains that it was first given to an ancestor with a cleft in the tip of his nose resembling a chickpea, and says that Cicero refused to change the name when he entered politics.

His first major appearance in the courts came in 81 BCE, at 26. In 80 BCE he defended Sextus Roscius of Ameria on a charge of parricide in Pro Roscio Amerino, his first criminal case. He accused Chrysogonus, a freedman of the dictator Sulla, of fabricating the proscription of Roscius's father to obtain the family's property, while tactfully avoiding any charge against Sulla himself. He won and gained a good reputation as an orator.

Cicero was elected consul for 63 BCE with the support of every unit of the centuriate assembly. He suppressed the Catilinarian conspiracy, but because he had executed five of the conspirators without trial he was exiled in 58 BCE and recalled the next year. In 60 BCE he refused Julius Caesar's invitation to join the partnership of Caesar, Pompey and Marcus Licinius Crassus, fearing it would undermine the Republic.

In 51 BCE he reluctantly took the proconsulship of Cilicia, where he restored calm by mild government and recovered public property embezzled by previous governors. In Caesar's civil war he favoured Pompey and followed the Pompeian forces to Pharsalus, but after Caesar's victory there on 9 August 48 BCE he refused to take command and returned to Rome in 47 BCE.

After Caesar's assassination in 44 BCE Cicero opposed Mark Antony in a series of speeches called the Philippics, and he praised Caesar's heir Octavian to play him against Antony. When Octavian and Antony joined with Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate, Cicero was proscribed and executed in late 43 BCE, on 7 December, while trying to escape Italy. On Antony's order his head and hands were displayed on the Rostra.

Cicero is considered the master of Latin prose. He coined much of Latin's philosophical vocabulary. Of his speeches 88 were recorded and 52 survive. Petrarch's rediscovery of his letters is often credited with starting the 14th-century Renaissance, and his authority peaked in the 18th-century Enlightenment.
cleopatra-vii: Cleopatra VII was born in Alexandria in early 69 BCE, the daughter of Ptolemy XII Auletes and an uncertain mother, presumably his wife Cleopatra V Tryphaena. She belonged to the Macedonian Greek Ptolemaic dynasty, descended from Ptolemy I Soter, a general and companion of Alexander the Great. Earlier Ptolemaic rulers refused to learn Egyptian; she was the first known to have done so, and Plutarch implies that she spoke several other languages as well.

Her father tried to ward off Roman annexation by lavish gifts to statesmen such as Pompey and Julius Caesar, which bankrupted him, and in 58 BCE he was exiled from Egypt. Before he died, some time before 22 March 51 BCE, he named her his heir.

Cleopatra began to reign alongside her brother Ptolemy XIII. Her first act as queen was installing a sacred Buchis bull at Hermonthis, and she faced famine caused by drought and a low Nile flood. A falling-out with her brother led to civil war. When Pompey fled to Egypt after losing at Pharsalus in 48 BCE, Ptolemy XIII had him ambushed and killed, and Caesar then occupied Alexandria and was besieged with Cleopatra in the palace. After Ptolemy XIII drowned in the Nile, Caesar made Cleopatra and her brother Ptolemy XIV joint rulers; her son Caesarion was born of her affair with Caesar. After Caesar's assassination she named Caesarion co-ruler.

In the civil war of 43–42 BCE she sided with the Second Triumvirate of Octavian, Mark Antony and Marcus Aemilius Lepidus. After meeting Antony at Tarsos in 41 BCE she had three children with him, and he came to rely on her for funds and military aid. The Donations of Alexandria declared their children rulers of territories under his authority, and Octavian presented this as treason and declared war on Cleopatra. She ruled as an absolute monarch and chief religious authority.

After Octavian defeated the fleet of Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE, his forces invaded Egypt in 30 BCE and Antony killed himself. Cleopatra reportedly killed herself too, probably by poison, to avoid being paraded in a Roman triumph. Her three surviving children were sent to Rome in the care of Octavian's sister Octavia.

Plutarch's Life of Antonius gives the fullest surviving account and draws on eyewitness sources as well as the Augustan view. Roman historiography and Latin poetry produced a generally critical view of the queen that shaped medieval and Renaissance literature.
cold-war: Animosity between the Allies of the Second World War predated its end. After the death of Franklin D. Roosevelt in April 1945, the administration of Harry Truman took a harder line, and diplomats disputed how to read the Yalta agreements, the composition of the Polish government and the running of the United Nations. In February 1946 George F. Kennan's Long Telegram from Moscow helped shape American strategy, and on 5 March Winston Churchill gave his Iron Curtain speech at Fulton. The term itself was used by George Orwell in 1945 and applied to the confrontation by Bernard Baruch on 16 April 1947.

The United States declared the Truman Doctrine of containment in 1947, launched the Marshall Plan in 1948 and founded NATO in 1949; the Soviet-led Warsaw Pact followed in 1955. Early confrontations were the Berlin Blockade of 1948 to 1949 and the Korean War of 1950 to 1953, which ended in a stalemate. The Soviet Union tested its first nuclear weapon in 1949. After Joseph Stalin died in 1953, Nikita Khrushchev denounced him in 1956, the year the Soviet Union crushed the Hungarian Revolution. The Cuban Missile Crisis of 1962 is widely considered the closest the war came to nuclear conflict.

Both powers courted the newly decolonised states, and the Vietnam War of 1955 to 1975 ended in a North Vietnamese victory. In Indonesia from 1965 to 1966 the military, with the aid of the United States and other Western governments, led the mass killing of more than 500,000 members and sympathisers of the Indonesian Communist Party. The Soviet Union invaded Czechoslovakia with the Warsaw Pact in 1968, and a period of détente in the 1970s brought treaties limiting nuclear arsenals. The Soviet invasion of Afghanistan in 1979 renewed tensions.

Mikhail Gorbachev became leader of the Soviet Union in 1985. In June 1987 he announced perestroika, an agenda of economic restructuring, and introduced glasnost, or openness. These reforms contributed to the revolutions of 1989 in the Eastern Bloc and to the collapse of the Soviet Union in 1991, which ended the Cold War.

By 1989 the United States had military alliances with 50 countries and 526,000 troops stationed abroad. Nearly 100,000 Americans died in the Korean and Vietnam Wars, and millions died in the proxy wars around the globe, most of all in eastern Asia. Historians have disagreed over who was responsible for the breakdown of relations: orthodox accounts blame the Soviet Union, revisionists place more responsibility on the United States, and post-revisionists see a more nuanced pattern.
cologne: Cologne is centred on the left bank of the Rhine, about 35 kilometres south-east of Düsseldorf and 22 kilometres north-west of Bonn, in the Cologne Lowland of the central Rhineland. The city's highest point is 118 metres above sea level and its lowest 37.5 metres. It is regularly affected by flooding from the Rhine, and its flood control system was redesigned after a flood in 1993 that caused heavy damage.

The first urban settlement on the site was the Oppidum Ubiorum, founded in 38 BCE by the Ubii, a Germanic tribe. In 50 CE the Romans founded Colonia Claudia Ara Agrippinensium, named after Emperor Claudius and his wife Agrippina the Younger, who was born here. It became capital of the province of Germania Inferior in 85, and from 260 to 271 was the capital of the Gallic Empire under Postumus, Marius and Victorinus. Emperor Constantine I had a bridge built over the Rhine at Cologne in 310. The Franks occupied the city in 462. Its population is put at about 40,000 in 100–200 CE, 20,000 in 1000 and 50,000 in 1200.

Cunibert, made bishop of Cologne in 623, advised the Merovingian King Dagobert I. In 795 Charlemagne's bishop Hildebold was promoted to archbishop, and the Treaty of Verdun of 843 placed the city in Lothair I's Middle Francia.

Its position on major trade routes between eastern and western Europe made it a free imperial city of the Holy Roman Empire and a major member of the Hanseatic League, and one of the largest European cities of the medieval and Renaissance periods. French forces occupied it in 1794, and the Treaty of Lunéville of 1801 made the left bank of the Rhine part of the French Republic. The Napoleonic Code, introduced under French rule, remained in use there until 1900. In 1815 the Congress of Vienna gave Cologne to the Kingdom of Prussia.

Cologne is the fourth-most populous city of Germany and the largest city of North Rhine-Westphalia, with over one million inhabitants. It was one of the most heavily bombed cities in Germany during the Second World War, which reduced its population by 93%, mainly through evacuation, and destroyed around 80% of the old city centre. Most major historic landmarks were restored, among them Cologne Cathedral, built to house the Shrine of the Three Kings and the world's tallest building from 1880 to 1890, and the Romanesque churches. Eau de Cologne has been produced in the city since 1709.
colorado: Colorado is a landlocked state in the Mountain West. It shares the Four Corners region with Arizona, New Mexico and Utah, and is bordered by Wyoming to the north, Nebraska to the northeast, Kansas to the east and Oklahoma to the southeast. It takes in most of the Southern Rocky Mountains, the northeastern portion of the Colorado Plateau and the western edge of the Great Plains, and its landscape includes alpine mountains, high plains, deserts with huge sand dunes and deep canyons.

In 1861 the United States Congress defined the boundaries of the new Territory of Colorado exclusively by lines of latitude and longitude, from 37°N to 41°N and from 102°02′48″W to 109°02′48″W. After 165 years of government surveys the borders were officially defined by 697 boundary markers and 697 straight lines. Colorado, Wyoming and Utah are the only states whose borders are defined solely by straight lines with no natural features. The Four Corners Monument is the only place in the United States where four states meet.

The region has been inhabited by Native Americans and their Paleo-Indian ancestors for at least 13,500 years and possibly more than 37,000. The Lindenmeier site contains artifacts dating from approximately 8720 BCE. The Ancient Pueblo peoples lived in the valleys and mesas of the Colorado Plateau in the far southwest, and the Ute Nation inhabited the mountain valleys of the Rocky Mountains. The Apache and Comanche lived in the east and southeast. In the 17th century the Arapaho and Cheyenne moved west from the Great Lakes region to hunt across the High Plains.

The United States acquired the territorial claim to the eastern Rocky Mountains with the Louisiana Purchase from France in 1803. In 1806 Zebulon Pike led an army reconnaissance expedition into the disputed region. Spanish cavalry arrested him and his troops in the San Luis Valley the following February, took them to Chihuahua and expelled them from Mexico in July.

In 1848 much of the Nuevo México region was annexed to the United States by the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo. The Pike's Peak Gold Rush of 1858-1862 brought an influx of settlers. On 28 February 1861 President James Buchanan signed the act creating the Territory of Colorado, and on 1 August 1876 President Ulysses S. Grant signed Proclamation 230, admitting Colorado as the 38th state.

Denver is the capital, the most populous city and the centre of the Front Range Urban Corridor. Colorado Springs is the second-most populous city. The state is the eighth-largest by area. Its economy rests on government and defense, mining, agriculture, tourism and manufacturing.
conakry: Conakry was originally settled on the small Tombo Island, one of the Îles de Los, and later spread to the neighbouring Kaloum Peninsula, a stretch of land 36 km long and between 0.2 and 6 km wide. The expanding urban area has since spread north-eastwards to occupy the whole of the peninsula. The climate is tropical monsoon, with a wet season of very heavy rainfall, more than 1,100 mm in both July and August, and a dry season dominated between December and April by the harmattan wind.

The city was essentially founded after Britain ceded the island to France in 1887. In 1885 the two island villages of Conakry and Boubinet had fewer than 500 inhabitants between them. Conakry became the capital of French Guinea and prospered as an export port, particularly after a railway to Kankan, now closed, opened the interior of the country to the large-scale export of groundnuts.

After Guinea gained independence in 1958 the population boomed, from 50,000 in 1958 to 600,000 in 1980. The city's small land area and relative isolation from the mainland, an advantage to its colonial founders, created an infrastructural burden after independence. In 1970 the conflict between Portuguese forces and the PAIGC independence fighters in neighbouring Portuguese Guinea spilled into the Republic of Guinea, when 350 Portuguese troops and Guinean loyalists landed near the capital, attacked the city and freed 26 Portuguese prisoners of war held by the PAIGC before withdrawing. Camp Boiro, a feared concentration camp, stood in Conakry during the rule of Sekou Touré.

Conakry is the capital and largest city of Guinea and its administrative, communications and economic centre. It forms a region and a prefecture of its own, the Conakry Special Zone, divided into communes. Its port ships alumina and bananas, and its manufactures include food products, cement and metal goods. Among its buildings are the Grand Mosque and the Roman Catholic Cathedral of Sainte-Marie, and the Sandervalia National Museum and the National Library of Guinea are in the city. Its population is roughly one fifth of that of Guinea, more than eight times that of the next city, Kankan.
concepcion-chile: Concepción was founded by Pedro de Valdivia in 1550 north of the Bío Bío River, at the site now known as Penco. It was named Concepción de María Purísima del Nuevo Extremo. The settlement lay a few kilometres north of La Frontera, the boundary between Spanish territory and the land of the Mapuche, who remained independent until the 1870s. Spanish authorities formally recognised it as a town two years later by royal decree and gave it a coat of arms still in use today. When the Spanish arrived, the chronicler Jerónimo de Vivar noted that local Mapuche wore gold and silver bracelets and crown-like ornaments, interpreted either as Incan gifts, war spoils or the adoption of Incan metallurgy.

The city was the capital of the Kingdom of Chile between 1565 and 1573 and kept the unofficial position of military capital for the rest of the colonial period. After a serious earthquake in 1751 it moved to the Valle de la Mocha, where the city centre and historic district now stand. Its inhabitants are still called penquistas, after Penco. The city was an important site in the struggle for Chile's independence, and the declaration of independence was held at the Plaza de la Independencia. Until the election of Manuel Montt as president in 1851, executive power in independent Chile was dominated by Concepción elites.

Concepción is the capital of the Biobío Region and of Concepción Province, about 500 km south of Santiago. It is the core of the Greater Concepción metropolitan area, the second largest city in Chile by urban area, and sits in the most heavily industrialized region of the country. It is known as the university city, with the Universidad de Concepción, the Universidad del Biobío and the Catholic University of the Most Holy Conception. Like most of Chile it is seismically active: an earthquake in 1939 destroyed much of the city, one in 1953 damaged 15 per cent of its buildings, and a major earthquake in 1960 had a nearby epicentre.
confucius: The name Confucius is a Latinized form of the Mandarin Kǒngfūzǐ, meaning roughly Great Master Kong, coined in the late 16th century by early Jesuit missionaries to China. His family name was Kong and his given name Qiu, meaning hill or mound. His courtesy name was Zhongni, the Zhong indicating that he was the second son in his family.

It is thought that he was born on 28 September 551 BCE in Zou, in modern Qufu, Shandong. The area was formally controlled by the kings of Zhou but effectively independent under the local lords of Lu. His father Kong He, an elderly commandant of the local Lu garrison, died when Confucius was three years old, and his mother Yan Zhengzai raised him in poverty.

Traditional accounts trace the family back through the dukes of Song to the Shang dynasty, though not all modern scholars accept this descent. He was born into the class of shi, between the aristocracy and the common people, and was educated at schools for commoners. At 19 he married Qi Guanshi, and a year later their son Kong Li was born. He is said to have held various government jobs in his early 20s and to have mourned his mother for three years.

In the Analects, Confucius presents himself as a transmitter who invented nothing. He put the most emphasis on study and wanted his disciples to master older classics rather than build a systematic theory. Tradition credits him with authoring or editing the Five Classics, but modern scholars are cautious about attributing particular assertions to him, since some of the texts and philosophy associated with him are more ancient, and the Analects were compiled many years after his death. His ethics stress self-cultivation and emulation of moral exemplars over rules, and he taught a negative form of the Golden Rule, sometimes called the Silver Rule.

His disciples and his grandson Zisi continued his school, and Mencius in the 4th century BCE and Xunzi in the 3rd century BCE elaborated his ideas in different ways. The Qin state, which conquered all of China in 221 BCE, adopted Legalism as its official doctrine. Under Emperor Wu of Han, works attributed to Confucius were made the official imperial philosophy and required reading for civil service examinations in 140 BCE, a practice continued nearly unbroken until the end of imperial China in 1912.
congo-river: The Congo River, formerly also called the Zaire, is the only major river to cross the equator twice. Its basin covers about 4 million square kilometres and ten countries, around 13 percent of Africa. The Chambeshi River in Zambia is generally taken as its source, and the Lualaba is the river upstream of the Boyoma Falls. From Kisangani it flows north-west, then south-west to Pool Malebo, where Kinshasa and Brazzaville face each other. Below the Pool it falls through the Livingstone Falls, a series of 32 falls and rapids, to the sea at Muanda. Its flow is stable because its basin lies on both sides of the Equator, and it is one of the deepest rivers in the world.

The whole basin is populated by Bantu peoples, whose expansion is estimated to have reached the middle Congo by about 500 BCE. The name Congo comes from the Kingdom of Kongo, once on the southern bank, formed in the late 14th century. The name Zaire is a Portuguese adaptation of the Kikongo nzere, river. European exploration began in 1482, when the Portuguese explorer Diogo Cão found the estuary and made contact with the Kingdom of Kongo. The full course remained unknown throughout the early modern period.

Henry Morton Stanley's expedition of 1876-77 proved that the Lualaba fed the Congo and not the Nile. It reached Boma on 9 August 1877, having most probably lost 132 people to disease, hunger, drowning, killing and desertion. Stanley founded Kinshasa as a trading post in 1881, named Léopoldville for Leopold II of Belgium, who claimed the basin privately as the Congo Free State in 1885.

The Democratic Republic of the Congo and the Republic of the Congo are both named after the river. Although the Livingstone Falls block access from the sea, nearly the whole river above them is navigable in sections, especially between Kinshasa and Kisangani, and it remains a lifeline in a land with few roads or railways. Its basin holds the Congo rainforest, the second-largest rainforest area in the world, and almost 800 fish species have been recorded there, many found nowhere else.
connecticut: Connecticut is bordered by Long Island Sound to the south, New York to the west, Massachusetts to the north and Rhode Island to the east. It is named after the Connecticut River, the longest in New England, which roughly bisects the state. The river's name derives from anglicized spellings of Quinnetuket, a Mohegan-Pequot word for long tidal river. Many coastal towns lie less than 20 feet above sea level, and because the coast is on Long Island Sound, an estuary, it is relatively protected from high storm waves.

Evidence of human presence dates back 10,000 years. The peoples were semi-nomadic and shared Algonquian languages. In the early 17th century about 8,000 Pequots lived in the south-east, a number roughly halved by the smallpox epidemic of 1633–34, and 1,500 to 2,500 Mohegans lived west of the Thames. Their economies combined hunting, shellfishing, gathering and maize agriculture, and wampum from quahog and whelk shells served as currency and as a record of agreements.

In 1633 the Dutch West India Company established a short-lived settlement, House of Hope, in Hartford. The Dutch colony of New Netherland initially claimed half of Connecticut, but the English founded the first major settlements at about the same time. Thomas Hooker led followers from the Massachusetts Bay Colony to form the Connecticut Colony, and the Saybrook and New Haven Colonies, founded by other settlers from Massachusetts, had both merged into it by the mid-1660s. The Fundamental Orders of 1638–39 framed its first government, and King Charles II granted a charter in 1662.

Connecticut was one of the Thirteen Colonies that rejected British rule. At the Constitutional Convention of 1787 its delegates Roger Sherman and Oliver Ellsworth proposed the Connecticut Compromise, a bicameral Congress with proportional representation in the House and equal representation of the states in the Senate. In January 1788 Connecticut became the fifth state to ratify the Constitution. Hartford became the sole capital in 1875; before then New Haven and Hartford alternated.

Hartford is the capital and Bridgeport the most populous city. Connecticut is the third-smallest state by area. Its nickname, the Constitution State, was adopted in 1959. Yale University stands in New Haven, and the United States Coast Guard Academy in New London.
copenhagen: Copenhagen lies on the eastern shore of the island of Zealand, partly on the island of Amager and on a number of natural and artificial islets between the two. It faces the Øresund, the strait that separates Denmark from Sweden and connects the North Sea with the Baltic Sea. The Swedish city of Malmö lies directly across the sound, 42 kilometres away by road.

The Danish name København reflects the city's origin as a harbour and a place of commerce. The Old Norse form was Kaupmannahǫfn, meaning 'merchants' harbour', and the present form developed through sound changes that took place around 1400. The Latin name Hafnia is the source of the name of the element hafnium.

Flint tools show settlement in the Stone Age, and many historians believe the town dates to the late Viking Age, possibly founded by Sweyn I Forkbeard. The first habitations were probably centred on Gammel Strand, 'old shore'. The natural harbour and good herring stocks attracted seasonal fishermen and merchants from the 11th century and more permanent residents in the 13th. Excavations have uncovered the remains of a large merchant mansion from about 1020 near Kongens Nytorv, and a well from the late 12th century in Pilestræde.

Copenhagen became the capital of Denmark in the early 15th century, and the University of Copenhagen was founded in 1479. In the 16th century it served as the de facto capital of the Kalmar Union and its monarchy, and by the 17th century it was the centre of the Danish government and military. The 18th century brought a devastating plague outbreak and urban fires, followed by the building of the district of Frederiksstaden and of institutions such as the Royal Theatre and the Royal Academy of Fine Arts. In this period the city was the centre of the Danish slave trade.

A British fleet bombarded the city in 1807 during the Napoleonic Wars. The Danish Golden Age that followed gave Copenhagen a neoclassical look. After the Second World War the Finger Plan guided the growth of housing and businesses along five urban railway routes running out from the centre.

Copenhagen is the capital and largest city of Denmark and its cultural, economic and governmental centre. Since the completion of the Øresund Bridge it has been increasingly integrated with Malmö and the Swedish province of Scania in the Øresund Region. Its landmarks include Tivoli Gardens, the Amalienborg and Christiansborg palaces, Rosenborg Castle and Frederik's Church, and the University of Copenhagen is the oldest university in Denmark.
copper: Copper is a chemical element with the symbol Cu, from the Latin cuprum, and atomic number 29. It is a soft, malleable and ductile metal with very high thermal and electrical conductivity, second only to silver among pure metals at room temperature. Pure copper is orange-red, one of the few metals with a natural colour other than grey or silver. In air it slowly forms a protective layer of copper oxide, and on old roofs and the Statue of Liberty a green layer of verdigris appears. Copper is also one of the few native metals, found in nature in a directly usable, unalloyed form.

The use of native copper dates to about 9000 BCE in the Middle East, and a native copper pendant found in northern Iraq dates to 8700 BCE. The history of copper metallurgy is thought to run from cold working of native copper to annealing, then smelting, and finally casting. The earliest archaeological evidence of hot metallurgy in Eurasia, in the Balkans and Carpathian Mountains, dates to between 6200 and 5000 BCE. An amulet from Mehrgarh in Pakistan, dated to 4000 BCE, is the earliest example of lost-wax casting in copper. Ötzi the Iceman, who lived between 3300 and 3200 BCE, was found with a copper axehead of 99.7 per cent purity.

Smelting was probably discovered in China before 2800 BCE, in Central America around 600 CE and in West Africa about the 9th or 10th century. Experience with copper helped the development of other metals, and copper smelting likely led to the discovery of iron smelting.

Copper was alloyed with zinc to make brass and with tin to make bronze, and copper-tin bronzes have been used to make bells for centuries, the composition of the alloy affecting the tone. Alloys of copper and nickel, called cupronickel, are used in low-denomination coins. In Japan, shakudō is a decorative alloy of copper with 4 to 10 per cent gold, which can be patinated to dark blue or black. For more than two centuries copper paint has been used on boat hulls to control the growth of plants and shellfish.
corsica: Corsica is the fourth-largest island in the Mediterranean, lying south-east of the French mainland, west of the Italian Peninsula and immediately north of Sardinia. It is 183 km long at its longest and 83 km wide at its widest. It is the most mountainous island in the Mediterranean, a mountain in the sea: a single chain makes up two-thirds of the island, with Monte Cinto the highest peak at 2,706 metres. Its granite backbone on the western side formed about 250 million years ago.

People have lived on Corsica since the Mesolithic, and a permanent presence is documented from the Neolithic. After the western Roman Empire collapsed in the fifth century CE the island was invaded by the Vandals and the Ostrogoths, briefly recovered by the Byzantine Empire, then became part of the Kingdom of the Lombards. Pepin the Short, king of the Franks, expelled the Lombards and nominally granted Corsica to Pope Stephen II.

In the first quarter of the 11th century Pisa and Genoa together freed the island from the threat of Arab invasion, and it then came under the influence of the Republic of Pisa. Immigration from Tuscany gave the island its place names and made the language of the northern two-thirds close to Tuscan. The Republic of Genoa ruled Corsica from 1284 to 1755.

The Corsican Revolution against Genoa began in 1729 under Luiggi Giafferi and Giacinto Paoli, later led by Giacinto's son Pasquale Paoli. An independent Corsican Republic was proclaimed in 1755 and remained sovereign until France conquered the island in 1769. Napoleon Bonaparte was born in Ajaccio in 1769. In 1814 British troops briefly occupied the island and the Treaty of Bastia gave the British crown sovereignty, but Lord Castlereagh later repudiated it. Corsica was freed in 1943, the first French department to be liberated.

Corsica is one of the 18 regions of France and a single territorial collectivity, with a Corsican Assembly that has more extensive powers than other French regional bodies. Ajaccio is the capital and Bastia the second largest town. The population is 365,636. French is the official and most widely spoken language, while Corsican, an Italo-Dalmatian language close to medieval Tuscan, is recognised as a regional language. The Scandola Nature Reserve, within the regional natural park, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
cotton: Cotton was domesticated independently in the Old and New Worlds. In the Americas the indigenous species Gossypium barbadense has been identified at a site in the Nanchoc District of Peru and dated to the 7th to 6th millennia BCE, and cultivation at Ancon in Peru has been dated to about 4200 BCE. It was the backbone of the coastal cultures of Norte Chico, Moche and Nazca, whose people grew it upriver, made it into nets and traded them to fishing villages for fish. In South Asia a cotton thread dated to the sixth millennium BCE was found at Mehrgarh in Pakistan. The Spanish who reached Mexico and Peru found people growing cotton and wearing clothes made of it.

Cotton is a soft staple fibre that grows in a protective boll around the seeds of plants of the genus Gossypium, in the mallow family. The fibre is almost pure cellulose. Four species are grown commercially, all domesticated in antiquity: upland cotton, native to Central America, Mexico and the Caribbean, which supplies about 90 per cent of production; extra-long staple cotton from tropical South America; tree cotton, native to India and Pakistan; and Levant cotton, native to southern Africa and the Arabian Peninsula. The English word derives ultimately from a Hebrew word for a garment of linen, which was the usual word for cotton in medieval Arabic.

Hand-held roller gins had been used in India since the 6th century, and dual-roller gins appeared in India and China between the 12th and 14th centuries. The earliest clear pictures of the spinning wheel come from the Islamic world in the 11th century. Under the Mughal Empire cotton production increased, helped by agrarian reforms that favoured cash crops.

The English East India Company introduced cheap calico and chintz in the 1660s, and the cloth overtook its spice trade by value in the late 17th century. Weavers objected, and Parliament passed the Calico Act of 1700 and a stricter act in 1721. The exemption of raw cotton led to a native industry and to mechanised spinning and weaving, with imports rising to seven thousand bales a year by the early 1770s. In the United States, before 1865 cotton was largely produced by enslaved African Americans and enriched both southern landowners and the textile industries of the north and of Britain.
crimea: Crimea covers 27,000 square kilometres on the northern coast of the Black Sea and the western coast of the Sea of Azov. It is almost an island, joined to the mainland only by the Isthmus of Perekop, a strip about 5 to 7 kilometres wide. It was called the Tauric Peninsula, after the Tauri, until the early modern period; the name Crimea comes from the Italian la Crimea. Most of the peninsula is semiarid steppe, scattered with the burial mounds of the ancient Scythians, while the Crimean Mountains shelter a narrow southern coast with a Mediterranean climate.

The recorded history of Crimea begins around the 5th century BCE, when Greek colonies were founded on the south coast, the most important being Chersonesos near modern Sevastopol, with Scythians and Tauri in the hinterland. The south later became the Bosporan Kingdom, a client kingdom of Rome from 63 BCE to 341 CE, and stayed Greek in culture under the Byzantine Empire, the Empire of Trebizond and the Principality of Theodoro, which ended in 1475. In the 13th century the Venetians and the Genoese held some ports, while the interior fell to the Golden Horde.

In the 1440s the Crimean Khanate formed from the collapse of the Horde and soon became subject to the Ottoman Empire, which also conquered the independent coastal areas. Raids on Eastern Europe for slaves were a major source of prosperity. The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca in 1774 made the Tatars of Crimea politically independent, and in 1783 Catherine the Great incorporated the peninsula into the Russian Empire. From 1853 to 1856 it was the site of the principal engagements of the Crimean War, in which Russia lost to a French-led alliance.

Crimea changed hands many times in the Russian Civil War, and Wrangel's White Army made its last stand there. In 1921 it became an autonomous republic within the Russian Soviet Federative Socialist Republic. Germany occupied it from 1942 to 1944, and after the Soviets regained control in 1944 they deported the Crimean Tatars and several other nationalities. It became an oblast in 1945 and was transferred to the Ukrainian Soviet Socialist Republic in 1954, on the 300th anniversary of the Treaty of Pereyaslav.

After Ukrainian independence in 1991 most of the peninsula became the Autonomous Republic of Crimea, and a 1997 treaty let Russia keep basing its fleet in Sevastopol, the largest city. In 2014 Russia occupied and annexed the peninsula, a step most countries do not recognise. Its population is about 2.4 million.
croatia: Croatia lies on the Adriatic coast, and the sea forms its entire southwest border. It covers 56,594 square kilometres and is divided into twenty counties within four historical and cultural regions. The Dinaric Alps rise to the highest point, the Dinara peak at 1,831 metres, near the border with Bosnia and Herzegovina. Insular Croatia consists of over a thousand islands and islets, 48 of them permanently inhabited; the largest are Cres and Krk.

In the north the hilly Hrvatsko Zagorje and the plains of Slavonia are crossed by the Danube, Drava, Kupa and Sava. Karst topography makes up about half of the country. The area around Dubrovnik is a practical exclave, separated by land from the rest by a short coastal strip belonging to Bosnia and Herzegovina, and linked to it by the Pelješac Bridge.

The area was inhabited throughout prehistory, and Neanderthal fossils from the middle Palaeolithic were found at Krapina. Illyrians and Liburnians lived there, and the first Greek colonies were established on the islands of Hvar, Korčula and Vis. In 9 CE the territory became part of the Roman Empire. Emperor Diocletian, a native of the region, built a large palace at Split and retired there after abdicating in 305 CE. In the 5th century Julius Nepos, the last de jure Western Roman Emperor, ruled a small realm from it after fleeing Italy in 475.

Avar and Croat invasions in the late 6th and first half of the 7th century destroyed almost all Roman towns. Survivors retreated to the coast, islands and mountains, and Dubrovnik was founded by survivors from Epidaurum. The origin of the Croats is debated: the predominant view is that the White Croats were a Slavic group who migrated during the Migration Period, while the Iranian theory proposes a Sarmatian-Alanic origin, drawing on names in the Tanais Tablets. The oldest stone inscription with the full ethnonym styles Duke Branimir as Dux Cruatorvm, probably between 879 and 892.

Croatia is a unitary constitutional republic with a parliamentary system. The president is directly elected for five years, and the Sabor, a unicameral parliament, holds legislative power. Its population was an estimated 3.87 million in 2024, down from a peak of 4.7 million in 1991. The 2021 census recorded 91.6% Croats and 3.2% Serbs, and about 4 million Croats live abroad. The country has ten sites on UNESCO's World Heritage List. The necktie derives from the cravat worn by 17th-century Croatian mercenaries in France.
crusades: Sites linked to Jesus's ministry, including the Church of the Holy Sepulchre in Jerusalem, were popular pilgrimage destinations in Roman Palestine. Jerusalem fell to Caliph Umar in 638, and by the mid-10th century three rival caliphates had emerged: the Umayyads in al-Andalus, the Shi'ite Fatimids in Egypt and the Abbasids in the Middle East. By the late 11th century, Christian just war theory, increasing aristocratic piety and the popularity of penitential journeys to the Holy Land had created a context for armed pilgrimages. In March 1095 Pope Urban II received envoys from Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, who asked for military aid at the Council of Piacenza.

On 27 November 1095, at the Council of Clermont, Urban announced a military campaign against the Turkomans. According to most accounts he promised spiritual rewards, though accounts differ on whether he offered reduced penance or full remission of sin. Popular enthusiasm outran his wish to enlist only trained warriors, and Peter the Hermit attracted thousands of peasants and townsfolk. No crowned ruler joined; the leaders included Godfrey of Bouillon, Bohemond of Taranto and Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count of Toulouse, who led the largest force.

The campaign's successes led to four Crusader states: the Kingdom of Jerusalem, the Principality of Antioch and the counties of Tripoli and Edessa. When Edessa fell on 26 December 1144, most of its Frankish population was killed or enslaved, and the Second Crusade failed in 1148. Saladin destroyed the Jerusalemite field army at the Battle of Hattin on 4 July 1187, and Jerusalem surrendered on 2 October. The Fourth Crusade, first aimed at Egypt, was diverted to the Byzantine Empire and ended in the Sack of Constantinople and the Latin Empire in 1204. Jerusalem was regained by negotiation in 1229, but the Mamluks, who had reunited Egypt and Muslim Syria by 1260, captured the Crusaders' last mainland strongholds in 1291.

The fall of the Frankish East caused dismay rather than shock in the West, and Western Christians mostly blamed the Franks' alleged immorality. Schemes to recover the Holy Land inspired treatises, and only the Alexandrian Crusade briefly revived crusading activity in the region in 1365. Over time the crusading movement expanded to campaigns against pagans, Christian dissidents and other enemies of the papacy, promoted with similar spiritual rewards and continuing into the 18th century. The Crusades created national mythologies, tales of heroism and a few place names, and modern Muslim thinkers have drawn parallels between them and later political developments.
cuba: Cuba is an archipelago of 4,195 islands, cays and islets in the northern Caribbean Sea, where the Gulf of Mexico meets the Atlantic Ocean. Key West, Florida, lies about 150 kilometres across the Straits of Florida to the north and northwest, Mexico 210 kilometres west across the Yucatán Channel, Haiti 78 kilometres to the east and Jamaica 148 kilometres to the south. The main island is 1,250 kilometres long and makes up most of the land area of 104,338 square kilometres. It consists mostly of flat to rolling plains apart from the Sierra Maestra in the southeast, whose highest point is Pico Turquino at 1,974 metres. The second-largest island is Isla de la Juventud.

Humans first settled Cuba around 6,000 years ago. The Arawakan-speaking ancestors of the Taíno arrived from South America about 1,700 years ago and, unlike the earlier settlers, produced pottery and practised intensive agriculture. The earliest evidence of the Taíno on Cuba dates to the 9th century. Descendants of the first settlers persisted in the west of the island until European contact as the hunter-gathering Guanahatabey. Christopher Columbus first arrived on 27 October 1492, claimed the island for Spain and named it Isla Juana after John, Prince of Asturias.

The first Spanish settlement was founded by Diego Velázquez de Cuéllar at Baracoa in 1511, and San Cristóbal de la Habana was founded in 1514 and moved to its present place in 1519, becoming the capital in 1607. The Taíno were forced to work under the encomienda system.

Within a century they suffered high mortality, primarily from Eurasian infectious diseases against which they had no immunity, aggravated by harsh colonial subjugation. In 1529 a measles outbreak killed two-thirds of the few who had survived smallpox. Cuba remained part of the Spanish Empire until the Spanish–American War of 1898, was then occupied by the United States, and became independent in 1902. The Cuban Revolution of January 1959 overthrew the government of Fulgencio Batista and established a communist government under Fidel Castro.

Havana is the capital and largest city. Cuba is a socialist republic whose constitution names the Communist Party as the leading force of society and the state. Spanish culture, West African culture and the Guanahatabey and Taíno inheritance together shape Cuban culture. Cuba's population descends primarily from Spanish settlers, sub-Saharan Africans brought through the transatlantic slave trade, and pre-Columbian peoples, chiefly the Taíno and Ciboney. Havana, Camagüey, Cienfuegos and Trinidad, with colonial centres in Baroque and Neoclassical styles, are inscribed as UNESCO World Heritage Sites.
cudjoe: The name Cudjoe corresponds to the Akan day name Kojo or Kwadwo, given to a boy born on a Monday. The Leeward Maroons most likely emerged in 1690, when a Coromantee rebellion broke out on Sutton's estate in western Jamaica and most of the enslaved Africans there ran away into the mountainous interior. Cudjoe was probably the son of one of the leaders of that revolt. The oral history of the Accompong Town Maroons, as told by Milton McFarlane, holds that he was the freeborn son of Naquan, who led those who fled from the estate.

According to contemporary white enslavers, Cudjoe challenged a Madagascan for the leadership of the Leeward Maroons in 1720, and by defeating and killing him became their undisputed leader. His community was known as Cudjoe's Town, or Trelawny Town. For about half a century, until the treaties of 1739 and 1740, the Maroons operated outside direct British control.

During the First Maroon War of the 1730s the English colonial forces failed to win any significant victory over Cudjoe's Leeward Maroons. The agreement of 1739 recognised them as a semi-autonomous entity and freed their land from taxes. In the 1740s some Leeward Maroons who opposed the treaty rose in revolt, and Cudjoe crushed these risings.

Two descriptions of him survive from colonial writers. The physician R. C. Dallas, writing half a century after Cudjoe lived, claimed that he was short and stout, with a large lump of flesh on his back. The slaver Thomas Thistlewood, who met him in 1750, noted in his diary that he wore a feathered hat, with a sword at his side and a gun on his shoulder, barefoot and with "somewhat a Majestic look".

One source claims that Cudjoe died in 1744, but Edward Long and Thistlewood wrote of meeting him in the 1750s and 1760s. Long described him leading his Maroons in a martial performance at Montego Bay for Governor Sir William Lyttleton in 1764, and in the same year Thistlewood heard that he had been dead for some time. The treaty had named Accompong as his successor, but Governor Roger Hope Elletson had the Trelawny Town badge of authority given instead to a Maroon officer named Lewis, leaving Accompong authority over Accompong Town only. Cudjoe Day is celebrated in Jamaica on the first Monday in January.
cyprus: Cyprus is the third largest island in the Mediterranean, after Sicily and Sardinia. It measures 240 kilometres from end to end and 100 kilometres at its widest, and lies 75 kilometres south of Turkey. Two mountain ranges, the Troodos Mountains and the smaller Kyrenia Range, enclose the central Mesaoria plain. The highest point is Mount Olympus, at 1,952 metres, in the Troodos range. Some sources place the island in Europe and others in Western Asia, within the Levant.

Hunter-gatherers first reached Cyprus around 13,000 to 12,000 years ago, at about the time the island's pygmy hippopotamus and dwarf elephant became extinct. Neolithic farming communities emerged by around 8500 BCE, and the village of Khirokitia dates to approximately 6800 BCE.

From around 1650 BCE copper from the Troodos Mountains drove trade and the growth of urban settlements, and the island, identified in whole or part as Alashiya, was ruled by kings who corresponded with the pharaohs of the New Kingdom of Egypt, as the Amarna letters document. Mycenaean Greeks traded there from around 1400 BCE, and a major wave of Greek settlement is believed to have followed the collapse of Mycenaean Greece.

Later the island was contested by the Assyrians, Egyptians and Persians, and Alexander the Great seized it in 333 BCE. Ptolemaic, Roman, Arab, Lusignan and Venetian rule followed, then Ottoman dominion from 1571 to 1878. Britain administered Cyprus from 1878 under the Cyprus Convention and annexed it formally in 1914. Independence came in 1960. Intercommunal violence in 1963 and 1964 displaced more than 25,000 Turkish Cypriots into enclaves.

A coup by Greek Cypriot nationalists and elements of the Greek military junta on 15 July 1974 was followed by the Turkish invasion of 20 July, which captured the north and displaced over 150,000 Greek Cypriots and 50,000 Turkish Cypriots. A Turkish Cypriot state declared in 1983 is recognised only by Turkey. The island is divided along a United Nations buffer zone, and two British sovereign military bases, Akrotiri and Dhekelia, remain in the south.

The Republic of Cyprus, a presidential republic, joined the European Union in 2004 and adopted the euro on 1 January 2008. Greek and Turkish Cypriots share many customs, such as the foods souvla and halloumi, but differ in religion: Greek Cypriots are traditionally Greek Orthodox and Turkish Cypriots Sunni Muslim.
czech-republic: The Czech Republic is a hilly, landlocked country of 78,871 square kilometres, bordered by Austria, Germany, Poland and Slovakia. It is traditionally divided into three lands: Bohemia in the west, Moravia in the east and Czech Silesia in the northeast. Bohemia is a basin drained by the Elbe and the Vltava, surrounded by low mountains such as the Giant Mountains, where Sněžka, at 1,603 metres, is the highest point in the country. Moravia is hilly and drained mainly by the Morava River.

Water from the country flows to three seas: the North Sea, the Baltic Sea and the Black Sea. The Czech Republic also leases the Moldauhafen, a lot in the Hamburg Docks awarded to Czechoslovakia by Article 363 of the Treaty of Versailles; the territory reverts to Germany in 2028.

The area has been inhabited since the Paleolithic, and the Venus of Dolní Věstonice, dated to approximately 29,000 to 25,000 BCE, is considered the oldest known ceramic figurine in the world. After Celtic migrations in the 3rd century BCE, Bohemia became associated with the Boii. In the 7th century the Frankish merchant Samo became ruler of Samo's Empire, the first documented Slavic state in Central Europe. Great Moravia reached its zenith in the 9th century under Svatopluk I, and was Christianized with the Byzantine mission of Cyril and Methodius, who codified Old Church Slavonic and the Glagolitic script.

The Přemyslid dynasty unified the Duchy of Bohemia in the late 9th century. In the early 13th century Přemysl Ottokar I obtained the Golden Bull of Sicily from the emperor, confirming his and his descendants' royal status, and the duchy was raised to a kingdom. German immigrants settled in the periphery in the 13th century, and the Mongols, in their invasion of Europe, were defensively defeated at Olomouc after raiding Moravia.

The Czech Republic is a pluralist parliamentary democracy with a bicameral parliament: the 200-member Chamber of Deputies and the 81-member Senate. From 1993 to 2012 the president was chosen by parliament, and since 2013 by direct election.

In the 2021 census 57.3% of inhabitants were Czechs and 3.4% Moravians. About 75% to 79% of residents declare no religion. The Jewish population of Bohemia and Moravia, 118,000 in 1930, was nearly annihilated in the Holocaust.
czechoslovakia: Czechoslovakia was founded in October 1918 as one of the successor states of the Austro-Hungarian Empire. It was championed by nationalists and by its first two presidents, Tomáš Masaryk and Edvard Beneš, and its sovereignty was affirmed in the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye. Masaryk served as first president from 14 November 1918 to 14 December 1935. The state consisted of Bohemia, Moravia, part of Silesia, Slovakia and Carpathian Ruthenia, a region of present-day Ukraine, and its territory included some of the most industrialized regions of the former empire. The Bohemian Kingdom ceased to exist in 1918 when it was incorporated into the new country.

Between the two world wars Czechoslovakia was a democratic state with a generally literate population. Beneš, as foreign minister, was the prime architect of the Little Entente, a Czechoslovak-Romanian-Yugoslav alliance directed against Hungarian attempts to reclaim lost areas, and he worked closely with France. After 1933 the German element within the country allied itself with the Nazis. On 29 September 1938 Britain and France ceded control of the Sudetenland to Adolf Hitler at the Munich Conference, and France ignored its military alliance with Czechoslovakia. On 14 March 1939 the Slovak State was proclaimed, Hungary annexed the rest of Carpathian Ruthenia and the German Protectorate of Bohemia and Moravia was proclaimed. Beneš formed a government-in-exile recognised by the Allies.

The state was re-established after the war, without Carpathian Ruthenia, which was annexed by the Soviet Union. Under the Beneš decrees the government confiscated the property of ethnic Germans and expelled about 90 percent of them, over 2 million people. The Communist Party seized power in a coup in 1948, and the country joined Comecon in 1949 and the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The Prague Spring of 1968 ended when the Soviet Union, assisted by other Warsaw Pact countries, invaded. The Velvet Revolution began on 17 November 1989, and on 28 November the top Communist leaders and the party itself resigned. Growing nationalist tensions later led parliament to dissolve the state peacefully into the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

Before the Second World War the economy was among the strongest in industrial Europe, producing cars, trams, aircraft, ships, turbines and arms, with firms such as Škoda, Tatra and Baťa. The Slovak lands relied more heavily on agriculture than the Czech lands. After 1948 the economy was centrally planned along Soviet lines, and the Communist Party held a political monopoly, with the media under its control. Education was free and compulsory from ages 6 to 15, and the vast majority of the population was literate. The national football team reached the World Cup final in 1934 and 1962 and won the European championship in 1976.
